For British investors in particular, the post-Brexit landscape has made multi-country positioning especially valuable. The 90-day Schengen rule limits how long UK passport holders can stay in any single EU country within a 180-day period. A three-country fractional portfolio effectively maximises your available European time by providing comfortable, fully-equipped homes in multiple locations.

The Exit Strategy

Flexibility That Whole Ownership Cannot Match

Perhaps the most underappreciated benefit of a multi-country fractional portfolio is the flexibility it provides at exit. Selling a fully-owned holiday home is a binary decision — you either have the property or you do not. The process is slow, expensive, and emotionally fraught.

Year 1–3: Build Your Foundation

Acquire your first two fractional shares in complementary locations — one beach, one mountain or lake. Enjoy both and learn the fractional model.

Year 3–5: Add Your Third Country

With experience and confidence, add your third share. Your portfolio now covers all seasons and spreads risk across three markets.

Year 5–10: Rebalance as Life Changes

Children growing up? Sell the family-sized share and downsize. Market outperforming? Take profits and reinvest. The fractional model lets you adjust without liquidating everything.

Year 10+: Transfer or Exit on Your Terms

Pass individual shares to different family members, sell in stages, or hold for continued appreciation. Each share moves independently.

Data from the European fractional ownership market shows that well-located shares in professionally managed properties typically resell within three to nine months, often at or above the original purchase price plus a share of capital appreciation. This is markedly faster than the twelve to twenty-four months that luxury whole-ownership properties commonly take to sell.

Building Your Portfolio

A Practical Framework for Three-Country Diversification

Constructing an effective multi-country fractional portfolio requires the same disciplined thinking you would apply to any investment strategy. Start with your usage requirements. Map out the twelve months of the year and identify when and where your family would ideally spend time.

Seasonal Complementarity

Each property should serve a different time of year. Beach + mountain + city/lake is the classic winning combination.

Travel Accessibility

All three locations should be reachable within 3–4 hours from your home base. Direct flights matter enormously for weekend usage.

Market Maturity Mix

Blend established markets (lower risk, steady returns) with emerging destinations (higher growth potential).

Management Quality

Every property must be professionally managed through an established fractional platform with transparent fees and governance.

Tax Efficiency Across Borders

How a Multi-Country Portfolio Can Optimise Your Tax Position

Each European country offers a different tax landscape for property owners, and a multi-country fractional portfolio allows investors to take advantage of the most favourable regimes for each component of their holding. Portugal’s Non-Habitual Resident (NHR) programme, while recently modified, established a precedent for preferential tax treatment that continues to attract international buyers. France offers specific advantages for fractional ownership in France structured through a Société Civile Immobilière (SCI), which can provide inheritance tax planning benefits that are particularly valuable for British families. Italy’s Flat Tax regime for new residents and its various renovation incentives create additional opportunities for fractional owners of Italian properties.

The key principle is that with one-eighth shares, the absolute amounts involved in each jurisdiction are relatively modest. This often keeps investors below thresholds that trigger more onerous reporting requirements or higher tax brackets. A property worth €1 million owned outright is a substantial taxable asset in any country; a one-eighth share worth €120,000 is a far more manageable position from a tax administration perspective. Professional fractional ownership platforms typically handle local tax filings as part of the management service, so the administrative burden on the owner remains minimal regardless of how many countries the portfolio spans.

It is essential to take professional cross-border tax advice before building a multi-country portfolio. Tax laws change frequently, and the interaction between your home country’s tax regime and each property country’s rules can be complex. That said, the structural advantage of spreading smaller fractional positions across multiple jurisdictions — rather than concentrating a large whole-ownership investment in one — is a principle that most international tax advisors endorse.

Why Fractional Makes This Possible

The Structural Advantage of Co-Ownership

The three-country portfolio strategy simply would not be viable through traditional whole ownership. The capital required, the management complexity, and the administrative overhead of maintaining three fully-owned holiday homes in three different countries would be prohibitive for all but the ultra-wealthy. Fractional ownership removes these barriers by providing institutional-grade property management, transparent legal structures, and a liquid resale market for each position.

Unlike timeshare — which offers usage rights without genuine ownership or capital appreciation — fractional co-ownership means you hold a legally registered share of the actual property. Your name appears on the title deed. If the property appreciates in value, your share appreciates proportionally. You can sell your share on the open market at any time, bequeath it to your children, or even use it as security for financing. This is real property ownership, structured intelligently to make geographic diversification accessible.

The professional management layer is what makes the multi-country approach truly practical. In each location, a dedicated management company handles cleaning, maintenance, guest services, key handover, local regulatory compliance, insurance, utility management, and garden or pool care. As a co-owner, you arrive to a home that has been prepared to hotel standards — fresh linens, stocked essentials, everything in working order — regardless of which country your property is in. This consistency of experience across multiple countries is something that individual holiday home owners rarely achieve, even with a single property.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are sophisticated buyers actually building cross-country property portfolios in 2026?

Several converging reasons. Lifestyle diversification — different countries deliver different climates, cultures, and seasonal experiences; a portfolio across Spain, France, and Italy provides genuine variety that a single country can't match. Currency and political diversification — holding euro-denominated property in multiple jurisdictions reduces concentration risk versus single-country exposure. Tax planning — different jurisdictions offer different inheritance, capital gains, and ongoing property tax treatments; a portfolio can be structured for optimal cumulative treatment. Wealth planning — multiple residences in different jurisdictions can support flexible future relocation options and family-member residency strategies. The portfolio approach has matured from rare to standard among ultra-high-net-worth fractional buyers.

What's a typical cross-country fractional portfolio for a sophisticated buyer in 2026?

A common pattern: one Mediterranean coastal share (Spain, Italy, or Portugal) for summer beach use; one Alpine ski share (France or Switzerland) for winter mountain use; one urban share (Paris, Lisbon, or Madrid) for cultural and remote-work use. Total capital deployment typically €800,000-€2 million across three shares, with combined annual operating costs of €15,000-€30,000. The lifestyle outcome is access to three distinct destinations with genuine seasonal variety, plus the financial and planning benefits of jurisdictional diversification. Some buyers extend to four or five positions; others concentrate in two with deeper engagement in each.

How does jurisdictional diversification actually provide tax-planning benefits?

Several specific mechanisms. Different inheritance treatments — a portfolio across Portugal (no inheritance tax for direct heirs), Italy (€1 million per heir exemption), and Madrid (effectively zero rates) gives heirs much better outcomes than concentration in higher-tax jurisdictions. Different capital gains regimes — long-holding allowances vary, allowing portfolio rebalancing strategies that minimise tax exposure on rotation. Different wealth tax treatment — IFI exposure in France, Spanish autonomous-community variations, no national wealth tax in Italy or Portugal. Different VAT and transaction-tax treatments at acquisition. The cumulative tax efficiency of a thoughtfully-structured cross-country portfolio can be meaningfully better than concentration in a single jurisdiction.

What are the practical challenges of managing fractional ownership across multiple countries?

Several. Multiple operator relationships — different fractional operators in each jurisdiction with different processes, apps, and account structures. Multiple advisers — typically a local accountant and a local lawyer in each jurisdiction, plus home-country specialists who can integrate the picture. Multiple tax filing obligations — each property generates its own filings, with home-country reporting of foreign assets potentially required. Currency management — euro-denominated obligations across jurisdictions with non-euro income. Travel logistics — managing visits and stays across multiple destinations. The complexity is real but manageable with appropriate adviser support. Most multi-country portfolio buyers report that the lifestyle benefits substantially exceed the management overhead.

Which jurisdiction combinations work best for cross-country fractional portfolios?

Several work well together. Spain plus France plus Portugal: similar legal traditions, EU-internal advantages, complementary climates. Italy plus France plus Switzerland: strong cultural overlap, established luxury infrastructure, dual-season opportunities. The UK plus continental EU: post-Brexit complexity manageable with appropriate residency planning. The US plus EU: significant tax complexity but legitimate diversification benefits for US ultra-high-net-worth buyers. Less optimal: combinations involving jurisdictions with unfamiliar legal traditions, weak fractional operator infrastructure, or high regulatory volatility. For most international buyers, two or three EU jurisdictions plus optionally one home-country position works cleanly.

How should buyers sequence acquisitions when building a cross-country portfolio?

Most experienced buyers recommend starting with the jurisdiction most aligned with the buyer's primary lifestyle preference — the destination they would most repeat-visit. The first share teaches the model in the most familiar context. Subsequent acquisitions can diversify to other jurisdictions with the operating experience already established. Two-year intervals between acquisitions allow each share to mature into the buyer's life before adding complexity. The slowest paths (1-2 acquisitions per year over 3-5 years) typically deliver better outcomes than rapid portfolio assembly that overwhelms the buyer's bandwidth for relationship management.

What's the resale and rebalancing flexibility of cross-country fractional portfolios?

Generally good. Each fractional share can be sold independently through its operator's secondary market — typically 6-14 weeks in mature operator markets. Portfolio rebalancing (selling one share to acquire another in a different jurisdiction) is technically straightforward though commercially involves two separate transactions. Some operators with international presence offer portfolio-level services that simplify cross-jurisdiction rebalancing. The combined exit liquidity of a multi-country portfolio is typically better than a single concentrated whole-property position because the individual shares can be sold independently. For buyers thinking about long-term flexibility, the portfolio approach offers structural advantage over concentration.

content:
The way we work has fundamentally changed, and with it, the way we think about where we live. As of 2026, over 52% of the global workforce operates in remote or hybrid roles, according to The Gignomist — a figure that has nearly doubled since pre-pandemic levels. This seismic shift has sent ripples through property markets worldwide, transforming once-sleepy resort towns into thriving hubs of year-round activity, premium dining, and co-working infrastructure. The result is a new class of buyer: location-independent professionals who want their home to double as a retreat.

For the property market, the implications are profound. Resort towns that once relied on seasonal tourism are now seeing sustained demand from buyers who plan to live, work, and play in the same postcode. Whether it is a ski-in chalet in the French Alps or a sun-drenched villa on Spain’s Costa del Sol, the concept of a second home has evolved from occasional escape to permanent lifestyle upgrade. And for those exploring co-ownership models, this shift presents a uniquely compelling entry point into markets that were previously out of reach.

The Shift

From Zoom Towns to Lifestyle Capitals: The Evolution of Resort Property

The term ‘zoom town’ entered the cultural lexicon during the pandemic, describing small communities flooded by remote workers fleeing expensive city centres. Towns like Truckee in California, Breckenridge in Colorado, and Chamonix in France saw property prices surge as tech workers, creatives, and entrepreneurs arrived with urban salaries and rural aspirations. In Truckee alone, median home prices reached $1,205,000 by mid-2025, a 4.7% increase year-on-year according to Chris Fajkos Real Estate, with high-end sales over $2 million now representing 23% of all transactions.

But the story in 2026 has matured beyond the initial rush. The first wave of zoom-town migration was reactive — people escaping lockdowns. The second wave, now well underway, is strategic. Buyers are making deliberate lifestyle choices, selecting locations based on climate, culture, connectivity, and community. They are not just working from home; they are building lives around the places they love. This evolution has elevated certain resort towns from seasonal destinations to year-round lifestyle capitals, with property values and local infrastructure rising in tandem.

In Europe, this trend is equally visible. Alpine villages such as Morzine and Megève have invested heavily in fibre-optic broadband and co-working spaces, recognising that the digital nomad demographic represents a stable, high-spending population base. Meanwhile, Mediterranean hotspots from Mallorca to the Costa del Sol have attracted a new generation of buyers who combine remote work with coastal living, driving demand for properties that offer both workspace and outdoor lifestyle.

By the Numbers

The Remote Work Economy Powering Resort Property Demand

The numbers behind the remote work revolution paint a compelling picture for resort property markets. Robert Half reports that 32.6 million Americans now work remotely, representing 22% of the US workforce. Among those with remote-capable roles, 52% operate on hybrid schedules and 27% are fully remote. In Europe, Eurostat data shows that remote work adoption has tripled since 2019 in countries like France, Spain, and Portugal — precisely the markets where resort property demand has surged.

This workforce transformation has created what economists call the ‘donut effect 2.0’ — a migration pattern that extends beyond nearby suburbs to entirely different regions and countries. According to Fortune Business Insights, the global vacation rentals market was valued at $174.84 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $481.8 billion by 2034, growing at a compound annual growth rate of 10.42%. Much of this growth is driven by medium-length stays from remote workers who blur the line between holiday and home.

For property investors, the opportunity lies in markets where infrastructure is catching up with demand. Towns that offer reliable high-speed internet, international schools, quality healthcare, and vibrant social scenes are outperforming those that rely solely on natural beauty. The smartest buyers are looking beyond peak-season appeal to year-round liveability — and co-ownership models make these premium locations accessible at a fraction of the full purchase price.

Europe Spotlight

Alpine Villages and Mediterranean Coasts: Europe’s Hottest Remote Work Property Markets

Europe’s resort property landscape offers a particularly rich tapestry for remote workers. The French Alps combine world-class skiing with summer hiking, mountain biking, and gastronomy, making them genuine year-round destinations. Resorts like La Plagne, within the vast Paradiski ski area, now boast co-working spaces and improved digital infrastructure that cater specifically to the remote-work demographic. Property in these areas commands premium prices during winter, but the growing summer season — boosted by climate-conscious travellers avoiding overheated southern beaches — is creating a more balanced demand curve.

On the Mediterranean side, Spain continues to dominate. The Costa Blanca and Balearic Islands have seen sustained interest from Northern European buyers seeking year-round sunshine and a lower cost of living. Spain’s digital nomad visa, introduced in 2023, has further accelerated this trend by offering non-EU remote workers legal residency. Meanwhile, Italy’s lake regions — Como, Garda, and Maggiore — attract a discerning buyer who values culture, cuisine, and proximity to Milan’s international airport.

Portugal’s Algarve and Lisbon coast round out the European picture. With favourable tax regimes, a well-established expat community, and some of the continent’s most affordable luxury property, Portugal has positioned itself as a top-tier destination for remote workers and property investors alike. The key across all these markets is that properties offering both lifestyle and connectivity command the strongest premiums.

“The remote-work revolution has not simply moved offices into spare bedrooms — it has permanently redrawn the map of desirable real estate, turning resort towns into the new prime residential markets of the 21st century.”

Americas Spotlight

Mountain Meets Coast: The US Resort Towns Leading the Charge

In the United States, the resort property boom is concentrated in two distinct corridors: the Rocky Mountain west and select coastal markets. Colorado remains the flagship state for luxury resort property investment. According to Moxie Property Group, Breckenridge leads the high-end rental market with average daily rates exceeding $400 during peak season, while Vail and Aspen attract ultra-high-net-worth buyers willing to pay premium prices for ski-in access and five-star amenities.

Park City in Utah has emerged as a strong contender, offering proximity to Salt Lake City’s international airport, two world-class ski resorts, and the cultural cachet of the Sundance Film Festival. Property here benefits from year-round occupancy rates of approximately 80%, well above the national resort average. Further west, Lake Tahoe straddles the California-Nevada border, offering both skiing and lake-based recreation — a dual-season appeal that has driven median prices above $1.14 million.

The coastal picture is equally dynamic. Florida‘s Gulf Coast communities, the Emerald Coast’s 30A corridor, and California’s Malibu and Santa Barbara markets continue to attract remote workers seeking beach lifestyle with metropolitan connectivity. The common thread across all these markets is infrastructure investment: fibre broadband, expanded healthcare facilities, and artisan dining scenes that make year-round living genuinely appealing.

Market Dynamics

What Drives Property Values in Remote-Work Resort Towns

Not all resort towns are created equal, and understanding what drives sustainable value growth is essential for buyers. Research from Knight Frank’s Wealth Report identifies five key factors that separate thriving resort markets from those vulnerable to correction: connectivity (both digital and transport), year-round appeal, limited housing supply, strong governance, and cultural vibrancy. Towns that score highly across all five tend to see steady appreciation rather than boom-and-bust cycles.

Digital infrastructure ranks first for a reason. A resort town may offer breathtaking scenery, but if video calls drop and file uploads crawl, remote workers will look elsewhere. The most successful communities have invested proactively — places like Verbier in Switzerland, which now offers gigabit fibre to residential properties, or Javea on Spain’s Costa Blanca, where municipal broadband initiatives have transformed the town into a digital nomad hotspot.

Transport links matter equally. Properties within 90 minutes of an international airport consistently outperform more remote alternatives. This explains the enduring appeal of the French Alps (Geneva and Lyon airports), the Costa del Sol (Málaga airport), and Colorado resorts (Denver International). For buyers considering co-ownership shares, these connectivity factors provide additional reassurance: a property that is easy to reach is a property that gets used — and that holds its value.

2020–2021

The First Wave

Pandemic lockdowns trigger mass migration from cities to resort towns. Zoom towns emerge as remote workers seek space, nature, and affordability.

2022–2023

Infrastructure Investment

Resort communities invest in fibre broadband, co-working spaces, and expanded services. Spain launches its digital nomad visa programme.

2023–2024

Market Maturation

Overheated markets correct while well-connected, year-round destinations continue appreciating. Buyers become more strategic and data-driven.

2024–2025

The Lifestyle Premium

Properties combining workspace, outdoor access, and community amenities command 15-25% premiums. Co-ownership models gain mainstream acceptance.

2025–2026

The New Normal

52% of global workforce is remote/hybrid. Resort property markets stabilise around sustained year-round demand rather than seasonal speculation.

2026+

Next Frontier

Satellite internet eliminates last connectivity barriers. AI property management reduces costs. Emerging resort markets in the Pyrenees, Sardinia, and Portugal’s Silver Coast attract early adopters.

Buyer Strategy

Navigating the Market: Smart Approaches for 2026 and Beyond

For buyers entering the resort property market in 2026, timing and strategy matter more than ever. The initial zoom-town frenzy has subsided, replaced by a more measured market where informed buyers can find genuine value. The key is to look beyond the obvious headline destinations and consider emerging markets one step removed from the most saturated locations — what analysts call the ‘suburbs of the suburbs’ approach.

In practical terms, this means considering towns adjacent to established luxury resorts. In the Alps, that might mean looking at properties in the Pyrenees rather than competing in overheated Chamonix. On Spain’s coast, it could mean exploring the Costa Blanca or emerging areas of Sardinia rather than the most premium stretches of the Costa del Sol. In the US, towns like Winter Park, Colorado — with average daily rental rates of $285 and growing infrastructure — offer compelling alternatives to Aspen’s eye-watering price tags.

{{link:Co-ownership}} represents perhaps the smartest strategy of all for accessing these markets. Rather than stretching to afford a full purchase in a premium resort town, buyers can secure a share in a high-quality property — typically from around €65,000 for a one-eighth share — gaining all the lifestyle benefits of resort living without the full financial burden. With professional management handling maintenance, bookings, and upkeep, co-owners enjoy a genuine lock-up-and-leave lifestyle perfectly suited to the remote-work era.

Legal & Tax Considerations

Cross-Border Ownership: What Remote Workers Need to Know

Buying property in a resort town — particularly across borders — involves navigating legal and tax frameworks that vary significantly by country. In France, the SCI (Société Civile Immobilière) structure is commonly used by foreign buyers to hold property, offering flexibility in ownership transfer and inheritance planning. Spain requires a NIE (Número de Identidad de Extranjero) for any property transaction, while Italy’s notarial system adds a layer of due diligence that protects buyers.

Tax implications deserve careful consideration. Many European countries offer favourable regimes for non-resident property owners, but the rules change frequently. Spain’s Beckham Law, for example, provides a flat tax rate for qualifying foreign workers, while Portugal’s non-habitual resident regime has undergone several revisions since its introduction. In the US, state-level tax differences can be significant — Wyoming and Nevada offer no state income tax, making resort properties in these states particularly attractive to high earners.

For those exploring the buying process through co-ownership, much of this complexity is simplified. Reputable co-ownership providers handle the legal structuring, ensuring that ownership is properly constituted and that each co-owner’s rights are clearly defined. This professional management of legal and tax obligations is one of the less celebrated but most valuable aspects of the co-ownership model.

Future Outlook

The Next Five Years: Where Resort Property Markets Are Heading

Looking ahead, several structural trends suggest that the remote-work driven resort property market has significant room to grow. First, remote and hybrid work is not a passing fad — 90% of companies plan to maintain or increase remote work options, according to research cited by Chanty. Second, demographic tailwinds are strong: millennials are now the largest home-buying cohort, and their preference for experience-rich, flexible living aligns perfectly with resort property ownership.

Technology will continue to reshape expectations. Starlink and next-generation satellite internet are eliminating the last connectivity barriers in even the most remote mountain and coastal locations. AI-powered property management is reducing running costs and improving the owner experience. And virtual reality touring is making it easier than ever for international buyers to explore properties without travelling — accelerating the sales cycle for premium properties in desirable locations.

The most compelling long-term opportunity may lie at the intersection of lifestyle and investment. Properties in well-managed resort communities with strong year-round appeal are likely to outperform both urban and suburban residential markets over the next decade. For buyers who enter through co-ownership, the combination of lifestyle access, managed costs, and capital appreciation potential creates a genuinely compelling proposition. The remote-work revolution has not just changed where we work — it has permanently redefined what a dream home looks like.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

Which European resort towns have actually become viable for serious remote work as opposed to vacation work-from-home?

Three categories matter. Established working hubs with reliable infrastructure — Lisbon, Barcelona, Madrid, Berlin — have fast fibre, large coworking ecosystems, year-round community, and aren't seasonal towns. Resort towns that have crossed the threshold into year-round work bases include Palma de Mallorca, Funchal (Madeira), the Algarve's Lagoa-Carvoeiro corridor, Las Palmas (Gran Canaria), and increasingly Sotogrande. The third category is genuinely seasonal resort towns where work is feasible but social infrastructure thins out off-season — Saint-Tropez, Porto Cervo, Mykonos. For a co-ownership share that you intend to use for work blocks of 2–4 weeks, the first or second category fits; the third category works for vacation but isolates you professionally.

What's the realistic state of internet infrastructure in Mediterranean luxury resort areas in 2026?

Better than the reputation. Spain has near-universal fibre coverage in coastal resort areas (300+ Mbps available in even small Andalucian villages); Portugal is similar in the Algarve and Madeira. The French Mediterranean coast has been retrofitted aggressively — even Saint-Tropez and Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat have full fibre to most addresses now. Italian coverage is more variable: Costa Smeralda is good in the main population centres but patchy in remote villas; Tuscan and Ligurian rural villas often max out at 100 Mbps. For a co-owner planning serious work use, ask the operator for actual speed tests at the property in writing, not the carrier's advertised maximum. Backup options (Starlink, mobile hotspot) are worth considering for any property.

Do European countries' digital nomad visas accept fractional ownership as proof of accommodation?

Mostly yes, with variation. Spain's Digital Nomad Visa requires proof of accommodation but accepts owned property, rented property, or evidence of arrangements — a fractional ownership share with documented usage rights generally qualifies, although immigration officers occasionally request supplementary documentation. Portugal's D8 (digital nomad) and D7 are similar. Italy's nomad visa, launched in 2024, has more rigorous documentation requirements and generally expects rental contracts or owned property in the applicant's name. The cleanest position is to bring both the share certificate and a usage-rights document confirming your guaranteed annual access. Operators experienced with visa-applying owners can provide the right documentation pack.

How do tax residency rules interact with extended stays at a co-owned property?

Most European countries apply a 183-day test for tax residency, with additional 'centre of life' tests that can pull you into residency below 183 days if your economic and family centre shifts. For a fractional owner using a property for 4–8 weeks per year, residency risk is essentially zero. For owners planning extended remote-work blocks of two months or more, the calculation matters. The Schengen 90/180 rule constrains non-EU residents (including UK passport holders) regardless of tax residency. EU citizens face no immigration cap but can still trigger tax residency. Consult both home-country and destination-country tax advisers before any planned stay over 60 days; the marginal tax exposure can be material.

What workspace setup do experienced remote workers actually want in a co-owned property?

A dedicated quiet room with a door, ideally not the bedroom. Two monitors (or a single ultrawide) — laptop-only setups become painful within a week of serious work. A proper office chair, not a kitchen stool. Reliable backup internet (Starlink or 5G hotspot). A well-positioned camera for video calls — natural light from the front, not behind. Coffee infrastructure that doesn't require a barista. Properties marketed as 'remote-work friendly' that lack two or more of these tend to disappoint. Operators investing in these features typically see better booking utilisation across owners and stronger resale demand from work-aware buyers. Ask the operator what their nomad-aware properties have, and look at recent owner photos rather than marketing copy.

How does the time-zone of a destination affect remote-work fit?

More than people think. CET (most of continental Europe) maps cleanly to UK working hours, partially to Eastern US (overlap window 2pm–6pm CET vs 9am–1pm Eastern), and poorly to West Coast US. WET (Lisbon, the Canary Islands, the UK) extends the US overlap by an hour. For a remote worker on Eastern-US calls, Lisbon and the Algarve give an extra useful hour over Spain or France. For someone working Asia-facing hours, none of the European destinations help much. Co-owners who do significant US client work tend to gravitate toward the Western Atlantic side of Europe; Asia-facing workers tend to choose destinations less for time zone and more for travel access via the Gulf hubs.

Are the resort properties marketed as 'nomad-ready' actually delivering on the promise?

Mixed. Properties that have invested seriously in the work experience — true office rooms, professional-grade chairs, multiple workstations for couples both working, fast verified internet, coworking-space partnerships in the local town — perform very well in owner satisfaction surveys. Properties that have simply added a desk in the corner of a guest bedroom and called it a 'home office' tend to score badly with owners trying to do real work. The market is bifurcating: serious nomad-ready properties are emerging as a distinct category with appropriate pricing, while properties that retro-fitted superficial work facilities are starting to lose share to better-equipped competitors. Specific operator certification (e.g., 'Nomad Verified' programmes) is becoming more common as a quality signal.

title: Selling Your Co-Ownership Share: The Complete Exit Strategy Guide
subtitle: Discover exactly how to sell your co-ownership property share — pricing, buyers, legal steps, timelines and tax in one authoritative 2026 guide.
excerpt: Discover exactly how to sell your co-ownership property share — pricing, buyers, legal steps, timelines and tax in one authoritative 2026 guide.
content:
One of the most common questions asked by prospective co-ownership buyers — and one of the most important — is: what happens when I want to sell? Understanding your exit strategy before you buy is not just prudent financial planning; it is the hallmark of a sophisticated property investor. The good news is that co-ownership property shares are fundamentally more liquid than many buyers realise, and when handled correctly, a share sale can be completed smoothly, at a fair price, and on a timeline that suits your life.

This guide covers everything you need to know about exiting a co-ownership arrangement: how the process works in practice, how to price your share accurately, where buyers come from, the legal mechanics of transfer, realistic timelines, and the tax implications you should plan for. Whether you are years away from selling or actively considering an exit, this is the definitive resource for co-ownership share disposals in 2026. Browse our co-ownership FAQs or explore what is fractional ownership for further context.

Understanding the Framework

Why Exit Strategy Is Built Into Quality Co-Ownership Structures

The most reputable co-ownership property programmes are designed with exit in mind from day one. Unlike informal property-sharing arrangements between friends or family — where exiting can be emotionally and legally fraught — professionally structured co-ownership agreements include clearly drafted exit clauses, pre-emption rights, share transfer protocols and dispute resolution mechanisms. These provisions exist not because exits are expected to be problematic, but because clarity at the outset makes every subsequent step straightforward.

A typical co-ownership agreement will specify: the minimum holding period before a share can be offered for sale (commonly one to three years, though not universal), the right of first refusal held by existing co-owners, the process for agreeing a sale price, the role of the management company in facilitating the transfer, and the legal fees and transfer costs payable. Reading and understanding these clauses before you purchase is as important as understanding the usage calendar or the maintenance budget. Our co-ownership buying process guide walks buyers through every stage, including the exit provisions they should look for.

The co-ownership market has matured considerably over the past decade. The global fractional ownership market was valued at approximately $3.32 billion in the equity-share segment alone by 2025, according to market research data, and this growth has driven the development of more sophisticated secondary market platforms and resale processes that simply did not exist ten years ago. This maturing infrastructure is one of the strongest arguments for confidence in the long-term liquidity of co-ownership properties.

Valuation

How to Price Your Co-Ownership Share Correctly

Pricing a co-ownership share is both more straightforward and more nuanced than pricing a whole property. The starting point is the current market value of the whole property, divided by the number of shares — but this simple calculation is typically adjusted by a pricing multiplier that reflects the premium or discount associated with fractional ownership in the relevant market. Industry data suggests fractional pricing multipliers ranging from 1.2 to 1.6 times the proportionate whole-property value, depending on the prestige of the location, the quality of the management structure, and demand dynamics.

In practice, the most reliable approach is a three-point valuation: obtain a current appraisal of the whole property from a local estate agent; cross-reference this with recent comparable whole-property sales in the immediate area; and then consult with a specialist who understands fractional market dynamics. Your management company should be able to facilitate this process and may have access to data on recent share transactions within the same development. Co-ownership shares in prime European and US resort locations have historically tracked the appreciation of the underlying whole property — meaning sellers who have held for five or more years typically see meaningful capital gains.

One common mistake is pricing too high out of optimism or sentiment. Unlike a whole property — where buyers have widespread mortgage access and established comparables — a co-ownership share buyer pool, while growing, is more defined. Competitive pricing generates quicker interest and can actually result in a higher net outcome when you factor in the carrying costs of a delayed sale. See our co-ownership vs full ownership comparison for a broader financial context.

Finding a Buyer

Where Co-Ownership Share Buyers Come From

The buyer for your co-ownership share is most likely to come from one of four sources: existing co-owners within the same property exercising their right of first refusal; the management company’s existing database of qualified buyers who were unable to purchase when the property originally launched; specialist co-ownership brokers and platforms with active buyer databases; or open-market listing through channels targeting the affluent second-home buyer audience.

The right of first refusal is often underestimated as a sales channel. Co-owners who are already familiar with the property, trust the management structure, and perhaps want to increase their usage allocation are highly motivated buyers. A well-run management company will actively facilitate this introduction. If existing co-owners do not exercise their right within the stipulated period — typically 30 to 60 days — the share moves to the open market. Our dedicated best co-ownership properties marketplace and destination-specific pages in locations such as French Alps co-ownership, Spanish coastal properties, Balearic Islands properties, and Italian Lakes co-ownership all generate consistent inbound buyer demand.

Specialist co-ownership portals maintain databases of buyers who have registered interest in specific destinations, property types and budget ranges. These buyers have already self-qualified; they understand co-ownership and are not being introduced to the concept for the first time. This dramatically shortens the education phase of the sales process and accelerates transactions. For sellers, listing with a specialist platform is almost always more effective than a generic estate agent who may lack the vocabulary and experience to represent fractional property confidently. Review our co-ownership case studies to see how the process has worked for previous buyers and sellers.

“A well-structured co-ownership exit is not a crisis — it is a feature. The best programmes are designed so that selling your share is as straightforward as buying it in the first place.”

Legal Mechanics

The Share Transfer Process Step by Step

The legal transfer of a co-ownership share follows a defined process that mirrors elements of a full property conveyance but is typically simpler and faster. The process begins with the seller formally notifying the management company of their intention to sell, triggering the pre-emption period for existing co-owners. Once a buyer is identified, a share purchase agreement is drafted — in most professionally structured programmes, a template agreement already exists within the co-ownership deed, reducing legal costs significantly.

Both parties will instruct solicitors, who review the agreement, conduct due diligence on the property management accounts, the maintenance reserve fund balance, and any outstanding obligations. The transfer is then registered with the relevant land registry (or equivalent authority in the jurisdiction of the property) and the management company updates its records. In France, where many co-ownership properties are held through an SCI (Société Civile Immobilière) structure, the share transfer is a transfer of company shares rather than a real estate transaction — which can be administratively simpler and may carry different tax treatment.

Typical costs associated with a share transfer include legal fees for both parties (often €1,500–€3,500 each depending on jurisdiction), registration fees, any applicable transfer taxes, and a management company administration fee. These costs are known in advance and should be factored into your net sale calculation. Our guide to benefits of co-ownership covers the financial structure in more detail, and for a full breakdown of ongoing costs, see management company costs explained.

Planning Ahead

Realistic Timelines: How Long Does a Share Sale Take?

A realistic timeline for a co-ownership share sale — from decision to completed transfer — ranges from six weeks at the fast end to six months at the slower end, with the majority of transactions completing in two to four months. This compares favourably with whole-property sales in many European markets, which commonly take three to six months and can extend considerably longer.

The key variables that influence timeline are: the pre-emption period specified in your agreement; how quickly a buyer is found (which depends heavily on pricing competitiveness and the quality of the platform you list through); the efficiency of the legal process in the property’s jurisdiction; and whether any complications arise in due diligence. Properties in French Alpine resorts and Spanish coastal locations tend to have well-established local legal infrastructure for fractional transactions, which supports faster completions.

The most important thing a seller can do to shorten the timeline is to prepare documentation in advance. This means having your co-ownership deed, management company accounts, maintenance fund statements, and any recent property valuations ready before you formally list. Buyers who receive comprehensive documentation promptly are far more likely to proceed quickly and with confidence. Our co-ownership buying process overview also explains what documentation a buyer will expect to see during due diligence.

Week 1–2

Intention to Sell

Notify the management company in writing. Obtain a current valuation. Review your co-ownership agreement for exit provisions and pre-emption periods.

Week 2–6

Pre-Emption Period

Existing co-owners are formally notified and given first right of refusal at the agreed price. This period typically runs 30–60 days per the co-ownership deed.

Week 4–10

Marketing & Buyer Identification

If existing co-owners do not exercise their right, the share is listed on specialist platforms and the management company’s buyer database. Offers are received and evaluated.

Week 8–14

Legal Process & Due Diligence

Both parties instruct solicitors. The share purchase agreement is drafted and reviewed. Financial due diligence on property accounts is conducted and documents are prepared for signing.

Week 12–18

Completion & Transfer

Agreement is signed, funds are transferred, and the share ownership is formally registered with the relevant land registry. Management company updates its records.

Tax Planning

Understanding the Tax Implications of Selling Your Share

Tax treatment on the sale of a co-ownership share varies significantly depending on the structure of ownership (direct title, SCI, trust, LLC, etc.), the jurisdiction of the property, your country of residence, and the length of your holding period. It is essential to take qualified tax advice specific to your circumstances before completing a sale. The following is an overview of the most common scenarios.

In France, co-ownership shares sold by non-resident individuals are typically subject to French capital gains tax at a flat rate of 19% plus social charges of 17.2%, though taper relief applies for properties held for more than five years, reducing — and eventually eliminating — the taxable gain after 22 years (for income tax) and 30 years (for social charges). In Spain, non-resident sellers face a withholding tax on the sale proceeds, with the buyer required to retain 3% on account of the seller’s capital gains liability. In the United States, co-ownership shares in resort properties are typically treated as second-home real estate for tax purposes, with federal capital gains tax and potentially state tax applying on any gain. The bar chart below illustrates French taper relief as a planning reference.

Many sellers are pleasantly surprised to find that, combined with the ongoing lifestyle value they have enjoyed, the tax-adjusted net return on their co-ownership investment compares favourably with alternative asset classes over similar holding periods. Working with a tax adviser who understands cross-border property taxation — ideally before you purchase — is one of the highest-value steps you can take as a co-ownership investor.

Maximising Value

How to Prepare Your Share for Sale and Maximise the Price

While co-ownership sellers do not need to stage a property for photography or manage viewings in the traditional sense, there are meaningful steps that distinguish well-presented shares from those that sit on the market. The most impactful is ensuring all financial records are clean and current: up-to-date management company accounts, a healthy maintenance reserve, no outstanding special assessments, and a clear record of any improvements made to the property during your ownership.

Timing your sale relative to the property season can also affect buyer appetite. A ski chalet share listed in October — as the season anticipation builds — is likely to attract more interest than the same share listed in May after the season has ended. Similarly, a coastal property share listed in January and February, when aspiring buyers are actively planning their summer, tends to attract more engagement than one listed in September. Understanding the seasonal psychology of your target buyer is part of selling a lifestyle asset effectively.

Consider the narrative you can offer. If the property has been professionally managed, consistently maintained and — where usage rules permit — generating rental income, these are compelling points for a buyer’s decision. Quantifying the value you have received from the property and being transparent about costs and returns builds trust and reduces negotiation friction. A buyer who feels well-informed is a buyer who proceeds. For further preparation tips, see our co-ownership FAQs buyer guide.

Alternatives to Selling

Other Options: Share Exchange, Splitting and Temporary Arrangements

Before committing to a full share sale, it is worth exploring whether a partial exit or alternative arrangement might better serve your needs. Some co-ownership programmes allow share-splitting, where — with the agreement of co-owners and the management company — a single share is divided between two buyers, each receiving a proportionate usage allocation. This can unlock liquidity while maintaining some connection to a property you value. Review what is fractional ownership for an explanation of how share structures work.

Another option worth considering is a share exchange, where you swap your share in one property for a share in a different property within the same management company’s portfolio. This route is particularly attractive if your lifestyle has changed — perhaps you originally wanted a ski property but now prefer coastal sun — and you want to retain the co-ownership model without a full cash exit and re-entry. Our co-ownership destinations section shows the breadth of options available across Europe and the USA.

Finally, consider whether a temporary suspension of usage rather than a sale might address your needs. If the reason for considering a sale is primarily financial pressure, some management companies can facilitate a temporary rental arrangement for your weeks that generates income without requiring you to permanently divest an asset you may later wish you had kept. Exploring all your options is the foundation of a decision you will be confident in long-term. Book a no-obligation consultation with our team to discuss your specific situation in detail.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

When does it actually make sense to sell a fractional share rather than continue holding?

Several common triggers. Life events — divorce, retirement relocation, family circumstance changes that affect property usage patterns. Capital needs — funding other major purchases, business opportunities, or consolidating wealth into different asset classes. Portfolio rotation — selling one share to acquire a different destination as preferences evolve. Operator concerns — declining service standards or operator-specific issues making continued ownership less attractive. Market timing — strong appreciation creating opportunity to lock in gains. Most sellers exit for life or portfolio reasons rather than dissatisfaction with the asset itself; operator surveys consistently show high satisfaction among exiting owners.

How long should a typical fractional ownership cycle last for the math to work?

Most operators and advisers recommend 5-7 year minimum holding to amortise transaction costs and capture meaningful capital appreciation. Holding 10+ years typically optimises the cumulative cost-per-night economics. Holding less than 3 years often produces marginal financial outcomes because transaction costs (acquisition plus disposal) don't get amortised over enough usage. For buyers, the implication is that fractional ownership rewards medium-to-long term commitment; if your circumstances suggest you'll want to exit in less than 3 years, fractional ownership may not be the right structure compared with rental flexibility.

How does the operator's secondary market quality affect exit decisions?

Critically. Mature operator secondary markets with active buyer waiting lists, transparent historical resale data, and well-defined processes deliver predictable exit timing and pricing. Less mature operator markets create exit uncertainty — longer timelines, more negotiated pricing, more administrative burden. For owners considering exit, the operator's specific secondary market performance is the most important practical factor affecting outcomes. Buyers should evaluate secondary market quality at acquisition (it predicts future exit experience), not wait until exit when limited options remain. Strong secondary market is one of the most important operator quality markers.

What's the role of the operating agreement in shaping exit options?

Substantial. The operating agreement defines: notice periods for intent to sell, right of first refusal procedures and pricing methodology, valuation requirements, restrictions on who can be buyers (e.g., subject to operator approval for AML/KYC compliance), commission structures, completion procedures. Well-drafted agreements provide clear, predictable exit mechanics that protect both selling owners and remaining co-owners. Poorly-drafted agreements create ambiguity that surfaces only at exit when it's hardest to resolve. Read the operating agreement's exit provisions carefully before purchase; these provisions matter more at exit than during ownership.

Are there alternative exit structures beyond traditional secondary market sale?

Several. Buy-back by the operator at predefined prices in some structures (typically at modest discount to current market). Exchange for share in a different operator property (some operators with multi-property portfolios offer this). Family transfer to children or other family members as part of estate planning. Trust transfer to bring the share into a family wealth vehicle. Each alternative has different tax implications and operational requirements. For owners with specific exit objectives, the standard market sale may not be optimal; explore alternatives with the operator and specialist advisers before committing to any specific exit path.

How should owners think about exit timing relative to broader market cycles?

Several considerations. Property markets have cycles — exiting during strong appreciation periods captures more capital gain than exiting during downturns. Currency cycles matter for cross-border owners — strong destination-currency periods improve realised value in home currency. Operator-specific timing — operators with active buyer waiting lists support faster, stronger-priced exits than periods when waiting lists are thin. Personal life timing — major life events often dictate exit timing more than market timing. For owners with flexibility, monitoring market and operator conditions can meaningfully improve outcomes; for owners with timing constraints, the structure delivers reasonable exits in most market conditions.

What should sellers expect after exit completion in terms of ongoing obligations?

Generally clean break. After completion, the share has transferred to the new buyer, the share register has been updated, and the seller's obligations to the holding entity end. Some final administrative items — final pro-rata of operating costs through completion date, any year-end tax filings covering the partial year of ownership. Some operating agreements include modest post-exit provisions (e.g., information sharing about specific property issues that arose during the seller's ownership period). Specialist tax counsel should handle the capital gains filing in both the property's jurisdiction and the seller's home jurisdiction. The whole post-exit administrative process typically completes within 6 months of completion.

title: Why Prime Real Estate Is Running Out — And How Smart Buyers Are Still Getting In
subtitle: Prime real estate inventory is shrinking as demand surges. Discover how co-ownership gives affluent buyers access to luxury properties before they're out of reach.
excerpt: Prime real estate inventory is shrinking as demand surges. Discover how co-ownership gives affluent buyers access to luxury properties before they're out of rea
content:
Something structural is happening in the global luxury property market, and most buyers are only noticing it when they’re already too late. The inventory of genuinely prime real estate — the villas, chalets, and apartments in the world’s most coveted locations — is not just tight. It is shrinking in any meaningful sense, as a combination of constrained new supply, rising ultra-high-net-worth demand, and increasingly restrictive planning environments conspire to make co-ownership of luxury property a less attainable aspiration for even affluent buyers. The question is no longer whether prime locations are becoming more exclusive. The question is what smart buyers are doing about it.

The answer, increasingly, is fractional ownership. Not as a compromise or a stepping stone, but as a deliberate, financially rational strategy that allows buyers to access prime real estate on their own terms — without the capital concentration, the vacancy problem, or the management burden that outright second-home ownership demands. This article examines the market forces driving the squeeze on prime property, what the data says about where this is heading, and why a growing cohort of affluent buyers is choosing co-ownership not because they can’t afford more, but because it simply makes better sense.

Market Reality

The Inventory Squeeze Is Real — And It’s Structural

Knight Frank’s Prime Global Cities Index tracks prime residential prices across the world’s most sought-after urban and resort markets, and the pattern it reveals is consistent: in locations where supply is genuinely constrained — whether by geography, planning policy, or heritage restrictions — prices grow faster, recover more quickly from downturns, and retain value through economic cycles. What differentiates these markets from broader residential real estate is not just price; it is scarcity by design.

In the French Alps, for example, the most desirable ski villages have had near-zero new residential development for decades. Conservation rules and the finite geography of the mountains mean that the total number of ski-in, ski-out chalets in premier resorts like Méribel, Courchevel, or Val d’Isère is essentially fixed. The same applies to Ibiza and Mallorca properties: strict construction moratoriums, introduced to protect UNESCO Biosphere Reserve designations, mean that the supply of authentic fincas and luxury villas is declining as properties are consolidated or absorbed into private family estates rather than entering the open market. On Spain’s prime costas, the story is similar — while lower-end development continues, genuinely premium sea-view properties in established resort areas like Marbella’s Golden Mile or Sotogrande simply do not come onto the market very often.

This is not a temporary post-pandemic tightening. Savills’ Prime Residential Price Forecasts identified supply constraints as the primary driver of price resilience in markets like Sydney, Geneva, and prime London. Knight Frank’s Wealth Report 2025 noted that global ultra-high-net-worth individuals — those with assets exceeding $30 million — increased their real estate holdings through 2025 even as broader market volumes softened. When the wealthiest buyers keep buying, and new supply is restricted, the pool of available prime properties available to the next tier of affluent buyers contracts.

Demand Dynamics

The Demand Side: More Buyers, Fewer Opportunities

If supply is structurally constrained, demand is doing the opposite. The Coldwell Banker Global Luxury 2026 Trend Report projects that Gen X and Millennials will inherit approximately $2.4 trillion in US real estate wealth over the next decade, creating a wave of newly capitalised buyers entering the luxury market. Globally, the great wealth transfer — estimated by Knight Frank at $6 trillion transferred in 2025 alone — is producing a generation of buyers with both the assets and the ambition to acquire prime international property.

Meanwhile, existing ultra-high-net-worth buyers are not stepping back. Spending on luxury homes among this cohort is projected to rise 18.5% in the near term, outpacing growth in every other luxury category. In practical terms, this means that the competition for the best properties — the ones in genuinely irreplaceable locations, with authentic character, and proper luxury amenity — is intensifying, not easing. Data from Redfin confirms that US luxury home prices outpaced the broader market throughout 2025, with median luxury sale prices reaching record highs in several key markets.

For buyers in the €500,000 to €2 million range — the classic profile of a serious second-home purchaser — this creates a real dilemma. The properties they actually want, in the locations they actually want, are competing against an expanding pool of significantly wealthier buyers operating in cash, often through family offices or private banks with preferred access. The gap between aspiration and attainability is widening faster than income growth alone can bridge.

The Numbers

What the Data Shows About Prime Property Performance

The performance data on prime real estate makes a compelling case for access at virtually any price point. According to the JamesEdition Global Prime Market Index 2025, prime residential properties in the top 20 global resort and city markets have delivered strong annualised price appreciation over the past decade — significantly outperforming broader residential indices in the same periods. Supply-constrained resort markets showed the strongest long-run appreciation, with Alpine ski resort properties and Mediterranean island villas consistently in the upper performance quartile.

The growth of fractional and co-ownership models as a market segment reflects this dynamic directly. The global fractional ownership market reached USD 9.4 billion in 2024, according to Growth Market Reports, with a projected CAGR of 13.7% through to 2033, when the sector is forecast to reach USD 29.3 billion. This is not a niche curiosity. It is a structural shift in how affluent buyers are approaching luxury second home ownership, driven by the very same forces — capital efficiency, access to constrained markets, and a preference for managed, hassle-free experiences — that are reshaping attitudes to premium assets across every category.

“The buyers choosing co-ownership in 2026 are not doing so reluctantly. Many previously owned full second homes and made a deliberate decision to switch — because it simply makes better financial and practical sense.”

The Ownership Problem

Why Outright Ownership Has Become a Poorer Proposition

Even setting aside the access problem, the economics of outright second-home ownership have deteriorated meaningfully. A buyer who purchases a prime villa in Mallorca or a ski chalet in the French Alps for full ownership faces a reality that rarely matches the aspiration: most luxury second homes sit empty for between 200 and 280 days per year, accruing running costs — maintenance, insurance, property management, taxes — proportionate to the entire asset, not just the portion being used. For a €1.5 million property, annual carrying costs can easily reach €30,000–€60,000, regardless of how many days the owner actually spends there.

This fundamental inefficiency has been tolerated for decades because the alternative — selling and losing access entirely — felt worse than the waste. But the calculus is changing. Buyers with genuine financial sophistication are beginning to ask the obvious question: why tie up €1 million or more in an asset you use for 6 weeks a year when co-ownership shares can deliver the same access, in the same property, with a fraction of the capital deployed and none of the management burden?

The running costs of fractional ownership answer this directly. Under a properly structured co-ownership arrangement, costs are shared proportionately between all co-owners — so a 1/8th owner pays 1/8th of maintenance, taxes, insurance, and management fees. The management itself is fully handled by professional teams; there is no need to source cleaners, coordinate between owners, manage rental schedules, or deal with property maintenance. Owners simply arrive and the home is prepared for them. When they leave, their belongings go into storage and the property is returned to pristine condition for the next owner.

Strategic Access

How Co-Ownership Solves the Prime Property Access Problem

The core advantage of well-structured co-ownership is that it decouples access from capital concentration. A buyer who wants a genuine luxury villa on the Costa del Sol luxury homes, a chalet above Méribel, or a contemporary apartment overlooking Lake Como does not necessarily need to own the whole thing. They need access: reliable, premium, flexible access, at the times they want to use it, in a property that is maintained to the standard they expect.

Co-Ownership Property offers exactly this structure. Buyers purchase a deeded share — typically 1/8th — in a registered LLC that holds the property as a real asset. This is not a points system or a holiday club membership. It is genuine real estate ownership: the kind that appears on a title deed, can be sold on the open market at market value, and benefits from the same appreciation dynamics as outright ownership. The share can be resold at any time, with the management company first offering it to existing co-owners in the property and then listing it openly — the average resale time across COP properties is around one month.

Usage is managed through a flexible booking app that allows owners to reserve stays from two days to two years in advance, with no fixed-week rotations or points hierarchies. Each 1/8th owner gets somewhere between six and eight weeks of personal use a year. In practice, most owners find this more than sufficient — the constraint has never been the number of days available, but the ability to get there with a property properly prepared and ready to deliver a genuine luxury experience without the pre-arrival logistics that personal ownership demands.

Shares across the COP portfolio start from under €100,000, with most properties falling in the €150,000–€600,000 range — a fraction of the capital that outright ownership would require, with equivalent access to prime assets in markets where that capital would not begin to acquire a full ownership position.

Traditional Second-Home Ownership Dominates

Mainstream recognition of co-ownership as a legitimate, financially sophisticated property strategy. Global market reaches USD 9.4 billion. COP expands portfolio across Europe and the USA.

2026 Onwards

Supply Constraints Deepen; Co-Ownership Becomes the Smart Default

With prime inventory shrinking further and ultra-HNWI demand accelerating, co-ownership is increasingly seen not as a compromise but as the optimal access strategy for most affluent buyers.

Location Intelligence

The Markets Where Scarcity Is Most Pronounced

Not all prime real estate is equally supply-constrained. Understanding where the inventory squeeze is most structural — and therefore where access via co-ownership delivers the greatest long-term strategic value — is essential for buyers thinking beyond the next few years.

The French Alps represent perhaps the most extreme case of geographic scarcity in European luxury real estate. The combination of altitude restrictions on development, decades of conservation planning, and a fixed number of genuinely ski-in, ski-out positions in the top resorts means that prime Alpine property supply is not just constrained — it is declining as owners hold for generational transfer. Demand continues to grow as European skiing’s profile rises and as the longest-season resorts — those above 2,000 metres with glacier access — become increasingly valuable relative to lower-altitude alternatives.

The Balearic Islands sit at the intersection of supply restriction and demand acceleration in the Mediterranean. Both Ibiza and Mallorca have strict building moratoriums on new residential development in protected zones, which cover the most desirable interior and coastal areas. These islands attract annual influxes of ultra-high-net-worth buyers from Northern Europe, the US, and the Middle East — and because there is virtually no new supply of authentic luxury villas in the most coveted areas, competition for existing stock is intense. Costa del Sol luxury homes, particularly in Marbella’s Golden Mile, Benahavís, and Sotogrande, show similar dynamics: established luxury areas with very limited new prime supply and a growing global buyer pool.

In USA fractional ownership markets, Colorado ski resorts — particularly Aspen and Vail — rank among the most constrained luxury real estate markets in the world. Land costs alone in central Aspen have made new development economically viable only at the ultra-luxury price tier, effectively removing these markets from reach for all but the very wealthiest buyers. Access via co-ownership in these markets is not a compromise. It is the only entry point that makes practical financial sense.

Buyer Psychology

The Shift in How Affluent Buyers Think About Property

Something deeper is happening alongside the market dynamics. The buyers who are most actively choosing co-ownership in 2026 are not doing so reluctantly. Many previously owned full second homes and made a deliberate decision to switch. The reasons they give are consistent: too much capital tied up in a single asset, too many responsibilities, too much time spent managing rather than enjoying, and a nagging awareness that the property sat empty for most of the year while the bills kept coming.

This shift in buyer psychology mirrors a broader trend toward access-over-ownership in premium consumption. The same high-net-worth individuals who no longer buy private jets outright — preferring fractional jet programmes or charter on demand — are applying the same logic to residential real estate. Why hold the whole asset when you only use a fraction of it, and when the management overhead of full ownership actively detracts from the enjoyment it was purchased to provide?

For co-ownership case studies that illustrate this journey, the pattern is remarkably consistent: more freedom, less hassle, better properties than full ownership at the equivalent capital level, and access to destinations that would otherwise be beyond reach.

Getting Started

How to Enter the Market Before the Window Closes Further

The combination of structurally constrained supply, rising ultra-high-net-worth demand, and improving performance data suggests that the window for accessing prime real estate at current price points — whether through full ownership or co-ownership shares — is finite. Markets that appear expensive today may look inexpensive in retrospect, as they consistently have across previous cycles in genuinely supply-limited locations.

For buyers considering co-ownership as their entry strategy, the buying process for co-ownership is straightforward. Initial consultations establish the buyer’s preferred destinations, budget, and usage profile. From there, available properties from the all properties catalogue are presented with full financial transparency — share price, estimated running costs, rental income potential where applicable, and resale data. Legal and tax structures are handled by specialists as part of the process, with the registered LLC structure optimised for cross-border ownership.

The benefits of fractional ownership extend beyond headline access and cost efficiency. Because co-ownership shares represent genuine real-property-backed ownership in a registered entity, they benefit from the same long-run appreciation that makes prime property one of the most reliable stores of value over multi-decade time horizons. Owners can hold, rent (where applicable), or sell — on their own timeline, at market prices, without the complex process that selling a full luxury property demands.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there actually a 'running out' of prime real estate in the luxury markets buyers care about?

Yes, in specific structural sense. European prime markets have static or declining supply because of planning rules that prevent new construction (Balearic UNESCO, French heritage zones, Italian protected coastlines), heritage protections that prevent footprint expansion of existing properties, and the inherent geographic constraint of finite coastline and finite established urban centres. Meanwhile, international demand continues to grow with global wealth distribution and the structural buyer-preference shift. The combination creates persistent supply scarcity in the most desirable addresses. The 'running out' framing is overdramatic but the structural dynamic is real — supply cannot expand to match demand in the addresses buyers most want.

How does fractional ownership specifically address the prime real estate scarcity?

By unlocking access to inventory that's structurally restricted at the whole-property level. A €15 million Saint-Tropez villa can be acquired by one buyer with €15 million of capital; the same villa as a fractional structure can be acquired collectively by eight buyers with €2 million each (entry plus transaction costs). The fractional approach expands the addressable buyer market by roughly 8x for prime inventory without increasing actual supply. For specific prime addresses where whole purchase is genuinely difficult, fractional ownership creates buyer access that would otherwise be impossible. The structural effect is that fractional ownership has effectively created a new buyer tier for ultra-prime real estate.

Which specific prime markets have the most acute supply-scarcity dynamics?

Several stand out. Costa Smeralda (Sardinia) has approximately 4,500 residential units total in the entire enclave, with planning rules preventing meaningful expansion. Saint-Tropez peninsula has roughly 12,000 residential units with the same constraint. Quinta do Lago has approximately 1,500 freehold units. The Mallorca southwest from Andratx through Calvià has supply constraints that have driven 7-10% annual appreciation despite high transaction volumes. Central Paris arrondissements 4, 5, 6, 7 have essentially zero net new housing supply each year. Central Lisbon historic quarters similar. These are markets where structural scarcity will persist for the foreseeable future regardless of demand patterns.

What's the practical buyer experience of trying to access these prime markets in 2026?

For whole-property acquisition: long search times (often 12-24+ months to find suitable inventory), competition from multiple qualified buyers on individual properties, pricing well above asking on competitive transactions, sometimes off-market deal structures requiring local connections. For fractional acquisition: operator inventory is typically pre-vetted and available for direct purchase, secondary market provides additional access to existing shares being sold, transaction timelines compressed to 6-12 weeks. The fractional path provides materially easier access to the same underlying addresses, with the trade-off being shared usage rather than exclusive ownership.

How are operators acquiring inventory in supply-constrained prime markets?

Three main channels. Direct acquisition of whole properties brought to market through traditional brokers — operators compete with whole-property buyers and often pay full market prices. Off-market sourcing through specialist relationships with local agents and family-office networks. Increasingly, conversion of existing whole-property ownership into fractional structures (the 'sell some shares, keep some' model). The conversion route is growing fastest because it provides supply without depending on traditional resale channels; it also brings to market inventory that wouldn't otherwise sell, since the existing owner can retain partial use. Sophisticated operators have built dedicated origination teams for these channels.

Are there prime markets where the supply scarcity narrative is overstated?

Some. Markets with significant new luxury construction underway (parts of the Algarve outside the Golden Triangle, parts of southern Spain coastal developments, certain Caribbean luxury developments) have supply expansion that moderates the scarcity dynamic. Markets at the edges of established prime zones (peripheral Marbella vs Golden Mile, outer Costa Smeralda zones vs Porto Cervo prime) have more elastic supply than the absolute prime addresses. For buyers, the implication is that supply scarcity is concentrated in specific addresses rather than uniform across markets; choose carefully within markets to focus on the genuinely supply-constrained positions.

What's the long-term trajectory for prime real estate access through fractional ownership?

Continued expansion. The combination of operator inventory growth (5-15% annually in established markets), conversion of inherited whole properties into fractional structures, and continued buyer preference shift suggests fractional ownership will continue to grow its share of access to prime markets. The forecast is that by 2030, fractional ownership will represent 20-30% of luxury second-home transactions in major European markets, up from approximately 12% in 2024. Specific markets where fractional ownership reaches 35%+ market share will see increasingly normalised dual-track activity — buyers choosing between whole and fractional acquisition based on financial structure preferences rather than because fractional is novel or scarce.
