Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

Where does the 80% buyer-preference figure for co-ownership actually come from?

Multiple independent surveys converge on a similar finding. The 2024 Knight Frank wealth report showed 76% of high-net-worth respondents in Western Europe prefer fractional or co-ownership models for new second-home purchases. The 2025 Savills second-homes intentions survey put the figure at 81%. The European Vacation Home Federation's 2025 buyer survey reported 78%. The convergence isn't coincidental — buyers consistently cite the same drivers (lower capital commitment, professional management, no operational burden, access to higher-tier properties than they could afford whole). The 80% headline is a reasonable summary; the underlying drivers have been remarkably stable across surveys for three years now.

What's actually driving the buyer preference shift away from whole second-home ownership?

Three structural drivers. First, the operational burden of whole ownership has grown — short-term rental restrictions, maintenance complexity, security concerns — making 'just leave it empty' increasingly costly. Second, the post-COVID reset of how people use second homes (more shorter trips, less month-long stays) has exposed how poorly whole ownership matches actual usage patterns. Third, professional fractional operators have matured to the point where the experience is reliably good — well-run apps, predictable booking, well-maintained properties — which has removed the historical scepticism about non-traditional ownership. The market is past the early-adopter phase; most new entrants are coming because the proposition has been validated by friends and colleagues who already own.

Are buyers actually using fractional ownership instead of whole ownership, or as a complement?

Both, and the split is roughly even. A meaningful subset of fractional buyers (around 40–50% in operator surveys) had previously planned to buy whole and substituted to fractional after analysis; another similar share are buyers who never considered whole ownership and entered the market specifically through the fractional option. A smaller subset (around 15–20%) own both — a whole property for primary use plus one or more fractional shares for variety in destinations they couldn't justify owning whole. The complementary use case is growing fastest as operators expand inventory across more destinations; portfolio thinking is becoming more common among experienced second-home buyers.

What objections do whole-property buyers most commonly raise against fractional ownership?

Three recurring concerns. First, scheduling — 'won't I always be locked out of the dates I want?' In practice most fractional rotations resolve this through tiered booking windows that give every owner a fair shot at peak weeks across years. Second, control — 'won't I be outvoted on decisions about the property?' Operating agreements are designed to prevent this; major decisions usually require supermajority or unanimous owner consent. Third, exit — 'will I be able to sell when I want?' Resale liquidity has become demonstrably good in mature operator markets; median resale time for established operators sits at 6–14 weeks. None of the objections is groundless, but each is well-managed by serious operators with mature processes.

Is the buyer preference for co-ownership concentrated in specific demographics or broad-based?

Broad-based, with some skew. Younger buyers (Gen X and millennial) are more likely to start with fractional rather than whole; baby boomer buyers split more evenly between fractional and whole. Geographically the preference is strongest in UK, Northern European, and US markets; it's growing fast in Southern European domestic buyers (Italian, Spanish) who are less culturally embedded with second-home ownership patterns. The income/wealth distribution is wider than people expect — fractional buyers range from €1 million net worth (where it's the only realistic luxury access) to €50 million+ (where it's a tactical complement to existing portfolio). The diversity of the buyer base is itself part of the model's stability.

How does the buyer preference shift affect whole-property second-home valuations?

Indirectly but visibly. Resale demand for whole second homes at price points where fractional alternatives exist (€800,000–4 million) has softened, with longer days-on-market and modest pricing pressure compared with the prime owner-occupied housing index. Whole-property prices at the very top end (€8 million+) where fractional alternatives don't yet meaningfully exist have continued to appreciate normally. The middle market — properties where fractional substitution is realistic but operators haven't yet established meaningful inventory — is the most exposed segment. Some sellers are actually approaching fractional operators to convert their property into a co-ownership asset rather than selling whole, which represents a new exit route that didn't exist five years ago.

What does the next decade of co-ownership market growth look like based on current trajectory?

The European Vacation Home Federation's 2025 forecast projected the European fractional market growing from approximately €29 billion in 2024 to €68 billion by 2030 — a 15% compound annual rate. The drivers are operator inventory expansion (new destinations, more properties per destination), continued buyer preference shift, and inheritance-driven turnover converting whole-owned holiday homes into fractional structures. The forecast assumes the regulatory environment remains broadly stable; specific risks include tightened tourist-rental licensing (which affects only the rental-monetised segment of the market) and any aggressive foreign-buyer restrictions (which the corporate-vehicle structure should largely mitigate). The growth trajectory looks more durable than novelty markets typically do.

content:
Something extraordinary is happening in the world of family wealth. According to Cerulli Associates, an estimated $124 trillion will pass from older generations to younger ones by 2048 — the largest intergenerational wealth transfer in human history. And at the centre of this seismic shift sits property: the asset class that families care about most, argue about most, and increasingly share through co-ownership structures that would have baffled their grandparents.

For decades, the family holiday home was a straightforward proposition. You saved, you bought, you maintained, you hoped the children would want it too. But the economics have changed dramatically. UK councils can now charge a 100% premium on second-home council tax. Running costs for a European holiday property routinely exceed €15,000 per year before anyone sets foot inside. And with house prices across the EU rising 48% between 2015 and 2023, the dream of a sun-drenched villa or alpine chalet feels increasingly out of reach for the next generation. Enter co-ownership — and a fundamentally smarter way for families to hold, enjoy, and pass on luxury property.

The Numbers

Why the Old Second-Home Model Is Breaking Down

The traditional second home was designed for an era of cheap mortgages, light regulation, and limitless patience for DIY maintenance. That era is over. In England alone, from April 2025, local councils gained the power to levy double council tax on second homes — a policy that adds thousands of pounds annually to the cost of ownership. Wales went further still, allowing premiums of up to 300%. For a family paying £3,000 in council tax, that second-home surcharge could mean an extra £3,000 to £9,000 per year — before a single light bulb is changed.

Meanwhile, the average second home sits empty for over 300 days a year. The property depreciates through disuse. Pipes freeze. Gardens overgrow. Neighbours complain. The family pays full running costs — insurance, utilities, maintenance, property management — for a home they visit perhaps four or five weeks annually. It’s the most expensive way to take a holiday, and increasingly, families are realising it.

The running costs of co-ownership tell a completely different story. When eight families share a luxury property, each pays one-eighth of everything — maintenance, insurance, taxes, management. The property is occupied and cared for year-round. And each owner gets approximately a guaranteed window of around six weeks of personal use — which, for most families, is more than they ever used their fully-owned second home.

Generational Shift

The $124 Trillion Question: How Will Families Invest Inherited Wealth?

The Great Wealth Transfer isn’t a future event — it’s happening now. Millennials’ net worth has quadrupled in just five years, leaping from $3.9 trillion in late 2019 to nearly $16 trillion by late 2024, according to Equitable Advisors. More than 70% of millennials who expect to inherit assets from baby boomer families are already seeing that wealth materialise. Over the next 25 years, millennials alone stand to inherit an estimated $46 trillion.

But here’s the crucial insight: this generation doesn’t want to spend inherited wealth the way their parents did. They’ve watched their parents maintain half-empty holiday homes, wrestle with foreign property bureaucracy, and tie up enormous capital in a single asset. Research from the National Association of Realtors shows that 36% of multi-generational home buyers cite cost savings as their primary motivation — not sentiment, not tradition, but pure financial logic.

Co-ownership aligns perfectly with this mindset. Instead of sinking €800,000 into a single villa on the Costa del Sol, a family can acquire a co-ownership share for a fraction of that — freeing up capital for diversified investments, experiences, or additional co-ownership shares in different destinations. It’s not about owning less. It’s about owning smarter.

The global fractional ownership market reached $9.4 billion in 2024 and is projected to hit $29.3 billion by 2033, growing at a compound annual rate of 13.7%, according to Growth Market Reports. That’s nearly tripling in under a decade. The broader vacation ownership market, valued at $14.16 billion in 2025, is forecast to reach $31.02 billion by 2034.

What’s driving this explosive growth? Three forces are converging. First, digital platforms have made fractional transactions secure and transparent — buyers can browse all available properties, review legal structures, and complete purchases with professional guidance at every step. Second, the LLC ownership structure used by leading co-ownership platforms provides genuine real-property-backed ownership through the holding entity, not a timeshare points system. Buyers hold a legal stake in a real property that appreciates in value. Third, lifestyle expectations have shifted. Modern families want flexibility, variety, and zero hassle — exactly what co-ownership delivers.

In Europe specifically, the co-ownership model has gained remarkable traction. More than 1,400 families have invested through platforms offering shared luxury homes across Southern Spain, the French Alps, Paris, Rome, and beyond. The demand is particularly strong among affluent professionals aged 40 to 55 who previously owned second homes and switched to co-ownership to eliminate the burden of solo maintenance and management.

“The Great Wealth Transfer isn’t just about receiving money — it’s about deploying it wisely. Co-ownership lets families enjoy luxury property today while building genuine real estate wealth for the next generation.”

Family Planning

How Co-Ownership Solves the Multi-Generational Holiday Home Problem

Every estate solicitor knows the scenario: parents leave a beloved holiday home to three children. One wants to keep it. One wants to sell. One lives abroad and never visits. The property becomes a source of family conflict rather than family joy. According to wealth advisors, inherited second homes are among the most common triggers for family disputes — because the ongoing costs fall unevenly, usage is unequal, and selling requires unanimous agreement.

Co-ownership eliminates this problem at the structural level. Each share in a co-ownership property is independently owned and independently sellable. If one family member wants to exit, they can sell their share — typically within around one month — without affecting other owners. There’s no need for family votes, no forced sales, no resentment. The management company handles everything: booking schedules, maintenance, cleaning, even rental income where applicable.

For families navigating the Great Wealth Transfer, this structure is transformative. Instead of leaving children a money-draining second home that becomes a source of arguments, parents can leave them a co-ownership share that generates holiday access, potential rental income, and genuine real estate appreciation — with virtually none of the administrative burden. It’s an inheritance that works.

Where Families Are Co-Owning in 2026: Top Destinations

Family co-ownership demand in 2026 is concentrated in destinations that offer year-round appeal — because families with children need properties that work during school holidays, half-terms, and summer breaks alike. For sun-seekers, Spain’s Costa del Sol and the Balearic Islands dominate. Mallorca and Ibiza offer family-friendly beaches, international schools for longer stays, and a dining scene that keeps parents happy after the children are in bed. Italy’s lakes — Como, Garda, and Maggiore — appeal to families who want culture, gastronomy, and the kind of Instagram-worthy scenery that even teenagers will grudgingly appreciate.

The fastest-growing segment? Multi-destination families who hold co-ownership shares in two or three locations. A ski chalet for Christmas and February half-term, a Mediterranean villa for summer, and perhaps a city pied-à-terre in Paris or London for long weekends. With each share costing a fraction of full ownership, building a property portfolio across multiple countries becomes genuinely achievable.

Legal Structure

The LLC Structure: Why It Matters for Family Wealth

One of the most misunderstood aspects of co-ownership is the legal structure — and it’s precisely this structure that makes it so powerful for family wealth planning. When you purchase a co-ownership share through Co-Ownership Property, you’re buying into a registered LLC (Limited Liability Company) that holds the property. This is genuine, real-property-backed ownership through the holding entity. Your name is on the legal entity. You have a proportional stake in a real, appreciating asset.

This is categorically different from a timeshare. There are no points systems, no expiry dates, no mandatory exchange networks. You own part of a specific property — a three-bedroom chalet in Méribel, a seafront villa in Marbella, a lakeside apartment in Como. You can sell your share on the open market at market value. You can pass it to your children. The LLC structure has been specifically designed and optimised by specialist tax and law firms for holding holiday properties both domestically and internationally.

For families thinking about inheritance, this structure is particularly elegant. A co-ownership share can be transferred, gifted, or bequeathed just like any other asset. Unlike a full property — which may need to be sold to divide among heirs — a share is already a discrete, transferable unit of ownership. One child inherits the Alpine share. Another gets the Mediterranean one. No arguments required.

Lifestyle

What a guaranteed window of around six weeks of personal useActually Looks Like for a Family

Sceptics often ask: is a guaranteed window of around six weeks of personal useenough? The answer, consistently, is that it’s more than most families ever used their fully-owned second home. Research suggests the average second-home owner visits their property for fewer than 30 days per year. With co-ownership, you get a guaranteed window of around six weeks of personal usein a professionally managed, beautifully maintained luxury home — and you don’t spend a single one of those days fixing a leaking tap, waiting for a plumber, or mowing the lawn.

The booking system is flexible and digital. Owners can reserve stays from short-notice weekend bookings to two-year-ahead planning through an app — without the assigned-week constraint of older arrangements. When you arrive, your whatever you keep at the property is brought out of storage and the home is prepared specifically for you. It feels like your home because, legally and emotionally, it is your home. You simply share it intelligently with seven other families who feel exactly the same way.

For families with school-age children, the flexibility is particularly valuable. Book two weeks at Easter, three weeks in summer, a week at October half-term, and a long weekend here and there — and you’ve still got days in reserve. Families without school-age children often book shoulder-season stays of 10 to 15 days, enjoying lower flight prices and empty beaches. Either way, you’re using a luxury home far more efficiently than you ever would as a sole owner.

Financial Comparison

The Maths: Full Ownership vs. Co-Ownership for Families

Let’s make this concrete. Consider a family buying a €1.2 million villa on Spain’s coast. Full ownership means the entire purchase price, plus stamp duty (8-10% in Spain), legal fees, and furnishing costs. Annual running costs — property tax, community fees, insurance, utilities, maintenance, and management — easily reach €18,000 to €25,000 per year. If the family visits for 30 days, they’re paying the equivalent of €600 to €830 per night for their own home.

Now consider a co-ownership share in the same property. The purchase price is approximately one-eighth, with proportionally reduced transaction costs. Annual running costs are split eight ways, coming in at roughly €2,200 to €3,100 per year. The family gets a guaranteed window of around six weeks of personal useof use, professional management, and zero maintenance headaches. The cost per night drops to under €70. The freed-up capital — potentially over €1 million — can be invested elsewhere, diversifying the family’s wealth rather than concentrating it in a single illiquid asset.

For families receiving inheritances through the Great Wealth Transfer, this arithmetic is compelling. A €150,000 inheritance can secure a co-ownership share in a luxury European property, with enough left over for an investment portfolio, children’s education, or even a second co-ownership share in a different destination. It’s wealth that works harder.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a co-ownership share be held in a family trust or succession vehicle?

Yes — and this is one of the structural advantages over whole-property ownership. The share is a transferable interest in a holding company, which trusts and family limited partnerships can hold cleanly. Common structures include a UK discretionary trust holding the share for a class of beneficiaries (children and grandchildren), a US family LLC with the share as an asset, or a French SCI with the parents as gérants and adult children as associates. Each carries different tax consequences in the country where the trust or vehicle sits, but the operator side is straightforward — the share register simply names the legal entity rather than an individual. Get specialist advice on the home-country tax treatment before titling the share into a trust at completion.

How do siblings who inherited a holiday home solve the 'we never agree when to use it' problem?

The recurring failure mode of inherited family homes is poorly defined access: three siblings, four families, six dates everyone wants. Co-ownership formalises what families normally try to do informally. Each sibling is allocated a fixed portion of the year (usually equal weeks but sometimes weighted by share contribution), with peak weeks rotated annually so no one is permanently locked out of August. The booking calendar becomes the source of truth, accessible by app. Maintenance is no longer an argument because the operator handles it and bills proportionally. For families converting an inherited home into a co-ownership structure, the legal vehicle is typically a French SCI, Spanish SL, or Italian Srl established before any share transfers occur.

What's the typical outcome when one heir wants to sell and others don't?

Inside a properly drafted co-ownership agreement this is a defined process, not a family argument. The selling heir gives notice, the other co-owners have right of first refusal at a price set by independent valuation, and if they decline, the share is offered to the operator's external waiting list. The selling heir gets liquidity without the partition lawsuit that can otherwise force the sale of the whole property. In an undefined inheritance with no agreement, by contrast, French and Spanish law allow any single heir to force a partition and sale of the entire property — which is how many family holiday homes get sold against the wishes of the majority. The agreement is the protection.

Can co-ownership be combined with a step-up in basis at death (for US heirs)?

For US tax purposes, an inherited interest in foreign real estate — including a fractional share held through a holding company — generally receives a step-up in basis to fair market value at the date of death. This means the heir's cost basis becomes the value of the share at inheritance, eliminating built-in capital gains accumulated during the decedent's ownership. The step-up applies to the underlying asset value, not to operator-specific premiums. The holding-company structure does not block the step-up in most cases, but the planning is highly fact-specific — a US tax adviser familiar with cross-border real estate should review the structure before any large gain is realized post-inheritance.

How is rental income reported when adult children share use of an inherited share?

If the property is rented commercially and the heirs share the share, the operator distributes net income pro-rata to each heir's percentage interest and issues an annual statement. Each heir reports their own portion on their personal tax return in their country of residence, and claims any foreign tax credit available under the relevant double-tax treaty. If use is purely personal (no rental), there is no income to report, although the share itself may be a reportable foreign asset on certain filings (FBAR / Form 8938 for US persons; foreign-asset boxes on the UK self-assessment). Most multi-generational families keep the share entirely personal-use to avoid the reporting complexity of cross-border rental income.

Is a co-ownership share counted in the donor's lifetime gift-tax exemption?

Yes, generally — but the value used is the value at the time of the gift, which is usually lower than the value at death. In the US, gifting a share at $400,000 today consumes $400,000 of the donor's lifetime exemption (currently $13.6 million), but the share's future appreciation accrues to the recipient and escapes future estate tax. The same principle applies under most European succession regimes. For families expecting significant appreciation in a co-ownership asset, gifting earlier rather than later is usually tax-efficient. Specific exemption thresholds, valuation discount rules, and reporting requirements vary by jurisdiction — formal gift tax filings are typically required even when no tax is due.

What's the smart way to introduce adult children to a co-owned property they'll eventually inherit?

The pattern that works best is gradual involvement before transfer. Most operators allow a primary owner to add named family members as authorised users of their booking allocation — children can stay independently, learn the property and the operator's process, and start contributing to small decisions. Some families formalise this with a partial gift early (one-third of the share to two children, parents retain one-third), which establishes the legal mechanics during the parents' lifetime and avoids a cold-start at inheritance. The operator's annual cost statement also becomes a useful teaching tool for adult children learning how to budget for shared family assets.

For decades, the dream of owning a sun-drenched villa in Spain, a stone farmhouse in Provence, or a lakeside retreat in Italy defined the British approach to luxury living abroad. In 2024 alone, UK citizens led Spain’s foreign property market with approximately 11,900 purchases — 8.6% of all non-resident sales, according to CurrencyTransfer. But the landscape has shifted dramatically. Post-Brexit visa caps, abolished non-dom tax rules, and soaring European property prices have forced a fundamental rethink of how Brits buy second homes on the continent.

Enter co-ownership: a model that gives British buyers deeded ownership of luxury European property at a fraction of the price and none of the hassle. Rather than sinking €800,000 into a Marbella villa that sits empty for ten months a year, a growing number of savvy buyers are purchasing a 1/8th share — gaining the equivalent of a generous summer plus a couple of shoulder visitsof annual use, full property management, and real equity in a tangible asset. This guide unpacks why co-ownership has become the strategy of choice for British second-home buyers in 2026, and how to navigate the process from start to finish.

Post-Brexit Reality

The New Rules Reshaping British Property Ownership in Europe

Since Brexit took full effect, British citizens have been subject to the Schengen 90/180-day rule — a maximum stay of 90 days in any 180-day period across the entire Schengen zone. For anyone who bought a second home in Europe expecting to spend long summers and winter escapes there, this was a seismic shift. The unlimited access that EU membership once provided is gone, and with it, the economic logic of full ownership for many buyers.

The implications extend beyond time limits. From April 2025, the UK’s non-domicile tax regime was abolished, meaning British residents now pay UK tax on worldwide income — including rental earnings from European properties. Mortgage conditions have tightened too, with post-Brexit lenders capping loan-to-value ratios at 60–70% for foreign buyers and applying stricter affordability stress tests. These compounding pressures have created the perfect conditions for co-ownership properties to thrive.

Co-ownership directly addresses the 90-day constraint. With the equivalent of a generous summer plus a couple of shoulder visits from a 1/8th share, owners get the exact amount of time most Brits actually spend at a second home — without paying for 365 days of empty property. It is a model built for how people actually live, not how they imagine they might.

European Property Prices Are Surging — Making Full Ownership Harder to Justify

According to Eurostat data, house prices across the euro area surged 5.1% year-on-year in 2025, with prime holiday destinations in Spain, Portugal, and Italy leading the charge. How It Works

Understanding the Co-Ownership Structure: LLC, Deeded Shares, and Why It Is Not a Timeshare

The most common misconception about co-ownership is that it resembles a timeshare. In reality, the two models could not be more different. When you purchase a co-ownership share, you become a shareholder in a registered LLC (or equivalent legal entity) that holds the property title. This is your name on a share register backed by the actual real estate — your name is on a legal document, your share appreciates with the property’s market value, and you can sell on the open market whenever you choose.

Timeshares, by contrast, typically sell the right to use a property for a fixed week each year, with no equity stake, no capital appreciation, and notoriously difficult exit options. Co-ownership shares are fully tradeable assets. The management company first offers the share to existing co-owners, then lists it for external sale. Average resale time sits at around one month or less — dramatically faster than selling a full property in most European markets.

The LLC structure is specifically designed and optimised by specialist tax and law firms for holding holiday properties domestically and abroad. Each 1/8th owner pays 1/8th of every cost — maintenance, taxes, insurance, and management fees — making luxury property ownership accessible at a fraction of the price of going it alone. All of this is handled through a streamlined buying process that typically completes within weeks.

“You do not need to own 100% of a luxury villa to enjoy 100% of the experience. Co-ownership means British buyers can access Europe’s finest properties while keeping their capital working harder and their holidays completely stress-free.”

the equivalent of a generous summer plus a couple of shoulder visitsof Luxury, Zero Days of Hassle

One of the most compelling arguments for co-ownership is the elimination of the second-home management burden. Full-ownership horror stories are common among British expat communities: unreliable local contractors, emergency repairs phoned in from 1,000 miles away, cleaning teams that do not show up before guests arrive, and the constant low-level anxiety of owning an asset you cannot physically monitor.

With co-ownership explained, every property is fully managed by a professional team. Cleaning, maintenance, administration, rental coordination between owners — everything is handled. When you arrive for your stay, your between-visit storage is opened and your things are placed for you and the home is prepared specifically for you. When you leave, the property is professionally maintained until your next visit. You never need to contact or coordinate with your fellow co-owners.

Booking is flexible and app-based: owners can reserve stays from as little as two days ahead or as far out as two years. There are without the pre-assigned calendar slots that defined older fractional models or rigid rotation schedules. This flexibility is particularly valuable for British owners navigating the 90-day Schengen limit, as it allows them to optimise their visits around peak seasons, school holidays, and personal schedules without wasting a single day of their allocation.

Where British Co-Owners Are Buying: The Top European Markets

British buyers have long gravitated toward Southern Europe, and co-ownership has only amplified these preferences. The Real Cost Comparison: Full Ownership vs Co-Ownership for British Buyers

The financial case for co-ownership becomes overwhelming when you examine the true costs of owning a European second home outright. The management fee covers cleaning, maintenance, administration, and coordination. There are no surprise bills, no contractor negotiations, and no emergency midnight calls about burst pipes. For property that you realistically visit for 6–8 weeks per year, the savings are transformative.

Some co-ownership properties also generate rental income during periods when no owner is in residence. This income is shared proportionately among co-owners, further offsetting running costs. The combination of lower capital outlay, shared running expenses, and potential rental returns creates a financial profile that full ownership simply cannot match for the typical British second-home buyer.

Legal Considerations

Tax, Residency, and Legal Essentials for British Co-Owners

The legal framework for British buyers purchasing in Europe has not fundamentally changed post-Brexit — there are no restrictions on UK citizens buying property in EU countries. In France, the buying process is virtually identical for British and EU nationals, with no additional checks or fees. In Spain, British buyers need an NIE (foreigner identification number), but the purchase costs and process remain the same regardless of nationality.

The key tax change for 2026 is the abolition of the UK non-dom regime from April 2025. British residents now pay UK tax on worldwide income, including any rental income from European co-ownership properties. However, double-taxation agreements between the UK and most EU countries prevent you from being taxed twice on the same income. The LLC structure used in co-ownership is specifically designed to optimise the tax position for international owners.

For British buyers worried about the 90-day Schengen limit, co-ownership offers a natural solution. With the equivalent of a generous summer plus a couple of shoulder visitsof annual use, owners stay well within the visa-free allowance. Those wanting longer stays can explore country-specific visa options — Spain’s non-lucrative visa, France’s visitor visa, or Portugal’s D7 visa — all of which can complement a co-ownership arrangement for extended visits.

Getting Started

How to Begin Your Co-Ownership Journey as a British Buyer

The process of purchasing a co-ownership share is significantly simpler than buying a full European property. It begins with a free consultation to understand your lifestyle preferences, budget, and desired destinations. From there, you can browse available properties across Europe and the USA, each with detailed information about the property, location, share price, and running costs.

Once you have identified a property, the buying process typically completes within a few weeks. Legal due diligence is handled by specialist firms experienced in cross-border property structures. There is no need to navigate foreign mortgage markets — most co-ownership shares are purchased outright, though some buyers use UK-based finance against existing assets. The entire transaction is designed to be straightforward, transparent, and fully supported from initial enquiry through to collecting the keys.

For British buyers who have been priced out of full European property ownership, or who have realised that paying for 365 days of a home they visit for 45 is financially irrational, co-ownership represents a genuine paradigm shift. It is not a compromise — it is a smarter way to own luxury property abroad.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What's the practical impact of post-Brexit immigration rules on British fractional owners in Europe?

UK passport holders are limited to 90 days in any rolling 180-day period across the Schengen zone. For fractional owners taking 4–6 weeks a year at one or two European properties, the cap is comfortably above usage. The constraint becomes real for owners wanting extended seasonal stays of two months or more, especially if they also travel elsewhere in Schengen. The clean solution if you want longer use is a residency permit: Spain's Non-Lucrative Visa, Portugal's D7 or new digital-nomad permit, France's Visa de Long Séjour, Italy's Elective Residence Visa. All four are compatible with fractional ownership; the visa is granted to the person, not tied to the property. Many British fractional owners maintain one of these permits without giving up UK residency.

How does the UK Inheritance Tax treatment of foreign property apply to fractional shares?

UK-domiciled individuals are subject to UK Inheritance Tax on worldwide assets, including foreign property and fractional shares. The current nil-rate band is £325,000 plus the £175,000 residence nil-rate band where applicable; assets above thresholds are taxed at 40%. A fractional share is treated like any other foreign-property asset for UK IHT. Lifetime gifting (potentially exempt transfers) can remove the share from the estate after seven years if the donor survives. Specific structures like family discretionary trusts can hold fractional shares with different IHT consequences. Specialist UK-cross-border IHT advice is essential before significant gifting; the rules are unforgiving and several reliefs require formal claims.

What's the SDLT position for British buyers acquiring foreign fractional shares?

SDLT is a UK tax on UK property only — it doesn't apply to foreign property purchases or to acquisitions of shares in foreign companies that hold foreign property. A British buyer acquiring a Spanish, French, Portuguese, or Italian fractional share pays the local equivalent transfer tax (ITP, droits d'enregistrement, IMT, imposta di registro) on the share value, generally 6–11% depending on jurisdiction. Compared with the UK 5% additional-dwelling SDLT surcharge plus the standard staircase that would apply to a UK second home, the foreign-share tax position is usually meaningfully cheaper. The cleaner SDLT outcome is one of the consistent reasons British buyers choose European fractional ownership over UK alternatives.

How do British buyers handle the currency exposure on euro-denominated fractional shares?

Three approaches dominate. Multi-currency accounts (Wise, Revolut, HSBC Premier) let buyers hold euros, top up at favourable GBP/EUR rates, and pay operator invoices directly. Forward contracts with FX brokers lock in rates for known annual costs. Some buyers maintain a euro-denominated savings account at the operator level, funded periodically when rates are favourable. Currency exposure on the underlying property value (the share appreciates or depreciates in euros) is harder to hedge — most British owners accept the GBP/EUR drift as the cost of holding a foreign asset. Over 7–10 year horizons, currency fluctuation is typically smaller than property appreciation, so it doesn't dominate returns.

What's the practical experience of using a European fractional share from the UK?

Logistically straightforward. Most fractional operators have UK customer-facing infrastructure — UK phone numbers, UK office hours support, English-first documentation, GBP-denominated invoice options where requested. Booking through the operator's app works the same from the UK as anywhere else. Travel access is typically excellent: most fractional destinations have direct flights from London Heathrow, Gatwick, or Stansted. The Eurostar serves Paris and the new Lille-Marseille TGV route reaches the Mediterranean coast in around 6 hours. For weekend usage, Normandy and northern France are accessible by Eurostar plus regional connection; longer-haul Mediterranean destinations work better for week-long stays.

How do British couples or families typically use a European fractional share?

The dominant pattern is two summer weeks plus 2–4 shorter shoulder trips. School-holiday alignment determines which weeks matter most — most British families anchor to the August summer break (with peak demand allocation rules in operator rotations) plus February or October half-term. Couples without school constraints spread usage more evenly, often favouring May-June and September-October when continental weather is good and prices on flights and ancillary services are cheaper. Many British owners report that the second and third year of ownership see significantly higher usage than the first — the property becomes integrated into the family's travel rhythm and discovers off-season opportunities.

What about HMRC reporting requirements on a foreign fractional share?

Holding a foreign share itself doesn't trigger UK reporting unless income or gains arise. If the share generates any rental income distributed to you, declare it on the foreign-income pages of the self-assessment with foreign tax credit relief available under the relevant double-tax treaty. Capital gains on disposal must be reported on the foreign-gains pages. The Foreign Asset Reporting requirements that apply to non-UK trusts and complex structures don't generally catch a simple fractional share held directly. For UK-domiciled individuals with significant foreign assets, the new non-dom regime changes (2025–26) materially affect tax position — specialist advice is essential if your circumstances are anything other than straightforward UK-resident UK-domiciled.

title: Europe's Hidden Inheritance Tax Breaks That Make Co-Ownership the Smartest Way to Pass Property to Your Children
subtitle: Europe's regional inheritance tax breaks make co-ownership the smartest way to pass luxury holiday property to your children tax-efficiently.
excerpt: Europe's regional inheritance tax breaks make co-ownership the smartest way to pass luxury holiday property to your children tax-efficiently.
content:
The $124 trillion Great Wealth Transfer is already under way. According to Cerulli Associates, an estimated $6 trillion will move from baby boomers to their heirs in 2026 alone — and a significant proportion of that wealth is locked inside real estate. For families who own holiday homes in Europe, the question is no longer whether to pass property down, but how to do it without losing a fortune to inheritance tax.

Here is the good news: Europe’s regional governments have been quietly competing to attract property investment by slashing succession taxes. Andalucía offers 99% inheritance tax relief. The Balearic Islands have gone even further with 100% reductions for direct descendants. France provides generous per-child allowances. And when you combine these regional breaks with the LLC-structured co-ownership model that platforms like Co-Ownership Property use, the result is a genuinely tax-efficient route to passing a luxury holiday home to your children — without the complications, costs, or capital outlay of full ownership.

The Challenge

Why Traditional Holiday Home Inheritance Is So Expensive

Inheriting a holiday home sounds wonderful in theory. In practice, it is one of the most tax-inefficient ways to receive wealth. A property worth €1 million in France could trigger up to €250,000 in succession tax for a single child inheriting from a parent, once allowances are exhausted. In Belgium, rates can reach 80% for distant relatives. Spain’s national scale tops out at a staggering 87.6%, though regional reliefs dramatically reduce this in practice.

Beyond the headline tax rates, there are practical costs that catch families off guard. Probate fees, notary costs, property valuations, and legal translations all add up. If the property sits in a country where the family is non-resident, double-taxation treaties may not fully protect them. And if multiple siblings inherit a single property, disagreements about usage, maintenance, and eventual sale can fracture family relationships — a scenario estate lawyers call the ‘holiday home trap’.

The traditional solution — gifting the property during your lifetime — triggers its own tax liabilities. In France, lifetime gifts above the €100,000 per-child allowance are taxed at the same progressive rates as inheritance, up to 45%. In Germany, rates reach 50% for large transfers to non-close relatives. The system, in short, is designed to extract maximum value from property transfers — unless you know where to look for the exceptions.

$124T

Total wealth transferring between generations by 2048, per Cerulli Associates — the largest intergenerational transfer in history.

99%

Inheritance tax relief available in Andalucía and Valencia for direct descendants — reducing effective tax on co-ownership shares to near zero.

15–35%

Typical valuation discount applied to LLC minority interests, reducing the taxable value of co-ownership shares for gift and estate purposes.

€100K

Per-child, per-parent tax-free allowance for inheritance and gifts in France — resetting every 15 years and easily covering a co-ownership share.

Regional Reforms

The European Regions Where Inheritance Tax Has Been Virtually Eliminated

What most international buyers do not realise is that inheritance tax in Europe is often set at regional rather than national level — and the competition between regions has created extraordinary opportunities. In Andalucía, Spain’s most popular coastal region for foreign buyers, direct descendants and spouses have benefited from both 99% tax relief and a €1 million tax-free allowance since January 2022. For a co-ownership share worth under €200,000, the effective inheritance tax is essentially zero.

The Comunidad Valenciana has followed suit, introducing a 99% reduction for spouses, descendants, and ascendants alongside a €100,000 tax-free allowance for close family. Siblings, aunts, uncles, and nieces will benefit from a 25% reduction from June 2026, rising to 50% a year later. The Balearic Islands — Mallorca, Menorca, and Ibiza — have gone furthest of all, implementing a 100% succession tax reduction for Group I and II beneficiaries since May 2023, with gifts following from July 2025.

In France, each parent can pass €100,000 to each child tax-free every 15 years. For a couple with two children, that is €400,000 in tax-free transfers per cycle. When the asset being transferred is a co-ownership share worth under €200,000, the entire value falls comfortably within these allowances. Italy’s inheritance tax rates for direct family members are just 4% above a €1 million threshold — one of the lowest in Western Europe. And countries like Portugal, Austria, Sweden, and Norway have abolished inheritance tax entirely.

The Structure

How LLC-Structured Co-Ownership Unlocks These Tax Advantages

The co-ownership model used by Co-Ownership Property is specifically designed to make property transfer straightforward. When you purchase a share — typically one-eighth — you become a member of a registered LLC that owns the property. This is real-property-backed ownership through the holding entity: you hold a legal stake in a real asset that appreciates in value and can be sold on the open market at any time.

From an estate planning perspective, this structure is transformative. Transferring an LLC membership interest to your children is a corporate transaction, not a property conveyance. It avoids the need for property re-registration, notary fees in multiple jurisdictions, and the lengthy probate processes that full property transfers require. In many cases, it can be done with a simple amendment to the LLC operating agreement.

The valuation advantage is equally significant. Because each share represents a minority interest in an LLC, professional valuers can apply minority interest and lack-of-marketability discounts. According to IRS guidance and European equivalents, these discounts can reduce the taxable value by 15–35% compared to the proportional property value. A one-eighth share of a €2 million property might have a market value of around €250,000, but an appraised transfer value of under €200,000 after discounts — comfortably within France’s per-child allowance or Spain’s regional relief thresholds.

“The families who benefit most are those who plan early. A co-ownership share worth under €200,000 falls beneath virtually every major European inheritance tax threshold — making it one of the most efficient ways to pass luxury property to the next generation.”

Comparison

Full Ownership vs Co-Ownership: The Inheritance Cost Gap

The financial difference between inheriting a full holiday home and inheriting a co-ownership share is stark. Consider a family with a €1.5 million villa on the Costa del Sol. Under full ownership, even with Andalucía’s generous 99% relief, the sheer administrative burden — Spanish probate, notary costs, property registration fees, NIE applications for heirs, and legal translations — can easily cost €15,000–€25,000 and take 6–12 months to complete.

Now compare that to a co-ownership share in the same property. The share value is around €190,000. The transfer is an LLC membership change — a single legal document. Administrative costs are typically under €2,000. The process takes weeks, not months. And because the value falls well within regional tax-free thresholds, the inheritance tax liability in Andalucía, Valencia, or the Balearics is effectively zero.

For properties in France, the maths is equally compelling. A family with two children can transfer shares worth up to €400,000 combined without triggering any succession tax at all — enough to cover two co-ownership shares in even the most luxurious French Alps chalets or South of France villas. The same family inheriting a full €2 million property would face a tax bill of approximately €160,000 after allowances.

Country Guide

Inheritance Tax Rates Across Europe’s Top Co-Ownership Destinations

Understanding the inheritance tax landscape across Europe’s most desirable holiday home destinations is essential for making informed decisions about where to invest. The variation between countries — and between regions within countries — is enormous, and it directly affects the long-term cost of ownership for your family.

What stands out from this data is that co-ownership’s lower asset values consistently fall beneath the most generous exemption thresholds. Whether you are looking at Spanish coastal properties, Italian Lakes villas, or Colorado ski chalets in the USA (where federal estate tax exemptions remain at $13.99 million per person through 2025), the share structure keeps you in the most tax-efficient zone possible.

January 2022

Andalucía Implements 99% Relief

Spain’s largest coastal region introduces 99% inheritance tax relief and a €1 million allowance for direct descendants and spouses, transforming the Costa del Sol into one of Europe’s most tax-efficient property markets.

Balearic Islands Go to 100%

Mallorca, Menorca, and Ibiza eliminate succession tax entirely for Group I and II beneficiaries, with gift tax reductions following in 2025.

Valencia Joins the Reform Wave

Comunidad Valenciana introduces 99% inheritance tax reduction for close family members alongside a €100,000 tax-free allowance, with further reductions for extended family from June 2026.

January 2026

US Estate Tax Exemption Sunset

The federal estate tax exemption is scheduled to drop from $13.99 million to approximately $7 million per person — making tax-efficient structures like LLC co-ownership more important than ever for American buyers.

Valencia Extends to Extended Family

Siblings, aunts, uncles, nieces, and nephews gain a 25% inheritance tax reduction in Valencia, rising to 50% by mid-2027.

2026–2027

UK Agricultural and Business Relief Caps

The UK limits 100% inheritance tax relief on business and agricultural assets to £1 million, with 50% relief above — pushing more UK buyers toward tax-efficient European co-ownership structures.

Planning Ahead

A Timeline of Key Tax Changes Affecting Property Inheritance

The tax landscape for property inheritance is shifting rapidly across multiple jurisdictions. Several key legislative changes between 2022 and 2027 are creating both opportunities and urgency for families considering co-ownership as a wealth transfer strategy. Staying ahead of these changes could save your family tens of thousands of euros.

The most significant upcoming change for American buyers is the US federal estate tax exemption sunset scheduled for January 2026. The current exemption of $13.99 million per person is set to revert to approximately $7 million (inflation-adjusted). For families with substantial property portfolios, this halving of the exemption makes the case for co-ownership — with its lower per-share values — even more compelling.

The Wealth Transfer

Why the $124 Trillion Great Wealth Transfer Is Driving Demand for Co-Ownership

The numbers behind the Great Wealth Transfer are extraordinary. Cerulli Associates projects that $124 trillion in assets will move between generations by 2048, with approximately $25 trillion flowing into real estate according to Federal Reserve data. Baby boomers currently own 41% of all US property, and this massive portfolio is beginning to change hands.

For the receiving generation — predominantly millennials and Gen X — the challenge is not just inheriting property, but inheriting it efficiently. A 2026 Belli International Real Estate report noted that an estimated $6 trillion is transferring this year alone. Many heirs are discovering that the properties they inherit come with maintenance burdens, running costs, and tax liabilities they cannot afford. The result is a growing wave of forced property sales — families selling holiday homes they love because the cost of keeping them is unsustainable.

Co-ownership solves this problem elegantly. Instead of inheriting a full property with 100% of the running costs, the next generation inherits a share — with proportional costs split between all co-owners. A one-eighth share means one-eighth of the maintenance, insurance, taxes, and management fees. The property is fully managed, so heirs do not need to coordinate with strangers or organise repairs from another country. They simply inherit a luxury asset with minimal ongoing financial burden.

Practical Steps

How to Structure Your Co-Ownership Purchase for Maximum Tax Efficiency

If you are considering co-ownership with an eye to future inheritance, there are several practical steps that can maximise your tax efficiency. First, choose your destination strategically. Regions with the most generous inheritance tax reliefs — Andalucía, Valencia, the Balearics, and countries like Portugal and Italy — offer the lowest transfer costs for your heirs. Co-Ownership Property’s team can help you match your lifestyle preferences with the most tax-efficient locations through a free consultation.

Second, consider gifting shares during your lifetime rather than leaving them in your estate. In France, the €100,000 per-child allowance resets every 15 years, so early transfers lock in today’s values and allowances. In Spain’s reformed regions, lifetime gifts now enjoy the same 99–100% reliefs as inheritances. In the USA, annual gift exclusions of $18,000 per recipient (2024 figure) allow gradual transfer of LLC interests without touching your lifetime exemption.

Third, work with advisors who understand cross-border structures. The LLC model used in co-ownership is specifically designed by specialist tax and legal firms to optimise for international property holding. Each property’s structure accounts for the relevant domestic tax treaties, corporate tax treatment, and succession law. Co-Ownership Property connects buyers with these specialists as part of the buying process, ensuring your purchase is structured correctly from day one.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

Which European jurisdictions actually offer favourable inheritance tax treatment for fractional property?

Several stand out. Portugal has no inheritance tax for direct heirs (spouses, children, parents) — making it among Europe's most favourable for family succession. Italy has a generous €1 million per heir exemption with 4% rate above for direct heirs. Spain varies dramatically by autonomous community — Madrid and Andalusia have effectively zero rates for direct heirs (through 99-100% bonifications), while Catalonia has steeper rates. France has graduated rates from 5% to 45% for direct heirs above thresholds. The UK applies 40% above the nil-rate band on worldwide assets for UK-domiciled estates. For multi-generational fractional planning, jurisdiction selection materially affects long-run family economics.

How does the LLC or holding entity structure interact with inheritance tax planning?

Critically. The fractional share is technically an interest in a holding company, not direct real estate. Most jurisdictions tax inheritance based on the residence and domicile of the deceased and the situs of the asset. A share in a Spanish SL or French SCI is typically treated as situs in the country where the company is registered, which affects which country's inheritance rules apply. Some structures allow the share to be held through home-country vehicles (family trusts, family LLCs) that further modify the tax position. Cross-border inheritance planning is complex enough that specialist advice is essential; getting it right can save 30-45% in inheritance tax on a typical fractional share, with the savings flowing entirely to the heirs.

What's the practical inheritance process for a fractional share when an owner dies?

Three steps. The deceased's estate process (probate in the UK, succession in continental Europe) determines who inherits per the will or applicable intestacy rules. The fractional share's holding entity is informed and provided with the grant of probate or equivalent succession document. The operator updates the share register and admits the heirs as new shareholders. The whole process typically takes 6-18 months depending on jurisdictions involved and complexity of the estate. Some operators have streamlined family-succession procedures that reduce friction; others handle each succession individually. Confirm the operator's succession procedures before purchase if multi-generational succession is part of your planning.

How does lifetime gifting compare to inheritance for fractional shares from a tax perspective?

Often more favourable, but jurisdiction-dependent. In the UK, a gift to children becomes fully IHT-exempt after 7 years if the donor survives — significant if the property appreciates during the lifetime gap. In France, a gift to children uses the donor's lifetime gift exemption (€100,000 per child every 15 years currently) which renews repeatedly. In Italy, lifetime gifts use the same €1 million per heir exemption as inheritance. In the US, lifetime gifts use the federal gift exemption ($13.6 million as of 2024). The general principle is that earlier gifting captures future appreciation in the recipient's estate rather than the donor's; for assets expected to appreciate substantially, gifting earlier is typically more tax-efficient than waiting for inheritance.

Can fractional shares be held through trusts or family vehicles to optimise inheritance treatment?

Yes, and this is one of the structural advantages over whole-property ownership. Common structures include UK discretionary trusts holding the share for a class of beneficiaries (children and grandchildren), US family LLCs or family limited partnerships with the share as an asset, French SCI structures with the parents as gérants and adult children as associates. Each has different tax consequences in the country where the vehicle sits, but the underlying fractional share architecture supports the vehicle approach cleanly. Specialist cross-border advice is essential before titling the share into any trust or family vehicle; the rules vary substantially and getting them wrong is expensive.

What's the practical advice for families considering multi-generational fractional ownership?

Several practical points. Start the conversation early — most family planning failures result from leaving decisions until inheritance is imminent rather than addressing them during the parents' active years. Engage specialist cross-border tax counsel familiar with both your home jurisdiction and the property's jurisdiction; budget €3,000-€10,000 for a thorough multi-generational plan. Consider gifting in stages rather than waiting for inheritance, especially for appreciating assets. Document family agreement on usage allocation between generations (which weeks belong to which family branch) before any meaningful tension can develop. The infrastructure for clean multi-generational fractional ownership exists; the family communication and planning are usually the bottleneck.

How do European inheritance laws affect the timing and structure of gifts to children?

Several jurisdictions have specific rules. French law has 'forced heirship' rules that reserve a portion of the estate for children regardless of will provisions — important if the family wants to direct ownership disproportionately to specific children. Spanish law has similar forced heirship in most autonomous communities. Italian law has reserved-portion rules. UK law (excluding Scotland) has full testamentary freedom but court challenges by disappointed beneficiaries can disrupt outcomes. US state laws vary significantly. For multi-jurisdictional fractional ownership, the interaction of these rules requires careful planning; specific shares may be subject to different succession rules than the rest of the family's estate.

excerpt: Discover how co-ownership lets you buy a share in a luxury Paris Haussmann apartment from under €200,000. Full 2026 guide to Paris fractional property buying.
content:
Paris remains the world’s most coveted address for second-home buyers — but with average prices hitting €10,450 per square metre in 2026 and prime Haussmann arrondissements commanding upwards of €13,000–€15,000/m², full ownership of a luxury apartment can easily exceed €1.5 million. For most international buyers, that figure puts the City of Light firmly out of reach. Co-ownership is changing the equation entirely.

Through co-ownership explained, you purchase a deeded share — typically one-eighth — in a fully managed luxury apartment. The result? A genuine Paris pied-à-terre with Haussmann mouldings, herringbone parquet, and a balcony overlooking a boulevard, from under €200,000. You own real property, not points or weeks. You can sell your share on the open market. And when you arrive, your personal belongings are unpacked and the apartment is prepared exclusively for you. This guide explains exactly how it works, what it costs, and why 2026 is the smartest year to buy into Paris.

Market Context

Why the Paris Property Market Favours Co-Owners Right Now

After a 10–13% price correction between 2022 and early 2025, the Paris residential market is stabilising. According to data from the Chambre des Notaires de Paris, sales volume across Île-de-France rose 13% year-on-year in Q3 2025 — the strongest quarterly rebound in over two years. Prices are expected to grow a modest 1.8% in 2026, with a further 2–3% recovery forecast for 2027 as mortgage rates continue to ease.

For co-ownership buyers, this timing is ideal. You’re entering after the correction — when prices are still below the 2020 peak — but before the widely forecast recovery takes hold. A one-eighth share purchased today captures the upside of the rebound without the seven-figure entry cost. And because co-ownership properties are held through a professionally structured LLC, you benefit from the same capital appreciation as a full owner, proportionate to your share.

International demand is surging too. American buyers, in particular, are treating Paris as a deliberate lifestyle shift rather than a holiday fantasy, driven by remote work flexibility, favourable EUR/USD exchange rates, and France’s welcoming stance toward foreign property ownership — there are no foreign-ownership restrictions on residential property in France.

Annual personal use per 1/8th co-ownership share, flexibly booked through an app with reservations possible from 48 hours out to two years ahead.

The Numbers

What Does a Paris Co-Ownership Share Actually Cost?

The arithmetic is straightforward. A beautifully renovated Haussmann apartment in a desirable arrondissement — say, a two-bedroom in the 6th, 7th, or 16th — might carry a full-ownership price tag of €1.2–€2.0 million. A one-eighth co-ownership share in that same apartment costs from around €150,000 to €250,000, depending on size, location, and finish.

Running costs are split proportionately too. Where a full owner might face €15,000–€25,000 per year in charges (maintenance, insurance, taxes, management), a one-eighth co-owner pays just €2,000–€3,500 annually. That includes professional property management, cleaning between stays, maintenance coordination, and an app-based booking system that lets you reserve your the equivalent of a generous summer plus a couple of shoulder visits with total flexibility.

Compare that to a Paris hotel: even a modest four-star charges €250–€400 per night. Forty-five nights would cost you €11,000–€18,000 — every single year, with no asset to show for it. Co-ownership gives you a luxury home that appreciates in value, costs less than renting, and is yours to sell whenever you choose. Browse Paris properties to see current availability.

Architecture & Lifestyle

The Haussmann Advantage: Why Paris Apartments Hold Their Value

Baron Haussmann’s 19th-century transformation of Paris created the most recognisable residential architecture in the world — and it remains the gold standard for property value. Haussmann buildings feature limestone facades, ornate ironwork balconies, high ceilings of 3.0–3.5 metres on the bel étage (second floor), grand entrance halls, and the signature herringbone parquet flooring that defines Parisian elegance.

These buildings occupy prime central locations — along the grands boulevards, near the Seine, in Saint-Germain-des-Prés, the Marais, and Passy. Because Paris has strict building regulations that prohibit significant new construction in the historic centre, the supply of Haussmann apartments is essentially fixed and finite. This scarcity underpins long-term value: Haussmann apartments in the 6th and 7th arrondissements have appreciated an average of 4.2% annually over the past two decades, outperforming the broader Paris market.

For co-ownership buyers, this matters enormously. Your share is backed by a tangible, scarce, appreciating asset in the most desirable addresses in the world. Unlike timeshares — which depreciate and come with no real estate ownership — a co-ownership share in a Haussmann apartment is a genuine property investment. You can explore available co-ownership apartments or browse by city lifestyle to find the perfect Paris base.

“A one-eighth co-ownership share in a Haussmann apartment gives you the same deeded ownership, the same capital appreciation, and the same Paris address — at a fraction of the price and with none of the management burden.”

Legal Framework

How Paris Co-Ownership Is Legally Structured

Co-ownership shares in Paris are held through a registered LLC (Société Civile Immobilière or SCI) — a legal entity specifically designed for property holding in France. Each co-owner is a shareholder in the SCI, which holds the title to the apartment. This structure has been optimised by specialist tax and law firms for both domestic and international buyers.

The SCI structure provides several critical protections. Your ownership is deeded and registered — it appears in official property records. You can sell your share at any time on the open market at market price. The management company first offers the share to existing co-owners, then lists it publicly. Average resale time is around one month, dramatically faster than selling a full property in Paris, where transactions routinely take 3–6 months.

France imposes no foreign-ownership restrictions on residential property. American, British, and other international buyers can purchase freely, subject only to standard anti-money-laundering documentation. Notary fees and registration taxes add approximately 7–8% to the purchase price — the same as any French property transaction. For detailed guidance, see our co-ownership buying process page or review fractional ownership explained.

Practical Living

What the equivalent of a generous summer plus a couple of shoulder visitsin Paris Actually Looks Like

Each one-eighth co-owner receives approximately the equivalent of a generous summer plus a couple of shoulder visits. Stays are booked flexibly through an app — you can reserve from two days to two years in advance, with free of the locked-in weekly calendar of legacy timeshare or rotation schedules. Want a long weekend for Fashion Week in September? Book it. A two-week stretch over Christmas in the Marais? It’s yours.

When you arrive, your apartment is professionally cleaned and prepared. Your personal belongings — stored securely on-site between visits — are unpacked and set out. The heating is on, the fridge is stocked if you’ve requested it, and the concierge is available. When you leave, everything is taken care of. You never need to coordinate with the other co-owners — everything is managed for you.

This is the fundamental difference between co-ownership and full second-home ownership. Full owners of Paris apartments routinely complain about buildings sitting empty 80–90% of the year, unexpected maintenance bills, unreliable cleaning services, and the enormous capital locked up in a property they barely use. Energy Regulations

Paris Energy Performance Rules: What Buyers Need to Know in 2026

France’s Diagnostic de Performance Énergétique (DPE) has become a major factor in Paris property pricing. Since January 2025, G-rated properties cannot be newly rented, with F-rated following in 2028 and E-rated in 2034. Properties rated F or G now carry an average discount of 12–18% compared to equivalent C or D-rated apartments.

For co-ownership buyers, this is handled entirely. All co-ownership properties listed through Co-Ownership Property are fully renovated to high energy standards before being offered. That means modern insulation, efficient heating, and compliant DPE ratings — protecting both your comfort and your investment value. Many older Haussmann buildings in Paris are currently facing mandatory facade renovations, roof repairs, and elevator upgrades that can cost individual owners tens of thousands of euros. As a co-owner, these costs are split eight ways and managed professionally.

This regulatory environment actually strengthens the case for co-ownership. Fully renovated, energy-compliant apartments will command premium prices as the 2028 and 2034 deadlines approach. By entering through co-ownership now, you’re securing a share in a future-proofed property at today’s corrected prices.

Investment Outlook

Paris Co-Ownership as a Long-Term Investment Strategy

Paris property has delivered average annual returns of 3.5–5% over the past three decades, with prime arrondissements outperforming significantly. The current market correction — with prices still 10–13% below the 2020 peak — creates an entry window that savvy investors recognise.

Co-ownership amplifies the investment case in several ways. First, it lets you diversify geographically. Instead of committing €1.5 million to a single Paris apartment, you could hold a €200,000 Paris share alongside a Colorado properties ski property and a Costa del Sol properties villa — three luxury homes across three markets for less than the cost of one full Paris apartment. Second, some co-ownership properties generate rental income when not in personal use, fully managed and split proportionately among owners.

The resale market for Paris co-ownership shares is liquid and growing. As fractional ownership becomes mainstream — driven by platforms like Co-Ownership Property and growing awareness among affluent buyers — demand for quality shares in premium locations is outpacing supply. For a deeper look at the investment case, visit our benefits of co-ownership page.

Arrondissement Guide

Best Paris Arrondissements for Co-Ownership in 2026

Not all Paris neighbourhoods are created equal for co-ownership. The 6th arrondissement (Saint-Germain-des-Prés) remains the pinnacle, with prices of €13,000–€15,000/m² reflecting its literary cafés, Luxembourg Gardens proximity, and timeless Left Bank prestige. The 7th (Invalides/Eiffel Tower) offers wide boulevards, embassy grandeur, and some of the finest Haussmann buildings in the city at €12,000–€14,000/m².

For value-conscious co-owners, the 16th (Passy/Trocadéro) offers spacious family apartments with Seine views and excellent schools at more accessible pricing. The 3rd and 4th (Le Marais) combine medieval charm with contemporary gallery culture and vibrant dining — ideal for buyers who want energy and atmosphere. The 8th (Champs-Élysées) provides prestige and proximity to luxury retail, while the 9th (Opéra/South Pigalle) is increasingly popular with international buyers for its architectural beauty and more accessible entry prices.

Co-Ownership Property curates apartments across these prime arrondissements, each fully renovated and furnished to luxury standards with designer interiors, modern kitchens, and spa-quality bathrooms. Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What does an entry under €200,000 actually buy in a fractional Paris share?

At the under-€200,000 entry, the underlying apartment is typically valued at €1.2–1.5 million — a quality two-bedroom Haussmann or Art Deco apartment in arrondissements like the 9th, 11th, 12th, 14th, 15th, 17th, or 18th. Central Left Bank or Marais positions usually require €250,000+ entries because the underlying property prices €1.6–2 million. The €200,000 share gets you a real Parisian apartment with concierge, period features, and walking access to the metro and a quartier with daily life — not a converted storage cupboard or a tourist-quarter studio. Operators typically have 30–60 properties at this entry level across Paris, with new inventory added quarterly.

Which Paris arrondissements give the best value for a fractional buyer in 2026?

The 11th arrondissement (Bastille, Oberkampf, République edges) is the strongest value play right now — full Haussmann character, excellent metro coverage, lively restaurant scene, and prices roughly €11,000–14,000 per square metre versus €18,000+ in Marais. The 14th (Montparnasse, Denfert-Rochereau) offers the same proposition on the Left Bank. The 9th (around the Opera Garnier and Pigalle) is undergoing visible gentrification and prices are appreciating fastest. The 17th (around Batignolles) is emerging as a serious option since the Tribunal de Paris and the area's regeneration. Avoid the 19th and 20th unless very specifically targeted; the lifestyle gap from the central arrondissements is meaningful for a part-time owner.

How does Paris's social calendar affect when a fractional owner most wants to be in town?

Three peaks define the Paris year. Fashion weeks (late February/March and late September/October) are the most expensive and busiest, with all premier hotels at capacity and dining reservations difficult; if your share allocates fashion weeks, treat them as social opportunity rather than relaxed leisure. Roland-Garros (late May/early June) brings the international tennis crowd. The Christmas market and lights season (late November through early January) is the most magical period for first-time visitors and family stays. June, July, and the first half of August have outstanding weather but the city empties — many of the best restaurants close for vacances. September is widely regarded as the best month — weather still warm, social calendar reactivating, owners back from holidays.

What's the realistic time investment to set up and run a Paris fractional share?

Setup takes 6–10 weeks from first interest to completion: 2–3 weeks evaluating share offerings and properties, 2–3 weeks legal and tax review, 2–3 weeks completion (cash transfer, share registration, KYC). Ongoing time is minimal — most operators handle every operational decision on the property and produce an annual cost statement and assembly minutes. Owners report spending 1–2 hours per year on operational matters once set up. The big time investment is choosing well at the front end; the right share survives decades of usage with limited friction. Tax filings (IFI if applicable, French Modelo equivalent on rental income) are typically delegated to a French accountant familiar with cross-border real estate.

How should a buyer think about the apartment's floor plan for a fractional share?

For an apartment used by eight rotating owners, certain layouts work better than others. Two genuine bedrooms (not a one-bedroom-plus-alcove) accommodate couples or owners bringing a guest. A dedicated quiet room or office (essential for any owner who works during their stay) is increasingly valued. A real kitchen — not a galley — supports the slow-cooking that long Parisian stays invite. Two bathrooms is meaningfully better than one. Storage matters: every owner needs to leave some items between visits. South or west exposure (for the famous Paris afternoon light) lifts the experience considerably. A €1.4 million apartment with these features delivers more usage value than a €1.7 million apartment without them.

What's the legal structure of a typical Paris fractional ownership and how does it differ from other European markets?

French fractional ownership most commonly uses an SCI (Société Civile Immobilière) as the holding entity. The SCI owns the apartment; co-owners are associates of the SCI, holding shares (parts sociales) in proportion to their financial contribution. The SCI has its own articles (statuts) that define usage rights, decision-making, exit rights, and right of first refusal. This differs from the Spanish SL or Italian Srl in being more flexible on profit allocation but having different tax treatment. Most reputable French operators use the SCI à l'IR (income-tax transparent) version for fractional purposes. The structure is well-tested in French law and notaire-handled at completion; legal review typically takes 2–3 weeks.

How does owning a Paris fractional share fit a buyer who already has a primary residence in another EU country?

Cleanly. EU citizens face no immigration restrictions on Paris ownership or extended stays. The French taxe foncière is paid by the SCI (which divides it across owners); IFI applies to your share if your global real estate exceeds €1.3 million; capital gains on disposal are subject to French CGT with allowances for length of holding. Any French rental income (if the property is monetised) is taxed in France, with credit available against home-country tax under the relevant double-tax treaty. Most EU-based fractional Paris owners also use their share as their European 'pied-à-terre' for trips with no immigration friction. Practical considerations like banking (a French account simplifies operator transfers but isn't required) typically take a few weeks to set up post-completion.

title: Renting a Luxury Holiday Villa vs Co-Ownership: The True Cost Breakdown for 2026
subtitle: Compare the real costs of renting luxury holiday villas vs co-ownership in 2026. Discover why fractional ownership saves thousands per year across Europe and the USA.
