content:
Every year, millions of families across Europe and the United States spend €3,000 to €10,000 per week renting luxury holiday villas — and most do it without ever questioning whether there’s a smarter alternative. Over a decade, that spending can quietly exceed €200,000 or more, with nothing to show for it at the end. No equity, no asset appreciation, and no guarantee your favourite property will even be available next summer.

Co-ownership — also known as fractional ownership — is fundamentally changing that equation. By purchasing a deeded share in a luxury holiday home, buyers secure guaranteed annual access, build real equity in a tangible asset, and dramatically reduce their cost per night compared to renting. In this guide, we break down the real numbers behind both options, drawing on 2025–2026 market data from Knight Frank, Savills, Statista, and Fortune Business Insights, so you can make a fully informed decision about how you holiday.

The Rental Reality

What Luxury Holiday Rentals Actually Cost in 2026

The luxury holiday rental market in Europe generated over €36.6 billion in revenue in 2025, according to Statista’s Vacation Rentals market forecast. That figure continues to climb as demand for premium short-term accommodation rises faster than supply. For families booking four-bedroom villas in popular destinations, weekly rates have become genuinely eye-watering.

In Spain’s Costa del Sol, a quality villa with a private pool and sea views now commands €2,500 to €5,000 per week during peak season, rising to €7,000 or more in hotspots like Marbella and Sotogrande. On the French Riviera and South of France, comparable properties start at €3,000 per week in the Languedoc and climb past €5,000 in the Côte d’Azur. Italy’s Lake Como and Sardinian coast regularly exceed €4,000 per week for lakeside or coastal villas. In Colorado’s ski country, a luxury chalet in Aspen or Vail during ski season can run $5,000 to $15,000 per week.

Now multiply those figures. A family taking six weeks of luxury holidays per year — two summer weeks, a ski week, a couple of long weekends, and a half-term break — could easily spend €25,000 to €50,000 annually on villa rentals alone. Over ten years, that’s €250,000 to €500,000 in rent, with zero equity to show for it. And that doesn’t account for the annual 5–8% price inflation in premium rental markets that Knight Frank has tracked since 2021.

The Co-Ownership Alternative

How Fractional Ownership Costs Compare — Year by Year

Co-ownership works on a fundamentally different model. Instead of paying for access each time you travel, you purchase a deeded share — typically one-eighth — of a specific luxury property through a registered LLC. That share is real estate you own, recorded in a legal entity, with all the rights and protections of property ownership. Through Co-Ownership Property, shares in premium European and American holiday homes range from under €100,000 to around €2 million for ultra-luxury residences.

A typical one-eighth share at around €200,000 gives you approximately the equivalent of a generous summer plus a couple of shoulder visits — more than most families take in total holiday time. Annual running costs, split eight ways, typically amount to €5,000 to €12,000 per share, covering management, maintenance, insurance, taxes, and cleaning. That means your total annual cost of occupancy, excluding the initial purchase, works out to roughly €110 to €270 per night — a fraction of what you’d pay renting an equivalent property.

Critically, this isn’t dead money. Your share is a real asset that appreciates with the property market. According to Savills, prime European residential property values have risen an average of 4.2% annually over the past decade. A €200,000 share purchased today could reasonably be worth €250,000 or more within five to seven years, effectively meaning you’ve holidayed in luxury while your capital has grown. Try getting that from Airbnb.

Running The Numbers

A 10-Year Side-by-Side Comparison

Let’s model a realistic scenario. Take a family that currently rents luxury villas for six weeks per year, spending an average of €4,000 per week — that’s €24,000 annually. Over ten years, assuming 6% annual rental inflation (conservative for premium European markets), their total rental spend reaches approximately €316,000. At the end of decade one, they own nothing.

Now consider the co-ownership route. The same family buys a one-eighth share for €200,000 in a comparable luxury property through co-ownership properties. Annual running costs average €8,000 per year, totalling €80,000 over ten years. Their total outlay is €280,000 — already €36,000 less than renting. But here’s the kicker: they still own their share. With 4% annual appreciation, that share is now worth approximately €296,000. Their net cost of a decade of luxury holidays is effectively negative — they’ve come out ahead financially while enjoying guaranteed access to a beautifully managed property.

Even if you factor in opportunity cost on the initial capital — say, 6% returns if invested in a stock index fund — the co-ownership model still breaks even or comes out ahead once you account for rental income potential and capital appreciation. The running costs of co-ownership are genuinely competitive with high-end rental spending, with the enormous added benefit of building equity.

“Over ten years, a family renting luxury villas at €4,000 per week spends over €316,000 with nothing to show for it. A co-ownership buyer spends less — and still holds an appreciating asset worth nearly €300,000.”

Beyond The Balance Sheet

What the Spreadsheet Doesn’t Capture

Cost comparison only tells part of the story. Anyone who has spent August frantically refreshing Airbnb for a last-minute cancellation, or arrived at a rental that looked nothing like the photos, understands the hidden friction costs of renting. With co-ownership, your property is always there, always maintained, always yours. Your personal belongings are stored and placed out before each visit. The kitchen has your coffee machine. The bookshelves have your favourite novels.

Through Co-Ownership Property, booking is managed via a flexible app — you can reserve stays as little as two days ahead or as far out as two years. There are no fixed rotation schedules. Everything from cleaning to maintenance to local administration is handled by a professional management team, so you never coordinate with other co-owners directly. It’s the emotional experience of owning a second home with none of the logistics headaches that drive so many people to sell theirs.

There’s also the question of consistency and quality. Rental properties vary wildly. One villa is immaculate; the next has a broken pool heater and stained sofas. Co-owned properties are maintained to a consistent luxury standard year-round because all owners have a vested interest in the asset’s condition and value. The management company ensures everything meets that standard between stays.

Market Context

Why 2026 Is the Tipping Point for Co-Ownership

The global fractional ownership market was valued at USD 9.4 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach USD 29.3 billion by 2033, growing at a CAGR of 13.7%, according to Growth Market Reports. The vacation ownership market specifically is forecast to grow from $15.45 billion in 2026 to $31.02 billion by 2034, per Fortune Business Insights. This isn’t a niche trend — it’s a structural shift in how affluent buyers access luxury property.

Several forces are converging to accelerate adoption in 2026. Rising rental regulation across Europe — particularly in Spain’s Balearic Islands, Amsterdam, and Catalonia — is pushing holiday rental prices higher through increased taxes and reduced supply. At the same time, prime property prices in resort markets have risen 18–25% since 2020, according to Knight Frank’s Global Resort Index, making full ownership increasingly unattainable. Co-ownership sits perfectly in the gap: it offers genuine property ownership at a fraction of the full price, in precisely the markets where rental costs are rising fastest.

For buyers who have been renting luxury holiday homes for years and watching prices climb, 2026 represents a clear buying opportunity. Interest rates in the Eurozone are stabilising, prime resort inventory remains limited, and the co-ownership infrastructure — legal frameworks, management platforms, resale markets — is now mature and battle-tested.

Property Types

Where Co-Ownership Delivers the Most Value

Not all property types offer equal advantages. Co-ownership delivers its strongest financial case in high-demand resort destinations where rental prices are highest and property values most resilient. Alpine chalets in the French Alps and Colorado ski towns offer particularly compelling numbers because ski-season rentals are among the most expensive in the world — $5,000 to $15,000 per week — while the properties themselves enjoy year-round demand for both winter skiing and summer hiking.

Beachfront villas on Spain’s Costa del Sol and the Balearic Islands represent another sweet spot. Summer rental demand pushes weekly rates above €3,000, while year-round sunshine means owners can enjoy their property across all four seasons. Italian Lake Como and Sardinia properties combine cultural richness with strong capital appreciation in markets where Savills reports prime lakeside values have risen 6% annually since 2019.

For US-based buyers, Napa Valley wine country estates and Florida coastal properties offer the dual benefit of strong rental income potential and lifestyle appeal. Park City and Breckenridge continue to attract buyers who want ski access without the $3–5 million price tag of full ownership in those markets. Co-ownership makes these aspirational destinations genuinely accessible.

The Resale Advantage

Your Exit Strategy Is Built In

One of the most common objections to co-ownership is: “What if I want to sell?” The answer is simpler than most people expect. Co-ownership shares can be sold at any time at market value. The management company first offers the share to existing co-owners in the property — who often want to increase their stake — then lists it on the open market. Average resale time is around one month or less, significantly faster than selling a full property.

This is a critical distinction from timeshares, which are notoriously difficult to resell and frequently depreciate. Co-ownership shares are a documented property interest backed by a real asset in a real location. When property values rise, your share value rises proportionally. When you sell, you sell at market price — not at some discounted points-based calculation. The co-ownership buying process is transparent, legally robust, and designed for straightforward entry and exit.

Who It’s For

Is Co-Ownership Right for You?

Co-ownership is ideal if you recognise yourself in any of these scenarios. You currently spend €15,000 or more per year on luxury holiday accommodation. You’ve considered buying a second home but can’t justify the €800,000+ price tag for a property you’d use six to ten weeks annually. You’ve owned a holiday home before and grown tired of the maintenance, management, and the feeling of paying a mortgage on a property that sits empty most of the year.

It’s also perfect for those who want diversification. Rather than putting €1.5 million into a single property, you could own shares in three different properties across Spain, France, and Colorado for a similar total investment — giving you beach, city, and mountain options throughout the year. Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What does it actually cost to rent a luxury villa in mainstream European destinations for 6 weeks per year?

A €2.5–3 million luxury villa typically rents at €1,500–3,000 per night in shoulder season and €3,500–7,000 per night in peak summer. Six weeks of mixed-season rental at the same property — say two summer weeks plus four shoulder weeks — totals €120,000–250,000 per year depending on destination, plus cleaning fees, security deposits, and damage liability. In premium destinations (Saint-Tropez, Costa Smeralda, Mykonos peak), the same six-week pattern can clear €350,000+. The same six weeks repeated annually for a decade represents €1.2–3.5 million in cumulative spend with no asset retained — material relative to the property's whole purchase price.

How does the cumulative cost of renting compare to acquiring a fractional share over a 7-year horizon?

A representative scenario: €350,000 fractional share entry plus €5,000 average annual operating cost over 7 years (€35,000 cumulative). Total cumulative spend: €385,000. Likely exit value at year 7 (assuming 6% annual property appreciation): €450,000. Net financial outcome: €65,000 positive plus 280–350 nights of luxury accommodation usage. The same 280–350 nights bought through rental at the same property would cost €420,000–700,000 cumulative with no asset retained. The break-even between renting and fractional ownership for typical usage patterns is generally crossed by year 3 or 4; from then on the math compounds in favour of ownership.

Are there usage patterns where renting still makes more sense than fractional ownership?

Yes. Buyers who want maximum destination variety — three different countries per year, never repeating — get more value from rental than from a single fractional share concentrated in one location. Buyers planning very short total annual usage (under 3 weeks per year) often find rental more efficient because the per-night cost of fractional ownership requires several weeks of usage to justify. Buyers who actively dislike commitment to specific dates years in advance prefer rental's flexibility. Travel-mode buyers (a different luxury experience each holiday rather than returning to the same beloved property) are better served by renting. The fractional alternative wins for buyers who want to return to the same property repeatedly across years.

What hidden costs of luxury rental do most buyers underestimate?

Several. Cleaning fees and turnover costs (typically €500–2,000 per stay on a luxury villa). Security deposits, often substantial (€10,000–30,000), tied up for weeks around each stay. Damage policy excess if anything goes wrong during the stay. Concierge and meet-and-greet service fees that aren't always bundled. Currency exposure for euro-paying renters from non-euro income, which can swing the cost 10–15% across years. Booking-platform fees on top of the headline rental price. Cumulatively these add 8–15% to the headline rental quote — important for accurate comparison against fractional ownership total cost.

How does the experience of repeated rental at the same property compare to fractional ownership?

Less convenient and less personal. Each rental requires booking commitment 6–12 months in advance for desired dates; popular peak weeks book out further ahead. Each arrival is a new experience — different sheet sets, different kitchen layout to relearn, no personal items pre-positioned. Each departure is a complete pack-out. Friends and family staying separately is more complicated. By contrast, fractional ownership delivers consistency: same property, same kitchen, same staff, personal items in storage between visits, predictable rhythm. Most buyers who have done both report that the difference is more meaningful than they expected — repeated rental at the same property approximates fractional ownership but never matches it.

Is rental yield from fractional ownership a meaningful financial offset?

It depends on the operator model. Closed-rotation fractional structures (no public rentals; weeks released to owner co-owners only) generate no rental income — the model is purely usage-based. Hybrid models that release unused weeks to short-term rental can generate €5,000–15,000 per year per share in net rental income, partially offsetting operating costs. Whether yield matters to your decision depends on intent: if you want to maximise personal usage, choose closed-rotation; if you want some financial offset, choose hybrid. Yield-driven models work best in destinations with strong year-round rental demand and stable licensing regimes.

What's the smartest hybrid approach for a buyer who wants both flexibility and a base?

Many experienced second-home users settle on a fractional share at one beloved destination (anchoring family rhythm and friend-group plans) plus rental flexibility for variety in other years. The fractional share covers 4–6 weeks per year of repeat usage; rental covers an annual exploratory trip elsewhere. This pattern delivers both the consistency benefits of ownership and the variety benefits of rental, with capital commitment significantly lower than whole ownership. Operators are increasingly designing share structures with built-in flexibility for this user pattern — for example, allowing owners to substitute between two or three properties in different destinations within the operator's portfolio.

subtitle: How Robin traded the hidden costs and headaches of full second home ownership for hassle-free luxury through co-ownership. A real buyer's story.
excerpt: How Robin traded the hidden costs and headaches of full second home ownership for hassle-free luxury through co-ownership. A real buyer's story.
content:
Robin was, by most measures, a success story. A senior partner at a UK consultancy firm, he had worked hard for two decades, built a comfortable life, and made what seemed like the natural next step for someone of his means: he bought a second home in southern Spain. A three-bedroom villa with a private pool and mountain views, purchased for just over £500,000. For the first few months, it was everything he had imagined. Then reality arrived — quietly at first, then all at once.

Today, Robin owns a co-ownership share in a beautifully managed luxury villa through Co-Ownership Property, spends around around six and a half weeks of personal use annually there with zero management responsibilities, and has freed up the capital that was previously locked away in a barely-used property. His story is not unique — it is, in fact, becoming increasingly common among affluent second home buyers who discover that full ownership is not the lifestyle upgrade they expected. This is his journey, and what it reveals about the smarter alternative.

The Reality Behind the Dream

When the Second Home Dream Turns Into a Second Job

Robin’s villa sat empty for roughly ten months of the year. Between work commitments, family obligations, and the sheer logistical effort of travelling to and from Spain, he and his wife managed three or four visits annually — totalling perhaps five or six weeks of actual use. The remaining 46 weeks? The property sat idle, accumulating costs, weathering the elements, and demanding constant attention from afar.

The financial reality hit hard in the second year. Property maintenance, pool servicing, gardening, insurance, annual community fees, Spanish property taxes (IBI), and the retainer for a local management company consumed over £18,000 annually — before a single flight was booked or a meal was eaten. Research from Bankrate confirms this experience is far from exceptional: hidden homeownership costs average $21,000 per year, with maintenance alone accounting for nearly $11,000. For luxury properties in prime European locations, those figures climb considerably higher.

Then came the rental experiment. Hoping to offset costs, Robin listed the villa on a holiday rental platform. The income helped — but managing bookings, turnovers, maintenance requests from guests, and the inevitable disputes consumed weekends and evenings. More than two-thirds of second home owners attempt exactly this approach, according to Savills research. Most discover, as Robin did, that being a reluctant landlord is not the same as generating passive income.

The Hidden Maths

What Second Home Ownership Actually Costs Per Day of Use

Here is the calculation Robin eventually did, sitting with a spreadsheet on a rainy November evening in London. Annual running costs: £18,000. Mortgage interest on a partial borrowing: £9,500. Opportunity cost of capital tied up (at a conservative 4% return): £20,000. Total annual cost of ownership: approximately £47,500 per year. Days used: 38. Cost per day of actual use: £1,250 — before food, travel, or activities.

This is the number that changes everything. Most second home buyers never calculate it, because the purchase feels like a one-time decision rather than an ongoing commitment. But amortised across actual usage, the per-day cost of a privately owned luxury second home frequently exceeds £1,000 — more than a five-star hotel suite in the same location. The property industry rarely advertises this reality, but once seen, it cannot be unseen.

Robin also sat on roughly £500,000 of capital that was doing nothing except maintaining a property he barely visited. In a period of rising interest rates and volatile equity markets, the opportunity cost of that lock-up was substantial. co-ownership vs full ownership comparison data shows that co-ownership consistently delivers a lower effective cost-per-day of use for buyers who want access to luxury property without the carrying costs of full ownership.

Market Context

Why Thousands of Affluent Buyers Are Making the Same Switch

Robin’s decision to explore co-ownership put him in increasingly well-populated company. The global fractional ownership market reached USD $9.4 billion in 2024, according to Growth Market Reports, and is projected to expand at a 13.7% compound annual growth rate through 2033 — driven primarily by affluent professionals who have done the same maths Robin did. The model is not new, but the platforms, legal structures, and quality of properties available have matured significantly.

The typical profile of a co-ownership buyer mirrors Robin almost exactly: 45–55 years old, high household income, previously owned or seriously considered a full second home, and motivated primarily by lifestyle rather than investment return. Many, like Robin, have already experienced the reality of full second-home ownership and are actively looking for an exit. Others are first-time second home buyers who have done their research and decided to skip the expensive learning curve altogether.

What is shifting the market most decisively is the combination of rising luxury property prices and rising operating costs. Property taxes for single-family residences rose an average of 27% from 2019 to 2024 in the United States, according to Bankrate, and similar trends are playing out across European resort markets. When the maintenance and tax burden of a property you use for 38 days a year approaches £50,000 annually, the case for an alternative becomes compelling. Read more in our overview of the benefits of co-ownership for second home buyers.

“I spent three years owning a luxury villa I could barely enjoy. In twelve months of co-ownership, I’ve used my property more, stressed about it less, and freed up capital I didn’t know was sitting idle.”

The Discovery

How Robin Found Co-Ownership Property — and What Changed

Robin’s introduction to co-ownership came through a colleague who had recently sold a ski chalet in the French Alps and reinvested in a co-ownership share in a French Alps chalet. The conversation lasted three hours. What struck Robin most was not the financial logic — though that was compelling — but the description of the experience. His colleague described arriving at the property to find it immaculately prepared: personal items retrieved from storage, the fridge stocked, the pool at temperature. No checklist, no cleaning rota, no messages to contractors. Just a luxury home ready to use.

Through Co-Ownership Property, Robin began exploring properties available for co-ownership across Spain, France, and Italy. He found the model straightforward: buyers acquire a 1/8th share in a registered LLC that holds a specific property — genuine equity in the underlying property via the holding company, not a timeshare, with a genuine stake in a physical asset. Each share entitles the owner to approximately around six and a half weeks of personal use annually, bookable flexibly through an app from two days to two years in advance. Running costs are split proportionately — so a 1/8th owner pays 1/8th of everything.

The legal and financial clarity mattered to Robin. He had spent months navigating the complexities of Spanish property law for his original purchase; the LLC structure that underpins co-ownership properties had been specifically designed and optimised by tax and legal specialists. He instructed his own lawyer to review the documentation. They confirmed what Co-Ownership Property had told him: this was genuine real estate ownership with full resale rights on the open market. Our detailed buying process guide explains every step from initial enquiry to completion.

The Numbers

Robin’s Financial Comparison: Before and After

Robin’s full ownership scenario involved £500,000 of capital, approximately £47,500 in annual costs, and 38 days of use. His co-ownership scenario involved a share purchase of under £180,000, annual running costs of under £4,000 for his 1/8th portion, and around six and a half weeks of personal use annuallyin a property that, by virtually every measure, exceeded the quality of his original villa. The capital released — roughly £320,000 — he reinvested. Our guide to the running costs of a co-ownership property breaks down exactly what owners should expect to pay.

There is also the resale consideration. Robin’s original villa had proven difficult to price for resale; the market for specific luxury properties in niche locations is illiquid, and estate agent fees alone would consume tens of thousands of pounds. Co-ownership shares, by contrast, are offered first to existing co-owners in the same property — a ready-made pool of motivated buyers who already know and love the home. Average resale time is approximately one month, compared to an average of six to twelve months for the outright sale of a comparable luxury villa. Read more about selling a co-ownership share.

Robin is also quick to note what the comparison does not capture: the value of time. Managing his Spanish villa had consumed an estimated four to six hours per week of his attention — fielding calls from the management company, reviewing invoices, arranging maintenance, monitoring rentals. Co-ownership eliminated that entirely. For someone billing at consultancy rates, reclaiming that time has a very real financial value.

A Year In

What Robin’s Life Looks Like Now

Robin made his first co-ownership booking three days after completing the purchase — a ten-day stay in late September, a period he could never have used the old property due to peak rental season restrictions. He arrived to find the villa prepared exactly as described. His golf clubs were out of storage in the garage. His preferred brand of coffee was in the kitchen. The pool was clean and heated. There was no checklist, no walk-through, no handover.

Over the past year, Robin has made four separate bookings: the ten-day autumn stay, a long weekend with his adult children over Easter, a solo working trip of five days, and a two-week summer holiday with his wife. Total days used: 41. He has not received a single maintenance call, invoice query, or management email. His co-ownership property produces a small rental income from the periods he is not using it — managed entirely without his involvement.

Perhaps most tellingly, Robin describes a shift in how he relates to the property. With his original villa, he felt a constant background anxiety — about the pool pump, the terrace tiles, the latest estimate from the gardener. With his co-ownership share, he experiences it simply as a home he visits and enjoys. The management layer that separates ownership from occupation has transformed the psychological experience of having a luxury second property. It has become, in his words, what he always thought a second home would be. Browse more co-ownership case studies to see how other buyers have made the same journey.

What This Model Solves

The Six Problems Co-Ownership Eliminates

Robin’s experience illustrates a cluster of problems that co-ownership is structurally designed to solve. The capital lock-up problem: rather than tying up £500,000 in a single asset used for 38 days a year, co-ownership distributes that capital across a more efficient ownership structure. The management burden problem: full management — cleaning, maintenance, admin, rental, co-owner coordination — is handled by the management company, leaving owners with nothing to do except book and enjoy.

Then there is the usage efficiency problem. A 1/8th share is sized almost precisely to the actual usage pattern of a typical affluent second home owner. Research consistently shows that second homes sit empty for around 90% of the year. Rather than paying for 100% of a home you use 10% of the time, co-ownership aligns the cost of ownership with actual usage. There is the liquidity problem too: whole properties are slow and expensive to sell; co-ownership shares transact in weeks.

The quality problem is perhaps the most counterintuitive benefit. Because properties on offer through Co-Ownership Property are fully funded by eight owners rather than one, the per-owner entry cost for a given quality of property is dramatically lower than full ownership. Robin’s co-ownership property is objectively better specified than his original villa — larger, better located, more recently renovated, and more professionally managed — at less than a third of the purchase price. Getting Started

How to Follow Robin’s Path

For buyers considering the move Robin made, the process begins with a consultation with Co-Ownership Property specialists to explore available properties and find a match for your lifestyle, location preferences, and budget. Shares are available from under €100,000 for well-positioned European properties, up to around €2 million for ultra-prime destinations. Most buyers in Robin’s profile — established professionals seeking European sun or mountain access — find compelling options in the €150,000–€400,000 range.

The legal and financial due diligence is straightforward. Co-Ownership Property provides full documentation on the LLC structure, the management agreement, and the resale mechanism. Buyers are encouraged — as Robin was — to involve their own solicitor. Completion typically takes four to eight weeks from reservation. Read our detailed buying process guide for a full step-by-step overview.

For buyers who currently own a second home and are considering converting to co-ownership, Co-Ownership Property’s team regularly advises on the transition — including the timing and mechanics of selling an existing property and reinvesting in a share. The conversion from full ownership to co-ownership is, for many buyers, both financially and emotionally liberating. Robin describes it simply: he got his weekends back, released his capital, and still has a luxury villa in the sun. The only thing he lost was the stress.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What's the typical 'before' situation for someone like Robin who switches from whole-property to fractional ownership?

A common pattern. Owner has held a luxury whole second home for 8-15 years. Annual usage has settled into the 30-50 night range despite original aspirations of much higher use. Operating costs run €40,000-€80,000 per year. The property requires meaningful owner attention (contractor coordination, vendor management, occasional dispute handling). Renovation cycles loom or have just been completed. The owner has done the math on per-night cost and concluded it's no longer justifiable. Increasingly the property feels like a financial and operational burden disproportionate to actual lifestyle benefit. This 'second home stress' state is common enough that operators have specifically targeted the conversion-from-whole buyer segment with dedicated services.

What's typically the catalyst that prompts the actual decision to convert?

Several common triggers. Major maintenance event requiring substantial unplanned spending (roof replacement, HVAC overhaul, pool re-tiling). Life change — children leaving home reducing family-property usage, retirement freeing flexibility for different travel patterns, divorce requiring property settlement. Inheritance complications — multiple heirs creating coordination challenges. Financial review with adviser highlighting opportunity cost on the locked capital. Comparison with friends or family who have switched to fractional. The decision rarely comes from sudden insight; it's usually a accumulated series of frustrations that finally crystallise into action.

How does the actual transition from whole ownership to fractional unfold in practice?

Several months to over a year typically. Discovery phase: research operators, understand the model, evaluate specific destinations and properties. Decision phase: choose specific share or shares to acquire, often after 1-3 property visits. Sale of whole property: list the existing whole second home, accept offer, complete sale (typically 4-6 months in luxury markets). Acquisition of fractional share(s): legal and tax review, completion (typically 6-12 weeks). Settlement: capital reallocation between sale proceeds, new acquisition cost, retained reserves for diversified investment. The total transition typically takes 12-18 months from initial decision to fully settled new lifestyle.

What are the most common positive outcomes converters report after the transition?

Several recurring themes. Operational simplicity — the freedom from contractor coordination and vendor management is consistently the most-cited benefit. Capital efficiency — the freed capital from selling the whole property generates meaningful investment return. More holiday time — the friction reduction enables more frequent shorter trips than the whole-property pattern allowed. Multi-destination access — many converters acquire 2-3 fractional shares in different destinations, gaining genuine variety. Reduced relationship friction — coordination of family use of an inherited or shared whole property no longer creates ongoing tension. Overall lifestyle satisfaction typically increases meaningfully.

What downsides or regrets do converters report after the transition?

Several. Initial emotional difficulty — selling the whole property is harder emotionally than expected, particularly for properties held for long periods or with deep family memories. Some converters report missing specific aspects of whole ownership (full control over decoration choices, ability to host very large gatherings beyond fractional capacity, casual neighbourly relationships in the same village over years). A small subset find that fractional usage doesn't fully replace what they had — but typically these are converters who genuinely used their whole property heavily (100+ nights per year) and shouldn't have converted. For owners with realistic 30-50 night usage, regret is rare.

How do converters typically structure their post-conversion property portfolio?

Several common patterns. Single-share conversion to a different destination — buyer takes the freed capital from selling the whole property and acquires one fractional share at a destination they wanted to explore but couldn't justify owning whole. Multi-share portfolio — buyer acquires 2-3 fractional shares in different destinations creating genuine multi-location flexibility. Fractional plus rental flexibility — buyer maintains one fractional share as anchor and uses freed capital for rental flexibility on other trips. The portfolio approach has become increasingly common; first-time converters often start with single-share conversion and add additional shares over subsequent years as they gain confidence with the model.

What advice do experienced converters give to people considering the same transition?

Several recurring themes. Start with honest data on your actual usage — not aspirational, actual nights. Visit several fractional properties in person before deciding, not just review marketing. Engage cross-border tax counsel before any meaningful capital movement. Don't rush — the right transition takes 12-18 months and rushing typically produces worse outcomes. Choose operators with strong secondary market data over operators making aggressive marketing claims. Consider portfolio thinking from the start (one share now, possibly more later) rather than committing all freed capital to one share. Most converters wish they had made the transition earlier than they did.

Speak with our co-ownership specialists about properties that match your lifestyle and budget. Like Robin, you may discover that the smarter path to luxury second home ownership has been there all along.

title: Why Your Holiday Home Costs More Per Night Than a Five-Star Hotel
subtitle: Most holiday home owners pay €500-€800 per night for their own property when you factor in true costs and utilisation. Discover smarter alternatives for 2026.
excerpt: Most holiday home owners pay €500-€800 per night for their own property when you factor in true costs and utilisation. Discover smarter alternatives for 2026.
content:
Here is a number that shocks most holiday home owners: when you divide every penny you spend — mortgage payments, maintenance, insurance, taxes, furnishing, management — by the nights you actually sleep in the property, the true cost per night often lands between €500 and €800. That is more than a suite at many five-star hotels, yet most owners never run the calculation. They bought for lifestyle, fell in love with a view, and quietly ignore the spreadsheet that tells a different story.

This is not an argument against owning a place in the sun. It is an argument for owning the right amount of one. Across Europe and the United States, a growing wave of buyers — many of them former full owners — are switching to co-ownership models that slash the per-night cost by up to 80 per cent while preserving every luxury they care about. In this article we will walk through the real maths, the hidden costs that inflate the number, and the structural fix that is reshaping how affluent families think about second homes.

The Numbers

The Per-Night Calculation Most Owners Never Do

Consider a fairly typical Mediterranean holiday villa purchased for €800,000. Add stamp duty, legal fees, and furnishing and the all-in acquisition cost is closer to €880,000. Annual running costs — property tax, insurance, community charges, utilities, a gardener, pool maintenance, and an annual deep service — easily reach €18,000 to €24,000 per year, according to 2025 data compiled by Savills and local fiscal advisors across Spain, France, and Italy.

Now divide by usage. Research from Knight Frank’s 2025 Global Buyer Survey and the European Holiday Home Owners Association suggests the average owner uses their property for just four to six weeks per year — roughly 30 to 42 nights. The rest of the time the property sits empty, slowly degrading, while the bills keep arriving. At 35 nights of personal use and €22,000 in annual costs alone — before mortgage interest — that is €629 per night. Layer on mortgage interest at current European rates and the figure can top €900.

Compare that with the nightly rate for a luxury hotel suite in Marbella or Chamonix: €300 to €500. The hotel includes daily housekeeping, concierge, breakfast, and zero maintenance headaches. Your own holiday home, by contrast, costs more and arrives with a to-do list every time you unlock the door.

Hidden Expenses

The Seven Costs That Never Appear in the Brochure

Purchase price is only the beginning. Stamp duty and transfer taxes range from 6 per cent in mainland Spain to over 10 per cent in parts of France and Italy. Legal fees, notary costs, and registration add another 1 to 3 per cent. Then there is furnishing a property to the standard you actually want to live in — designer kitchens, quality linens, entertainment systems — which commonly runs €40,000 to €80,000 for a four-bedroom villa.

Once you move in, insurance premiums for holiday homes can be two to three times higher than for a primary residence, according to Eurostat’s 2025 housing cost index, because insurers factor in extended vacancy periods. Utility standing charges continue whether you are there or not. In Spain, the IBI property tax must be paid even if the home generates no income. In France, both taxe foncière and taxe d’habitation sur les résidences secondaires apply to second homes — and the latter has been rising sharply since 2023 as municipalities use it to discourage empty properties.

Then come the surprises: a leaking roof discovered in January when you are 2,000 kilometres away, a broken boiler the week before your Easter visit, termite treatment in the Algarve, storm damage on the Côte d’Azur. Capital expenditure on a property you occupy just five weeks a year feels disproportionately painful — yet it is unavoidable. Industry data suggests owners should budget 1 to 2 per cent of the property’s value each year for maintenance and repairs, meaning an €800,000 villa needs an €8,000 to €16,000 annual reserve fund.

Opportunity Cost

What That Capital Could Be Earning Elsewhere

Perhaps the most overlooked cost of holiday home ownership is opportunity cost. The €880,000 locked into a Mediterranean villa could instead sit in a diversified investment portfolio. Historical data from Morgan Stanley and Vanguard shows that a balanced 60/40 portfolio has returned an average of 7 to 8 per cent annually over the past two decades. Even at a conservative 6 per cent, that €880,000 generates roughly €52,800 per year in growth.

Meanwhile, residential property in southern Europe has appreciated at an average of 2 to 4 per cent per year over the same period, according to Eurostat’s House Price Index. The gap between what your capital earns inside a holiday home and what it could earn outside is significant — often €30,000 to €40,000 per year in foregone returns. Over a decade, compounding turns that gap into hundreds of thousands of euros. Yale economist Robert Shiller’s long-run data is even more stark: a dollar invested in equities in 1945 is worth nearly 50 times more than a dollar invested in housing.

None of this means property is a bad investment. It means that tying up the full purchase price of a luxury holiday home — a property you use for 35 nights — is an extraordinarily expensive way to access that investment. The smart question is not whether to own, but how much to own.

“If you use a property for five weeks a year, you are paying for 52 weeks of ownership. Co-ownership means you finally pay only for the weeks that matter.”

The Utilisation Crisis

330 Empty Nights and the Emotional Toll

Beyond the financial spreadsheet, there is an emotional dimension that rarely gets discussed before purchase. Owners describe a nagging guilt about the empty property — 330 nights per year when the beds are unslept in, the terrace furniture is gathering dust, and the garden is growing unchecked. Some try to offset this by renting the property out, only to discover that short-term rental regulations have tightened dramatically across Europe.

Barcelona banned tourist apartment licences outright in April 2025. The Balearic Islands have capped new holiday rental permits. The French Riviera requires registration and limits annual rental days. Even where rental is permitted, management fees of 20 to 40 per cent of income eat into returns, and the wear and tear from guests accelerates maintenance cycles. Many owners find the net rental income covers barely half of the running costs — leaving them subsidising a property they are emotionally attached to but financially burdened by.

A 2025 survey by the European Holiday Home Owners Association found that 38 per cent of owners said they would not buy the same property again if given the choice, citing unexpected costs and low utilisation as the primary regrets. The dream of a place in the sun can become a financial anchor that limits flexibility, ties up capital, and creates ongoing stress.

The Structural Fix

Co-Ownership: Paying Only for What You Use

The principle is simple: if you use a property for five to six weeks per year, why pay for 52 weeks of ownership? {{link:Co-ownership}} divides a single luxury property into typically eight deeded shares. Each owner holds a legal stake in the LLC or SCI that owns the property — this is real, registered, appreciating real estate, not a timeshare points programme. You can sell your share on the open market at market value whenever you choose.

A 1/8th share in an €800,000 villa costs from around €100,000. Running costs are split eight ways, so your annual overheads drop from €22,000 to roughly €2,750. You get somewhere between six and eight weeks of personal use a year — more than the average full owner actually uses — booked flexibly through an app covering everything from spontaneous weekends to long-range family planning. When you arrive, your personal belongings are taken out of storage and the home is prepared for you.

Let us redo the per-night calculation. A €100,000 share with €2,750 in annual costs over 45 nights equals roughly €61 per night in running costs. Even adding mortgage interest on the €100,000 share, the total per-night cost lands at approximately €90 to €130 — a fraction of the €629 that the full owner pays, and significantly less than a hotel. The remaining €780,000 in capital stays invested, continuing to earn returns. This is the maths that is converting thousands of buyers across Europe and the USA.

Hassle Factor

Zero Management, Zero Coordination

One of the most underappreciated benefits of the co-ownership model is the complete elimination of management burden. Every property is professionally managed — cleaning, maintenance, garden care, pool servicing, emergency repairs, guest coordination, and regulatory compliance are all handled. You never need to find a reliable local plumber at 10pm or argue with a rental guest about a broken dishwasher.

Crucially, you also never need to coordinate with other co-owners. There are no awkward group chats about who left the terrace dirty or whose week takes priority at Christmas. The management structure handles scheduling, conflict resolution, and property upkeep invisibly. For owners who previously spent hours each month managing a holiday property from afar — chasing contractors, reviewing utility bills, coordinating cleaners — this alone justifies the switch. Your holiday home becomes genuinely what it was supposed to be: a place to relax.

Properties in the co-ownership portfolio are typically furnished to a high designer standard with turnkey luxury interiors. There is no need to spend €60,000 furnishing a villa yourself, or to replace worn sofas every few years. The management team maintains the property at the standard it was delivered — so it looks and feels as good on your tenth visit as it did on your first.

Resale & Flexibility

Liquidity That Full Ownership Cannot Match

Selling a holiday home is notoriously slow. In southern Spain, the average time to sell a property over €500,000 is 6 to 12 months, according to Idealista market data. In rural France it can take even longer. During that period you continue paying every running cost while the property depreciates through lack of use.

Co-ownership shares, by contrast, are significantly more liquid. The management company first offers the share to existing co-owners in the same property — people who already know and love the home — and then lists it on the open market. Average resale time is approximately one month or less. The lower price point (from around €100,000 versus €800,000+) also dramatically widens the pool of potential buyers. If your circumstances change — a new grandchild in a different country, a desire to switch destinations, a financial need — you can exit quickly without the stress and cost of a full property sale.

Some owners use this flexibility strategically: they hold a co-ownership share in the French Alps for ski seasons and another on the Costa del Sol for summer, spreading their capital across two luxury destinations for less than the cost of one full property. This kind of portfolio diversification is simply impossible at the full-ownership level for most buyers.

Who Is Switching

The Profile of the Modern Co-Ownership Buyer

The typical buyer is not a first-timer priced out of the market. According to data from leading co-ownership platforms, over 40 per cent of buyers previously owned a full holiday home and switched specifically because of the cost and utilisation problems described above. They are typically aged 45 to 60, affluent professionals or semi-retired individuals who value their time as much as their money.

Many are British buyers who owned Spanish or French properties for years and grew tired of the management burden, or American families who maintained Colorado ski cabins that sat empty from April to November. The common thread is not lack of wealth — it is a rational reassessment of value. As one case study buyer put it: ‘I was paying a quarter of a million euros every five years to use a property for 200 nights. Now I pay a fraction of that and the experience is actually better because the property is always immaculately maintained.’

The trend is accelerating. The fractional and co-ownership market grew by an estimated 25 per cent year-on-year through 2024 and 2025, driven by rising property prices, higher interest rates, and a cultural shift toward asset-light living. Explore properties currently available across Europe and the USA to see the model in practice.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

How is the per-night cost of a holiday home actually calculated, and what do most buyers leave out?

The honest calculation includes annual operating costs (taxes, insurance, utilities, maintenance, security), one-eighth of major maintenance cycles (€40,000–80,000 every 7–10 years), and opportunity cost on the underlying capital (typically calculated at 4–7% of the property value). Divide this annual total by actual occupancy nights. Most buyers calculate only the obvious operating costs and ignore both major maintenance reserves and opportunity cost — both of which are real economic costs. The honest per-night cost on a €2.5 million property used 40 nights per year typically falls between €1,200 and €2,800, depending on which costs you include. Compared with five-star hotel rates at the same destination (typically €600–1,500/night), the math frequently looks unfavourable to whole ownership.

Why is the actual occupancy of luxury second homes so much lower than buyers initially expect?

The pre-purchase imagination usually involves 6–10 weeks of family use plus weekend visits whenever convenient. The reality is usually 30–55 nights per year. Three drivers consistently surface in occupancy data. Real vacation time is more limited than expected — most working professionals can't actually take 6+ weeks of holiday at one destination. Family schedules are harder to coordinate than imagined. The friction of organising trips to a property the owner manages personally creates 'maybe next month' deferral. Owners who measure their own usage honestly are typically surprised at how low it is — and the realisation often triggers the move to fractional ownership or the sale of the whole property entirely.

How does the per-night cost compare across different holiday accommodation models?

A representative comparison for €1,500–2,500/night quality at a typical European luxury destination. Five-star hotel: €1,500–2,500/night, all costs included, no commitment. Luxury villa rental: €1,800–3,500/night, plus cleaning and damage deposit, no commitment. Whole second-home ownership: €1,200–2,800/night when honestly costed, with locked capital and operational burden. Fractional co-ownership: €450–900/night including all operating costs, with capital appreciation participation and minimal operational burden. The fractional model is structurally the cheapest per-night for buyers who use the property 30–60 nights per year — the very usage band most luxury second-home buyers actually inhabit.

What's the operational time cost of running a luxury second home that buyers underestimate?

Independent surveys show typical owners spend 30–80 hours per year on property-related operations: contractor coordination, vendor management, insurance renewal, tax filings, maintenance scheduling, key handover for occasional rentals, and dispute handling. For high-net-worth buyers whose time has significant opportunity cost, this represents real economic value foregone. A senior professional with €500/hour effective rate is spending €15,000–40,000 per year of time-value on second-home operations — in addition to the cash operating costs. Fractional ownership delegates this to professional operators; the time-value saving is substantial and often not captured in financial comparisons.

Are there usage patterns where the per-night math actually favours whole ownership?

Yes, in specific cases. Owners who genuinely use 120+ nights per year at a single property — typically retirees or remote workers with partial relocation — get the per-night math down to €400–700, competitive with or better than fractional. Owners with very large families regularly using full 8+ bedroom properties find rentals expensive enough that whole ownership scales better. Owners with strong personal preference for full control over significant renovation or modification get value that's hard to monetise but real. Outside these specific cases, the per-night math typically favours fractional ownership for buyers whose actual usage falls in the 30–80 nights per year band that defines most luxury second-home use.

How does the per-night cost calculation change when you include resale outcome?

Significantly. A whole property purchased at €2.5 million and sold seven years later at €3.4 million (33% appreciation, plausible in many European markets) generates €900,000 in capital gain — material against the cumulative operating cost. The same calculation on a fractional share produces proportionally similar capital gain on the share value, also offsetting operating cost. In both cases, including the capital outcome substantially improves the per-night-net economics, but the relative ranking is preserved: fractional ownership delivers better capital efficiency per night used. The key variable is the appreciation rate, which is destination-specific; markets with strong appreciation make both whole and fractional ownership look attractive against rental, but fractional's capital efficiency remains the differentiator.

What's the practical implication for buyers considering their first second-home purchase?

Run the math honestly before purchase. Estimate realistic annual usage (most pre-purchase estimates are 2–3× actual). Calculate per-night cost across all the realistic options at your usage level — hotels, rentals, fractional, whole. The exercise often shifts the decision dramatically: many would-be whole-property buyers end up choosing fractional after the math, and many would-be rental users discover that even modest annual usage justifies a fractional share over repeated rental costs. The lifestyle outcome is what matters; the financial structure should be chosen to deliver that outcome at the lowest justifiable cost. For most buyers the outcome that emerges is some combination of fractional ownership at a primary destination plus rental flexibility for variety.

title: How to Buy Property in Spain as a Foreigner: Tax, NIE and Legal Rules for 2026
subtitle: Everything foreign buyers need to know about Spanish property taxes, NIE numbers, golden visa changes, and co-ownership options in 2026. Expert guide.
excerpt: Everything foreign buyers need to know about Spanish property taxes, NIE numbers, golden visa changes, and co-ownership options in 2026. Expert guide.
content:
Spain remains one of the most popular destinations for international property buyers — and for good reason. Sun-drenched coastlines, world-class cuisine, excellent healthcare, and property prices that still offer remarkable value compared to northern Europe and the US have drawn a record nearly 100,000 foreign transactions in 2025 alone. But buying property in a different country is never as straightforward as browsing a listing and signing a cheque. Spanish tax law, residency regulations, and the recent abolition of the golden visa programme have reshaped the landscape for overseas buyers entering the market in 2026.

Whether you are a British retiree eyeing a villa on the Costa del Sol, an American remote worker looking at a Barcelona apartment, or a Dutch couple searching for a Balearic holiday home, you need a clear understanding of the legal and financial framework before you commit. This guide walks you through every step — from obtaining your NIE number to managing annual property taxes — and explains why an increasing number of savvy buyers are choosing co-ownership as a smarter route into the Spanish property market.

The Legal Foundation

What Is a NIE and Why Do You Need One?

The NIE (Número de Identidad de Extranjero) is a unique tax identification number assigned to every foreigner conducting financial or legal transactions in Spain. You cannot buy property, open a Spanish bank account, pay taxes, or sign a utility contract without one. Think of it as the single key that unlocks the entire Spanish property buying process.

Applying for a NIE is straightforward but requires planning. You can apply in person at a Spanish National Police station (you will need a cita previa — an online appointment) or through your nearest Spanish consulate abroad. The paperwork consists of a completed EX-15 form, your passport, a passport-sized photograph, and proof of payment of the Tasa 012 fee (approximately €12 in 2026). Processing typically takes one to three weeks in Spain, though appointment availability can add to the timeline.

For international buyers who prefer not to travel to Spain solely for this step, a common and perfectly legal approach is to grant power of attorney (poder notarial) to a Spanish lawyer. Your lawyer can then attend the appointment and obtain the NIE on your behalf. This is standard practice and is used by the majority of foreign buyers purchasing holiday homes in Spain. If you are purchasing through a co-ownership structure, the management team typically coordinates this process for you, removing one more hurdle from the buying journey.

Understanding the Costs

Property Taxes and Purchase Costs in Spain

One of the most common surprises for first-time foreign buyers in Spain is the total cost of purchase beyond the headline price. Budget for between 10% and 15% on top of the property price to cover taxes, notary fees, land registry fees, and legal costs. The exact percentage depends on whether you are buying new-build or resale, and which autonomous community the property sits in.

For resale properties, the main tax is the ITP (Impuesto de Transmisiones Patrimoniales), which ranges from 6% to 10% depending on the region. Andalucía, home to the Costa del Sol, charges 7%. The Balearic Islands use a sliding scale from 8% to 13% based on property value. For new-build properties, you pay 10% IVA (VAT) plus 1.5% stamp duty (AJD) instead of ITP.

On top of the purchase tax, expect to pay approximately 1% to 2.5% for notary fees, land registry fees, and your lawyer’s fees. With co-ownership, these costs are split proportionately between shareholders — so a 1/8th owner pays just 1/8th of the total, making luxury property acquisition dramatically more accessible. A property with total purchase costs of €80,000 becomes roughly €10,000 per co-owner.

Regulatory Change

The Golden Visa Is Gone — What Replaces It?

On 3 April 2025, Spain officially ended its golden visa programme. Previously, non-EU nationals who purchased property worth €500,000 or more qualified for a Spanish residence permit. That route is now permanently closed, driven by concerns over housing affordability in cities like Madrid and Barcelona, EU-level recommendations, and anti-money-laundering priorities.

This does not mean foreigners cannot buy property in Spain — they absolutely can. Non-residents purchase Spanish real estate every day without needing a visa or residence permit. What has changed is that property ownership alone no longer creates a path to residency. Buyers seeking to live in Spain now need to explore alternatives such as the non-lucrative visa (for those with passive income and no intention to work), the digital nomad visa (for remote workers), or the entrepreneur visa.

For buyers whose primary goal is a holiday home rather than permanent relocation, the golden visa abolition changes nothing practical. You can still buy, own, enjoy, and resell property freely. And with co-ownership, the proposition becomes even more compelling: rather than tying up €500,000 in a single property you might use for a few weeks a year, you can own a share in a luxury villa or apartment from under €100,000 and enjoy roughly one-eighth of the calendar — about 45 nights — fully managed, zero hassle.

“With co-ownership, you pay 1/8th of the taxes, 1/8th of the maintenance, and enjoy roughly one-eighth of the calendar — about 45 nightsof luxury living per year — while the management company handles every piece of Spanish bureaucracy for you.”

The Proposed 100% Tax

Will Spain Tax Foreign Buyers Out of the Market?

In early 2025, the Spanish government proposed a 100% additional property tax on purchases by non-EU, non-resident buyers. The proposal was submitted to parliament in May 2025 and, as of early 2026, remains under review — it has not been signed into law. Even if passed, it would target non-EU, non-resident purchases specifically, meaning EU citizens and non-EU residents in Spain would be unaffected.

Market analysts remain divided on whether the tax will pass in its current form. Many expect it to be significantly watered down or limited to specific regions experiencing acute housing pressure. Regardless, the proposal has created a sense of urgency among non-EU buyers considering Spanish property. British buyers — who post-Brexit are classified as non-EU — have been particularly attentive, with many accelerating their purchase timelines.

This is another area where co-ownership provides a strategic advantage. Because co-ownership shares represent a stake in an LLC that owns the property — rather than a direct personal property purchase — the legal structure may offer different tax treatment depending on how the final legislation is drafted. Buyers working with co-ownership specialists benefit from professional legal and tax guidance tailored to their specific situation and nationality.

Annual Obligations

Ongoing Property Taxes for Foreign Owners in Spain

Buying is only the beginning. Foreign property owners in Spain face several annual tax obligations that must be budgeted for. The most important is the IBI (Impuesto sobre Bienes Inmuebles) — Spain’s equivalent of council tax or property tax. IBI is calculated as a percentage of the catastral value (a government-assessed value typically well below market price) and varies by municipality, typically ranging from 0.4% to 1.1% of catastral value.

Non-resident property owners must also file an annual non-resident income tax return (Modelo 210), even if the property generates no rental income. For non-rented properties, the tax is levied on an imputed income of 1.1% to 2% of the catastral value, taxed at 19% for EU/EEA residents and 24% for everyone else. If you rent the property out, rental income is taxed at those same rates, with EU/EEA residents able to deduct expenses but non-EU residents taxed on gross rental income.

The running costs of co-ownership are shared proportionately. A 1/8th owner pays 1/8th of the IBI, community fees, insurance, maintenance, and management charges. With co-ownership properties, all of these obligations are handled by the management team — tax returns filed, bills paid, maintenance coordinated — so you never have to navigate Spanish bureaucracy yourself.

Step-By-Step

The Complete Spanish Property Buying Process

Understanding the full purchase timeline helps set realistic expectations. From first viewing to collecting the keys, a typical Spanish property purchase takes eight to twelve weeks, though this can vary. Here is the standard process that every foreign buyer follows.

First, obtain your NIE and open a Spanish bank account — both essential before any money changes hands. Next, once you have found your property, you sign a reservation contract (contrato de reserva) with a deposit of €3,000 to €10,000 to take the property off the market. Your lawyer then conducts due diligence: checking the property register, confirming the seller’s ownership, reviewing any debts or charges against the property, and verifying building licences and energy certificates.

If everything checks out, you sign the private purchase contract (contrato de arras) and pay a deposit of 10% of the purchase price. This contract is legally binding: if you pull out, you lose the deposit; if the seller pulls out, they must return double the deposit. Finally, you attend the notary (notaría) to sign the public deed (escritura pública), pay the balance, and the property is yours. Registration at the Land Registry follows, typically handled by your lawyer.

When buying through co-ownership, much of this complexity is handled for you. The legal entity is already established, the property has been fully vetted, and the management company coordinates the purchase of your share through a streamlined process — often completing in as little as four weeks.

Market Intelligence

Where Are Foreign Buyers Purchasing in Spain in 2026?

The geography of foreign buying in Spain reveals clear hotspots. The Balearic Islands consistently lead, with foreign buyers accounting for over 30% of all transactions — a figure driven by demand from Germans, British, and Scandinavian buyers for Mallorca and Ibiza properties. The Valencian Community (including the Costa Blanca) and Andalucía (the Costa del Sol and beyond) follow closely.

British buyers remain the single largest foreign nationality purchasing in Spain, with 5,731 transactions in the first half of 2025 alone — 8.1% of all foreign purchases. Dutch buyers have surged to second place, overtaking Germans, with strong interest in the Alicante and Málaga provinces. American buyers are a smaller but fast-growing segment, attracted by favourable exchange rates and the remote work revolution.

For those drawn to the Costa del Sol, the Balearic Islands, or Spain’s stunning coastlines, co-ownership opens doors to locations where full ownership would require budgets of €1 million or more. Browse all available properties to see current co-ownership opportunities across Spain’s most sought-after destinations.

The Smarter Alternative

Why Co-Ownership Is Changing How Foreigners Buy in Spain

The traditional model of buying a full holiday home in Spain is increasingly difficult to justify financially. Most second homes sit empty for over 90% of the year, yet the owner bears 100% of the costs — mortgage payments, taxes, insurance, maintenance, and the stress of managing a property from another country. When you factor in the regulatory complexity outlined in this guide — NIE applications, annual tax returns, evolving visa rules — the administrative burden compounds.

Co-ownership eliminates these pain points. When you purchase a 1/8th share through Co-Ownership Property, you acquire documented legal title to your share of the property in a registered LLC that holds the property. This is genuine asset ownership — not a timeshare, not a points system. Your share appreciates with the property market, can be sold on the open market at any time, and typically resells in under one month.

Each owner enjoys approximately roughly one-eighth of the calendar — about 45 nights of use, booked flexibly through an app across the full window from a weekend whim to a planned-far-ahead family gathering. When you arrive, your whatever you keep at the property is brought out of storage and the home is prepared exactly to your preferences. Every aspect of management — from cleaning and maintenance to tax filings and rental coordination — is handled for you. It is luxury property ownership without the weight of full ownership, and it is why an increasing number of international buyers are choosing this route into the Spanish market.

Ready to explore your options? Browse all co-ownership properties or book a free consultation to speak with a specialist about finding the right share for your lifestyle and budget.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What's the realistic tax bill for a foreign buyer purchasing a Spanish property in 2026?

The headline charges are ITP (transfer tax on resale property) at 6–11% of the share/property value depending on autonomous community, AJD (stamp duty on new-build) at 0.5–1.5% plus 10% IVA on new-build, notary and registry fees at roughly 1–1.5%, and legal/gestor fees at 1–2%. For a fractional share acquisition through an existing Spanish SL, the structure is different — share transfers in companies typically attract a much lower tax footprint than direct property purchases. Total acquisition cost on a typical fractional share usually runs 8–14% above the share's headline price; on whole property purchases the comparable number is 12–18%. Always model the all-in cost, not just the headline price.

How does NIE work for fractional buyers, and is it actually required for share acquisition?

The Número de Identificación de Extranjero (NIE) is the Spanish foreign-buyer identification number, required for any significant Spanish economic activity by non-residents — including direct property purchases, opening Spanish bank accounts, and signing notarial deeds. For fractional ownership through a Spanish SL, NIE is typically required for the buyer to be registered as a shareholder in the company. The application process can be done at a Spanish consulate in your home country (4–8 weeks) or in Spain at a designated police station (2–6 weeks). Most operators handle the application as part of the buying process. Budget around €15 in official fees plus €100–250 if you use a gestor to handle the paperwork.

What's the post-Golden-Visa residency landscape for foreign Spanish property buyers in 2026?

The Golden Visa (€500,000+ property investment for residency) closed to new applicants in April 2025. Three replacement routes have grown in importance. The Non-Lucrative Visa requires showing approximately €30,000 per year in passive income — for retirees and investment-income earners. The Digital Nomad Visa (in force since 2023) is open to remote workers earning at least €30,840 per year for non-Spanish employers. The Entrepreneur Visa fits buyers establishing a Spanish business. None of these is property-conditional; residency is granted to the person and the person can hold property (or a fractional share) independently. For fractional buyers not seeking residency, the closure changes nothing operationally.

How does Spain's wealth tax (impuesto sobre el patrimonio) affect a foreign fractional owner?

Spain's national wealth tax has been variably applied across autonomous communities. Madrid and Andalusia apply a 100% bonification (effectively zero); Catalonia, Asturias, and a few others apply progressive rates above thresholds. Non-residents with Spanish-situs assets are exposed to wealth tax on those Spanish assets only, with a typical exemption of €700,000 (and higher in some communities). For a typical fractional share value (€200,000–500,000), most non-resident owners fall well below thresholds. Owners with multiple Spanish shares or other Spanish property aggregate the values. A new national-level 'solidarity wealth tax' applies above €3 million globally — relevant only to high-net-worth buyers with substantial overall asset bases.

What's the position on Modelo 720 (foreign asset declaration) for fractional buyers?

Modelo 720 is the Spanish foreign-asset declaration required of Spanish tax residents holding foreign assets above €50,000 in any of three categories (bank accounts, securities, real estate). For non-resident Spanish property owners, Modelo 720 is not relevant — it applies only to residents declaring their foreign holdings. For Spanish residents who own foreign fractional shares, the share is reportable in the real-estate or securities category depending on structure. The 720 reporting regime was substantially modified after EU court challenges in 2022; current penalties for non-compliance are reasonable rather than confiscatory, but timely filing matters. Spanish-resident fractional owners should work with Spanish accountants familiar with cross-border reporting.

How does the proposed 100% transfer tax on non-EU buyers actually work in practice?

The 100% surcharge on residential property transfer tax for non-EU resident individuals was proposed in early 2025 as part of housing-affordability legislation. The text targets direct individual purchases of residential property; it doesn't (as drafted) target acquisitions of shares in Spanish companies that already own property. As of mid-2026 the proposal hasn't been enacted and faces significant legal challenge, including from EU equality-of-treatment principles. For non-EU buyers considering fractional ownership through a Spanish SL, the share-acquisition route through corporate transactions is currently understood to fall outside the proposed scope. This is an active area to watch; confirm the operator's specific legal positioning in writing if you're a non-EU buyer.

What ongoing tax filings does a foreign fractional Spanish owner have to manage?

Two main filings. Modelo 210 is the non-resident income tax return — used to declare deemed rental income (an imputed rent for personal-use second homes, calculated as 1.1–2% of cadastral value annually) and any actual rental income if the property is let. Modelo 211/213 covers withholding on certain corporate transactions and is mainly relevant at acquisition and disposal rather than ongoing. Most fractional operators handle filings on the holding LLC's behalf and provide owners with the supporting documentation for personal Modelo 210 filings. Budget €300–600 per year in adviser fees for typical fractional share filings; complex cases (multiple shares, rental income, currency conversions) cost more.
