Global Trends

From Colorado to Como: Where Energy-Efficient Co-Ownership Is Thriving

The demand for sustainable co-ownership property spans continents. In Colorado, where altitude and extreme temperature swings make energy efficiency critical, ski chalets built to high-performance standards are commanding premium prices and strong co-ownership demand. The state’s progressive building codes and buyer demographics — affluent, environmentally aware professionals — make it a natural market for Passive House co-ownership.

Across the Atlantic, the Italian Lakes region is seeing a new generation of eco-luxury developments around Lake Como, where restored villas are incorporating modern insulation, heat pumps, and solar arrays while preserving their historic facades. In the South of France, the combination of solar abundance and rigorous French energy regulations makes the region ideal for properties that generate as much energy as they consume.

The Balearic Islands offer another compelling case study. Mallorca, Ibiza, and Menorca face acute energy challenges — imported electricity is expensive, and summer cooling costs can rival winter heating bills on the mainland. A Passive House on Mallorca or Ibiza dramatically reduces cooling demand through intelligent orientation, shading, and insulation, making co-ownership shares in these properties exceptionally cost-efficient to maintain.

Buyer Education

How to Evaluate Energy Efficiency When Buying a Co-Ownership Share

Not every property marketed as ‘energy efficient’ meets the same standard. For co-ownership buyers conducting due diligence, several key indicators separate genuinely high-performance properties from greenwashed marketing. First, look for formal certification — Passivhaus, LEED Platinum, BREEAM Excellent, or a national equivalent. Second, check the EPC (Energy Performance Certificate) rating; anything below B should prompt questions about future regulatory risk.

Ask about the building envelope: insulation thickness, glazing specification, and airtightness test results. A genuine Passive House will have documented blower-door test results proving airtightness below 0.6 ACH. Check the mechanical systems — heat recovery ventilation (MVHR), heat pumps, and solar thermal are hallmarks of high-performance builds. Finally, ask for actual energy consumption data from existing properties, not just design estimates.

At Co-Ownership Property, every listing includes detailed property specifications, and our team can walk you through the energy performance of any property in our portfolio. Understanding what you are buying — and what it will cost to run — is central to the buying process.

Investment Outlook

The Financial Case for Green Co-Ownership in 2026 and Beyond

The convergence of rising energy costs, tightening regulations, and growing buyer preference for sustainable property creates a powerful investment thesis for energy-efficient co-ownership. The global green building market is projected to reach $1.37 trillion by 2034, more than doubling from its current $618 billion valuation. Properties that meet or exceed current energy standards are positioned to capture a growing share of buyer demand — and the price premiums that follow.

For co-owners specifically, the calculus is even more favourable. Lower running costs mean higher net returns from rental income, stronger demand from environmentally conscious holiday renters, and reduced exposure to energy price volatility. When combined with the {{link:co-ownership model’s}} inherent advantages — shared costs, professional management, and flexible usage — an energy-efficient co-ownership share represents what many advisors consider the smartest entry point into luxury property today.

Whether you are looking at a ski chalet in the European Alps, a villa on the Costa del Sol, or a city apartment in Paris, the question is no longer whether energy efficiency matters — it is whether you can afford to ignore it.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What does Passive House (Passivhaus) standard actually mean for a luxury fractional property?

Passive House is a rigorous voluntary standard for energy-efficient buildings, requiring extremely low heating and cooling demand through superinsulation, airtight construction, mechanical ventilation with heat recovery, and triple-glazing. Certified Passive House properties typically use 75-90% less heating energy than conventional construction. For luxury fractional properties, the practical implications include dramatically lower operating energy costs (€3,000-€8,000 annual savings on a typical luxury property), better thermal comfort year-round, reduced acoustic transmission (the airtightness is acoustically beneficial), and meaningful sustainability credentials. The certification adds 5-10% to construction cost but typically pays back within 7-10 years through energy savings.

Are there any luxury fractional properties actually built to Passive House standard?

Yes — the segment has grown significantly since 2020. Several Alpine fractional chalets in Switzerland and Austria have been built to Passive House or Minergie-P (Swiss equivalent) standards. Some Mediterranean luxury fractional properties have been built to PHPP (Passive House Planning Package) standards even where formal certification isn't sought. The number is still modest relative to total fractional inventory but growing rapidly as buyer awareness of energy performance increases. Operators with portfolios including Passive House properties typically use the certification as a meaningful marketing differentiator and command pricing premiums.

How does Passive House construction interact with traditional luxury aesthetic expectations?

Modern Passive House design has matured significantly from the technology-forward early implementations. Contemporary Passive House luxury properties successfully integrate the engineering requirements (superinsulation, airtight construction, MVHR systems) with traditional aesthetic vocabularies — Alpine chalet character, Mediterranean villa style, urban heritage facades. Window proportions and aesthetics can match historical references while delivering Passive House thermal performance. The aesthetic compromise that defined early Passive House work (chunky proportions, limited fenestration) has largely been resolved by current design and material technology. For fractional buyers, Passive House properties no longer look or feel different from conventional luxury construction.

What's the operating cost difference between Passive House and conventional luxury fractional properties?

Substantial on the energy line. Annual heating and cooling energy costs on Passive House construction typically run 70-85% below comparable conventional construction — material savings on a luxury property's operating budget. For a luxury Alpine chalet that might run €15,000-€25,000 in annual heating energy on conventional construction, Passive House standards drop this to €2,500-€6,000. Other operating costs (insurance, maintenance, taxes) are similar; the energy savings are the primary differential. Inside fractional structures, the savings are divided across owners — perhaps €1,500-€3,000 per share annually. Over 7-10 year holding periods this compounds to meaningful amounts.

How do energy efficiency regulations across European jurisdictions affect Passive House positioning?

Increasingly favourably. EU regulations have progressively tightened minimum energy performance standards through 2020s; by 2030 most major jurisdictions will require minimum performance levels for residential property transactions. Passive House properties significantly exceed these minimums and are essentially future-proofed against further tightening. Conventional construction may require renovation to meet 2030 standards; Passive House construction won't. For fractional buyers thinking about 7-10 year holdings spanning the 2030 regulatory milestone, Passive House positioning provides meaningful protection against compliance cost and resale-value erosion.

What are the wellness and comfort benefits of Passive House construction?

Several worth understanding. Indoor air quality is consistently excellent because of the mechanical ventilation system with filtration. Temperature stability is dramatically better than conventional construction — once a Passive House reaches setpoint, temperature variation is minimal regardless of external weather. Acoustic isolation from external noise is excellent due to the airtight construction and triple-glazing. Humidity control is automatic through the MVHR system. The cumulative effect on stay quality is often described by owners as profound — sleep quality improves, daytime alertness improves, the property feels effortless to use. The wellness benefits matter as much as the energy savings for many owners.

What questions should buyers ask when evaluating Passive House fractional properties?

Several specific points. Is the property formally certified by an accredited Passive House certifier, or built to Passive House principles without certification? What's the actual measured energy use post-completion versus the design prediction? How is the MVHR system maintained and what's the filter replacement schedule? What's the comfort feedback from owners who have used the property across seasons? How is the airtightness verified and maintained over time (e.g., periodic blower-door tests)? Each question yields useful information; serious Passive House operators can answer all of them with documented evidence. Properties marketed as 'Passive House inspired' without formal verification warrant additional scrutiny.

title: From Enquiry to Keys in 6 Weeks: How the Co-Ownership Buying Process Actually Works
subtitle: Discover the co-ownership buying process from first enquiry to keys in hand. Learn how just six weeks is all it takes to own a share in a luxury property in 2026.
excerpt: Discover the co-ownership buying process from first enquiry to keys in hand. Learn how just six weeks is all it takes to own a share in a luxury property in 202
content:
Most people assume buying a share in a luxury holiday home involves the same marathon of paperwork, negotiations, and sleepless nights that comes with purchasing a full property. They picture months of mortgage applications, surveyor visits, and legal wrangling. The reality of co-ownership properties is refreshingly different. From your very first enquiry to receiving the keys to a stunning villa or chalet, the entire co-ownership buying process typically takes just four to six weeks — a fraction of the time required for a traditional second home purchase.

In a market where the average property transaction takes four to six months according to 2026 homebuying data, co-ownership stands apart as a streamlined alternative that removes the biggest bottlenecks. There are no chains, no competitive bidding wars, and no agonising waits for mortgage approvals on seven-figure sums. Whether you are eyeing a ski chalet in the French Alps or a sun-drenched villa on the Costa del Sol, this guide walks you through every stage of the journey — week by week — so you know exactly what to expect before you commit.

Week 1

Discovery: Finding the Right Property and Share

The process begins the moment you browse properties on the Co-Ownership Property platform. Every listing shows the location, share structure, price per share, and a detailed breakdown of annual running costs. Unlike traditional property searches where you might spend months viewing dozens of homes, co-ownership narrows the field dramatically. You are choosing from a curated portfolio of fully renovated, designer-furnished luxury homes — each one already vetted, legally structured, and ready to move into.

During your first conversation with a co-ownership specialist, you will discuss your lifestyle preferences, budget, and how you plan to use the property. Are you a ski family wanting roughly one-eighth of the calendar — about 45 nightson the slopes each winter? A couple dreaming of long Mediterranean summers? Or perhaps you want a base in multiple destinations to mix beach, mountain, and city breaks throughout the year. This initial consultation is free, carries no obligation, and typically lasts 30 to 45 minutes.

By the end of week one, you will have a shortlist of properties that match your criteria — complete with floor plans, interior photography, local area guides, and a transparent cost breakdown. Many buyers tell us this first stage is where the excitement really builds, because they realise just how much luxury is accessible at a fraction of the full purchase price.

6 Weeks

Average time from first enquiry to receiving the keys to your co-ownership property share.

4-6 Months

Average timeline for a traditional second home purchase in 2026 — up to five times longer.

$9.4B

~1 Month

Average time to resell a co-ownership share — far faster than traditional property sales.

Week 2

Due Diligence: Understanding What You Are Buying

Co-ownership is real-property-backed ownership through the holding entity, not a timeshare and not a holiday club. When you purchase a share — typically one-eighth — you become a shareholder in a registered LLC that holds the property title. This LLC structure has been specifically designed and optimised by specialist tax and law firms to protect your investment, whether the property is in Europe or the USA. According to Growth Market Reports, the global fractional ownership market reached USD 9.4 billion in 2024 and is growing at 13.7% annually, reflecting just how mainstream this structure has become.

During week two, you will review the co-ownership explained documentation: the LLC operating agreement, the usage schedule system, the management contract, and the cost-sharing arrangements. Every co-owner pays one-eighth of all running costs — maintenance, insurance, taxes, cleaning, and property management. There are no hidden charges and no surprise levies. Your due diligence checklist covers everything from title verification to local planning restrictions.

This is also the stage where you can arrange a property visit if you have not already seen the home. Many of our properties are in destinations buyers already know and love — which means some buyers are comfortable proceeding based on the detailed virtual tours and photography alone. Either way, your co-ownership specialist will answer every question before you move to the next stage.

Market Context

Why the Traditional Second Home Process Is Broken

To understand why co-ownership is gaining momentum so rapidly, consider what the alternative looks like. A traditional second home purchase in 2026 involves four to six months of searching, viewing, negotiating, arranging finance, and completing legal work. According to Bankrate’s 2025 study, the average annual hidden costs of homeownership now exceed $21,400 — and that figure rises steeply for second homes that sit empty for most of the year.

Insurance premiums on second homes can be two to three times higher than primary residences due to vacancy risk. Property management fees consume 20% to 40% of rental income. And maintenance costs have climbed 42% in just five years. For a property you might use for only four to six weeks per year, the economics of full ownership are increasingly hard to justify — especially when co-ownership delivers the same lifestyle for a fraction of the cost and effort.

The co-ownership vs full ownership comparison makes the case clearly. With co-ownership, you get roughly one-eighth of the calendar — about 45 nights — more than most full owners actually use their second homes — while splitting every cost eight ways. The buying process is faster because the legal structure already exists, the property is already renovated, and the management framework is already in place.

“Co-ownership does not just make luxury property more affordable — it makes the entire buying experience faster, simpler, and fundamentally less stressful than traditional second home ownership.”

Weeks 3-4

Legal Completion: Signing, Payment, and Share Transfer

Once you have completed your due diligence and decided to proceed, the legal process moves quickly. You will sign the share purchase agreement, which transfers your ownership stake in the LLC. Because the property is already held within a corporate structure, there is no need for the lengthy conveyancing process that traditional property purchases require. No chain, no mortgage delays from other buyers, no gazumping.

Payment is typically made via bank transfer. For buyers who need financing, some properties offer payment plans or mortgage options — though the majority of co-ownership purchases are cash transactions, reflecting the fact that share prices start from around €65,000 rather than the six- or seven-figure sums required for full ownership. The costs of buying page breaks down exactly what you pay and when.

Your co-ownership specialist will coordinate with the legal team to ensure all documents are reviewed, countersigned, and filed. In most cases, the legal completion takes just seven to ten business days from the point of signing. For properties in the USA, the LLC registration process is handled domestically. For European properties, the structure is adapted to local regulations while maintaining the same investor protections.

Co-Ownership vs Traditional Purchase: A Side-by-Side Timeline

The speed difference between co-ownership and traditional second home purchases is not marginal — it is transformational. A conventional international property purchase can take anywhere from three to nine months depending on the country, the complexity of the transaction, and whether financing is involved. Cross-border purchases add additional layers of legal, tax, and currency complexity that can extend the process even further.

Co-ownership eliminates most of these variables. The LLC is already registered. The property is already purchased and renovated. The management company is already operational. All you are doing is acquiring a share in an existing, functioning structure — which is why the process can be completed in weeks rather than months. This is particularly attractive for buyers who want to secure a property ahead of a specific season, such as ski season in the Alps or summer in the Balearics.

Week 6

Weeks 5-6

Welcome: Your First Stay and the Owner Experience

Within days of completion, you gain access to the owner booking app. This is where you reserve your stays — from two days to two years in advance, with free of the locked-in weekly calendar of legacy timeshare or rigid rotation schedules. Each one-eighth owner gets approximately roughly one-eighth of the calendar — about 45 nights, and the flexible system means you can plan around school holidays, personal commitments, or simply book last-minute when the mood strikes.

When you arrive for your first stay, the property is prepared exactly for you. Your between-visit storage is opened and your things are placed for you and placed in the home. The property is cleaned, stocked, and ready. You never need to coordinate with other co-owners — the management company handles everything. This hands-off, five-star hospitality experience is one of the key reasons buyers choose co-ownership over traditional second home ownership, where arrival often means dealing with maintenance issues, stale air, and overgrown gardens.

From this point forward, you are a property owner in every meaningful sense. You have deeded ownership, asset appreciation potential, and the ability to sell your share at any time on the open market. Average resale time is around one month — a fraction of the time it takes to sell a full property.

Financial Clarity

What You Will Pay: A Transparent Cost Breakdown

One of the most common questions buyers ask is: what does co-ownership actually cost? The answer is refreshingly straightforward. Your share purchase price is the upfront investment — ranging from under €100,000 for apartments in emerging destinations to around €2 million for ultra-luxury chalets and villas. The running costs are then split proportionately among all co-owners.

For a one-eighth share, you pay one-eighth of everything: property taxes, building insurance, maintenance, cleaning between stays, garden upkeep, pool servicing, and professional property management. For most properties, this translates to an annual running cost of roughly €3,000 to €8,000 per share — depending on the size, location, and amenities of the property. Compare that to the full running costs of a luxury second home, which the running costs page estimates at €25,000 to €60,000 annually.

Some properties also generate rental income when not in use by owners. This income is shared proportionately and managed entirely by the property management company — you do not need to handle bookings, guest communications, or key handovers. The FAQs section covers rental specifics in more detail.

Buyer Confidence

What Happens If You Want to Sell Your Share?

Life changes, and co-ownership is designed to accommodate that. If you decide to sell your share, the process is simple. The management company first offers your share to existing co-owners in the property — who often want to increase their stake. If none of them take it up, the share is listed for sale through the Co-Ownership Property platform and its network.

Average resale time is approximately one month, compared to three to twelve months for a full property sale in most European and US markets. Because you are selling a share in a functioning, managed property with a proven usage track record, buyers have confidence in what they are purchasing. The resale and exit process is fully supported, and there are no lock-in periods or exit penalties.

This liquidity advantage is one of co-ownership’s most underappreciated benefits. Traditional second home owners often feel trapped by their investment — unable to sell quickly without accepting a significant discount. Co-ownership shares, by contrast, are smaller, more affordable, and appeal to a broader pool of buyers, which keeps the resale market active and healthy.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the actual six-week timeline look like step by step?

A representative timeline with a mature European fractional operator. Week 1: Initial enquiry, share offering documentation review, scheduling of property visit (or virtual tour). Week 2: Property visit, legal/structural Q&A with the operator's local counsel. Weeks 3–4: Buyer-side legal review (your lawyer reviewing the share offering, operating agreement, and holding-entity structure), KYC and source-of-funds documentation. Week 5: Reservation contract signing with deposit (typically 10% of share value), final legal and tax review, appointment booking with notary or legal completion. Week 6: Funds transfer to escrow, completion meeting (notary or operator office depending on jurisdiction), share register updated, app access activated. The timeline assumes no specific complications; cross-border situations or estate-planning structures can extend by 2–4 weeks.

What are the most common reasons a six-week timeline slips?

Three recurring causes. NIE or equivalent foreign-buyer ID delays (Spanish NIE, French numéro fiscal) can add 4–8 weeks if not started early — this is the single most common timeline slip. Cross-border tax structuring (US estate-tax mitigation through holding companies, UK trust arrangements) typically adds 3–6 weeks for specialist review. Buyer-side legal review timelines can extend if the buyer's lawyer is unfamiliar with fractional structures and conducts traditional whole-property due diligence — many operators recommend lawyers experienced with fractional purchases specifically. Setting expectations realistically — eight weeks for the average buyer, with NIE started immediately if not already held — produces fewer surprises.

How much money actually moves at completion, and through what mechanism?

The completion transfer covers the share purchase price plus all transaction costs (transfer taxes, notary fees, registry fees, operator's administration fee). For a €350,000 share with typical Spanish or French structure, the completion total runs €375,000–390,000. Funds transfer through escrow — the operator's notary or designated trust account — with the operator triggering release to the holding entity on receipt. Buyers should never transfer directly to operator personal accounts; reputable platforms always use escrow. Banking-level KYC requirements mean source-of-funds documentation typically needs to be in order 1–2 weeks before completion. Most buyers use SWIFT or SEPA transfers; some larger transactions use specialist FX brokers for better rates.

What's the actual content of the documents a buyer signs at completion?

The core documents are the share purchase agreement (transferring the specific share from the operator or selling co-owner to the buyer), the operating agreement (the constitutional document of the holding entity covering usage rights, voting, exit mechanics, dispute resolution — already in force, the buyer adheres to it), the management services agreement (the contract between owners and the operator for ongoing services), and the local-jurisdiction property-related documents (deed, escritura, atto, depending on country). KYC and AML compliance documents are signed before completion. Buyers should have read all of these in draft well before completion; the meeting itself is execution, not negotiation.

When does property usage actually start after completion?

Typically immediately, with the first booking available from the date of completion. Some operators have a 7–14 day setup window for app activation, key codes, and booking-system synchronisation. Peak-week allocation for the first year usually depends on when the buyer enters the rotation — joining mid-year often means the first peak-week pick is in year two. Most buyers don't physically visit the property in their first month of ownership; the typical first stay is scheduled 2–6 months after completion. Some operators include a 'welcome stay' as part of the purchase — a complementary 3–4 night visit in the first 90 days for the buyer to inspect the property and meet local staff.

What can go wrong between reservation and completion, and how is it handled?

Three main risk scenarios. Buyer-side cold feet — the deposit is typically partially or fully refundable within a defined cooling-off period, then forfeit. Title or legal issues identified during buyer-side due diligence — typically grounds for renegotiation or termination with deposit refund if material. Operator-side delay or default — typically grounds for termination with full refund. The reservation contract should specify all of these scenarios; read it carefully before signing. The most common actual outcome is no major issue and clean completion within the expected window; operator-side defaults are rare with established platforms but have happened with smaller operators, which is why diligence on the operator matters.

How does the timeline compare with a traditional whole-property purchase?

Substantially faster. A traditional whole-property purchase in Spain, France, or Italy typically runs 3–6 months from offer to keys. The longer timeline reflects more complex legal due diligence (full title searches, urbanism certificates, structural surveys), mortgage application processing if applicable, and longer conveyancing chains. Fractional ownership compresses this because the operator has already conducted the full legal due diligence on the property at the original acquisition; the buyer only diligences the share and the structure, not the underlying property to the same depth. For buyers who want to be using their European second home this summer rather than next, fractional ownership's faster timeline is a meaningful practical advantage.

Courchevel is a name that conjures images of fur-clad oligarchs, helicopter transfers, and six-figure weekly chalet rentals. But beyond the glitz of Courchevel 1850 lies a village that seasoned Alpine buyers have quietly favoured for years — Courchevel Moriond, formerly known as 1650. It shares the same lift system, the same 600 kilometres of Three Valleys pistes, and the same snow record, yet property here costs up to 50% less per square metre than its celebrity-magnet neighbour. For buyers exploring co-ownership properties, Moriond represents one of the most compelling value propositions in European ski real estate.

Co-ownership — purchasing a deeded one-eighth share in a fully managed luxury property — turns that value story into something genuinely transformative. Instead of tying up seven figures in a chalet you use for a few weeks a year, a co-ownership share in Moriond can start from under €200,000, giving you roughly around six and a half weeks of personal use annuallyof annual usage, zero management headaches, and a legal stake in appreciating Alpine real estate. This guide explains exactly why Moriond deserves your attention, how co-ownership works here, and what the numbers look like in 2026.

Location Intelligence

Why Moriond Is the Three Valleys’ Best-Kept Secret

The Three Valleys — Les Trois Vallées — is the world’s largest interconnected ski domain, spanning 600 km of pistes served by 183 lifts capable of moving 260,000 skiers per hour. It stretches across 25,916 acres of skiable terrain with 337 marked runs: 53 green, 136 blue, 113 red, and 35 black. From Courchevel in the east to Val Thorens in the west, every metre is linked by lifts — no buses, no walking between resorts. According to data from Les 3 Vallées, the domain attracts over two million skier visits per season, making it the most visited ski area on the planet.

Moriond sits at 1,650 metres altitude on the eastern flank of this vast network. A single eight-minute gondola ride connects the village to the Courchevel 1850 bowl, and from there the entire Three Valleys opens up. Yet Moriond has its own distinct character: a compact, walkable village centre with restaurants, ski shops, and bars clustered around the snow front. Unlike the sprawling, hotel-dominated layout of 1850, Moriond feels like a genuine Alpine community — quieter slopes in the morning, a lively après scene by four o’clock, and none of the queues that plague the higher stations during peak weeks.

For families, Moriond is especially appealing. The resort boasts an epic toboggan run from the top of the Ariondaz gondola into the village centre, plus Aquamotion — a world-class swimming, spa, and leisure complex just a ten-minute walk from the main lift. Green and blue runs surround the village, making it ideal for children and improving intermediates. And because Moriond sits on the outer edge of the Three Valleys, its local slopes see significantly less through-traffic than Méribel or Courchevel 1850.

Market Data

The Property Price Gap That Smart Buyers Exploit

According to Knight Frank’s Alpine Property Report (2025), prime property in Courchevel 1850 commands between €30,000 and €40,000 per square metre — the highest of any ski resort in France. Moriond, by contrast, sits at €16,000–€17,600 per square metre for equivalent prime stock. That is a discount of roughly 45–55% for access to the identical ski domain, the same season length, and comparable build quality in newer developments.

This pricing gap has historical roots. Courchevel 1850 was repositioned as an ultra-luxury brand in the early 2000s, attracting Gulf State and Russian clientele willing to pay trophy-asset premiums. Moriond, meanwhile, retained its family-friendly, owner-occupier character — which is precisely why its fundamentals are stronger for anyone who actually wants to use their property rather than simply park capital. Over the past decade, Courchevel property values have risen approximately 40% across all villages, according to Cimalpes market data, with Moriond tracking that growth curve while starting from a lower base.

For co-ownership buyers, the arithmetic is even more compelling. A one-eighth share in a four-bedroom Moriond chalet valued at around €1.6 million works out at approximately €200,000 per share — roughly the cost of a studio apartment in 1850. You get a full luxury chalet experience, professional management, and a deeded ownership stake in prime Three Valleys real estate.

How It Works

Co-Ownership in Courchevel: Structure, Usage, and Management

When you purchase a co-ownership share in a Courchevel Moriond property, you become a shareholder in a registered LLC that holds the title to the property. This is genuine equity in the underlying property via the holding company — not a timeshare, not a points club, not a holiday membership. You have a legal stake in a specific, identifiable property that appreciates (or depreciates) with the market, and you can sell your share on the open market at any time.

Each one-eighth owner receives approximately around six and a half weeks of personal use annually. Booking is handled through a dedicated app — you can reserve stays from two days to two years in advance, with no rigid week allocation, no preset rotation or rigid rotation schedules. When you arrive, your stored kitchen tools, sports gear and personal items come back out and the chalet is prepared exactly as you left it. When you leave, professional cleaners reset the property for the next owner. The entire coordination layer is invisible to you.

All running costs — maintenance, insurance, local taxes, cleaning, ski-room upkeep, garden and pool care where applicable — are split proportionately among the eight co-owners. A one-eighth owner pays one-eighth of everything. According to running costs data, this typically reduces the annual cost of Alpine property ownership by 80–85% compared to sole ownership of an equivalent home. And because the management is fully professional, you avoid the single biggest frustration of second-home ownership: the endless admin of finding reliable local contractors, cleaners, and property managers in a foreign country.

“Moriond gives you the same 600 kilometres of skiing as 1850 — at half the price per square metre and with a village atmosphere that actually feels like the Alps, not the lobby of a five-star hotel.”

Investment Lens

Rental Income, Resale, and Long-Term Value

Courchevel Moriond properties can generate meaningful rental income during the weeks co-owners aren’t using them. The Three Valleys’ global reputation ensures strong demand from December through April, with peak-season weeks in Moriond commanding premium nightly rates. Rental is fully managed — owners don’t need to list, communicate with guests, or arrange changeovers. Revenue is distributed proportionate to each owner’s share.

On the resale side, co-ownership shares in established Alpine properties have shown strong liquidity. The management company first offers any outgoing share to existing co-owners in the same property — a built-in demand pool — before listing it externally. Average resale time across the portfolio is around one month, significantly faster than selling a full chalet, which can sit on the market for six to twelve months in slower conditions. Crucially, co-ownership shares are priced at market value, not depreciated like timeshare weeks — because they represent real equity in real property.

Looking at broader market dynamics, Savills’ Alpine Homes Index projects continued price growth in the French Alps of 3–7% annually through 2027, driven by limited new construction, tightening energy regulations that favour modern builds, and sustained international demand. Moriond benefits from all these tailwinds while remaining accessible enough for co-ownership entry at realistic price points.

Comparison

Courchevel Villages Compared: Which One Suits Co-Ownership Buyers?

Courchevel operates as four distinct villages, each with a different character and price band. Understanding the differences helps co-ownership buyers choose the right fit for their lifestyle and budget. Le Praz (1,300m) is a traditional Savoyard village popular with cross-country skiers and summer hikers, but its lower altitude makes it less appealing for peak-season ski convenience. Courchevel Village (1,550m) is compact and affordable but has limited après-ski and restaurant options.

Moriond (1,650m) hits the sweet spot: high enough for reliable doorstep skiing, vibrant enough for families and couples, and connected enough to reach every corner of the Three Valleys in minutes. It offers the best balance between altitude, amenity, community feel, and value per square metre. Courchevel 1850 is the flagship — unmatched for luxury retail, Michelin dining, and celebrity-spotting — but its property prices place sole ownership beyond all but the wealthiest buyers, and its atmosphere can feel more hotel district than Alpine village.

For co-ownership, Moriond’s combination of lower entry cost and higher liveability makes it the standout choice. You spend less capital to secure your share, enjoy a more authentic mountain lifestyle, and retain full access to the exact same 600 km ski domain that 1850 buyers pay double to reach.

Lifestyle

Year-Round Appeal: Summer in the Three Valleys

A common mistake among first-time Alpine buyers is evaluating properties purely on winter merit. The smartest co-ownership investors look at year-round usage — and Moriond delivers. Summer in the Courchevel valley means mountain biking on dedicated downhill trails served by open lifts, road cycling on legendary Tour de France climbs, hiking through wildflower meadows, and paragliding above the Vanoise National Park.

Aquamotion remains open year-round, providing a rainy-day alternative for families. The golf course at Courchevel 1850 is an easy drive, and the summer programme includes outdoor cinema, trail running events, and local food markets. For co-owners with around six and a half weeks of personal use annuallyof annual usage, splitting time between a February ski week, an Easter break, and a July hiking fortnight maximises both enjoyment and property utilisation — a pattern that’s difficult to justify with full ownership but perfectly natural with co-ownership explained.

This dual-season appeal is increasingly reflected in property values. According to JLL’s European Resort Index, Alpine properties with documented year-round amenity access command a 15–20% premium over winter-only equivalents. Moriond’s infrastructure — heated pools, restaurants open twelve months, maintained hiking networks — places it firmly in the year-round category.

Process

How to Buy a Co-Ownership Share in Courchevel Moriond

The buying process for a co-ownership share in Moriond is straightforward and typically completed in around six weeks from initial enquiry to receiving your keys. It begins with a consultation to understand your usage preferences, budget, and lifestyle goals. You’ll be presented with available properties — each with detailed floor plans, interior photography, running cost breakdowns, and a clear explanation of the ownership structure.

Once you’ve selected a property and share, the legal process mirrors a standard French property purchase. The LLC structure is specifically designed and optimised by specialist tax and law firms for holding holiday properties, avoiding common pitfalls around French property taxation and cross-border ownership. A notaire oversees the transaction, and all documentation is provided in English. Completion typically includes a fully furnished, turnkey property — designer interiors, equipped kitchen, ski room, and all linens — so your first visit feels like coming home, not moving in.

After purchase, a dedicated management team handles every aspect of the property: cleaning between stays, seasonal maintenance, insurance, tax obligations, and coordination between co-owners. You never need to contact or coordinate with the other seven shareholders — everything is handled for you. This is the fundamental difference between co-ownership and simply buying a property with friends: professional, silent management that removes every friction point.

2025–26 Season

What’s New in Courchevel for the 2025–2026 Season

The Courchevel valley continues to invest heavily in infrastructure. The headline project for winter 2025/2026 is the complete renewal of the iconic Chenus gondola in Courchevel 1850. After 55 years of service, the lift is being replaced with a state-of-the-art POMA installation featuring 10-seater EVO 2 cabins that double capacity to 2,400 people per hour. For Moriond co-owners, this means faster connections through the 1850 hub and reduced wait times during peak periods.

The Three Valleys also continues to expand its snowmaking network, now boasting over 2,300 snow cannons maintained by 73 grooming machines operated in overnight shifts. This investment in snow security is critical for property values — resorts that can guarantee snow from early December through late April command measurably higher premiums than those dependent on natural snowfall alone. Moriond benefits from north-facing slopes above 1,650m that hold snow exceptionally well, supplemented by comprehensive artificial snowmaking on key return runs.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What makes Courchevel Moriond (1650) different from the more famous Courchevel 1850?

Three structural differences. Altitude — Moriond at 1,650m versus 1850 at 1,850m, both well above the snow-security threshold but with 1850 having a slight edge on early-season conditions. Character — 1850 is the international ultra-luxury brand address with the Maya hotel, designer boutiques, and concentrated Michelin dining; Moriond is more relaxed, more residential, more genuinely Savoyard with a working village character. Pricing — Moriond properties price 25–40% below equivalent 1850 positions for similar quality. Ski access — both are linked to the same Three Valleys network (600km of pistes), with 1850 having slightly more direct access to the highest pistes but Moriond having excellent intermediate-terrain access. For fractional buyers prioritising lifestyle over brand, Moriond consistently delivers better value.

How does access to the Three Valleys compare from Moriond versus other base villages?

Moriond has direct lift access to the entire Three Valleys network via the Ariondaz gondola and the connecting lift system to Courchevel 1850. Skiing across to Méribel and Val Thorens is straightforward via the established lift links. Compared with Méribel-based positions, Moriond is slightly less central in the network but offers easier connections to the upper Courchevel pistes and the snow-secure peaks. La Tania and Le Praz at lower altitudes have less direct access to the high pistes. For fractional ski buyers prioritising the broadest ski day across Three Valleys, Moriond offers excellent access without the price premium of central 1850.

What's the realistic snow-security profile at Moriond and the Three Valleys broadly?

The Three Valleys benefits from the highest-altitude ski terrain in France, with peaks reaching 3,230m at Cime Caron above Val Thorens. Lower-altitude pistes (below 1,800m) face increasing season variability, with December and April requiring artificial snow support; mid-altitude pistes (1,800-2,500m) maintain reliable conditions; high-altitude pistes (above 2,500m) offer essentially guaranteed conditions throughout the season. Moriond at 1,650m base has reliable conditions on lifts up from the village from late December onward, with the highest reliability in January-March. For fractional families prioritising snow security, the Three Valleys offers some of the best in Europe; specific village altitude affects when peak conditions begin and end at the resort itself.

What's the typical fractional ownership profile and operator presence in Courchevel?

Courchevel (1850 specifically) has been an established luxury fractional market since the early 2010s, with multiple operators maintaining inventory of premium chalets. Moriond fractional inventory has grown significantly since 2020 as operators have responded to the value proposition. Median property values in Moriond fractional offerings run €4–8 million whole, with shares typically priced €550,000–1,100,000. Compared with 1850's €15–35 million whole-chalet prices and €1.8–4.5 million share prices, Moriond opens fractional Courchevel ownership to a meaningfully broader buyer pool. Operator presence in Moriond is increasing; secondary market liquidity is solid and growing.

What's the practical reality of Moriond's village amenities for a fractional owner?

Moriond has a substantive village core — restaurants, ski schools, equipment rentals, basic shops, and several quality bars and après-ski venues. The famous Moriond après scene at Le Bel Air and similar venues is genuinely lively without the brand-luxury intensity of 1850's Le Cap Horn or Les Verdons. Restaurant prices are 20–35% below comparable 1850 establishments. The village is walkable end-to-end in 10 minutes, removing the need for car use during a stay. For fractional families, the practical experience is significantly easier than 1850 — children can walk to ski school, parents can dine without long transfers, the daily rhythm is calmer.

How do Courchevel community fees and operating costs compare with other Three Valleys positions?

Courchevel operating costs sit at the higher end of French Alpine fractional ownership — chalet operating costs typically €80,000–140,000 per property annually for the labour-intensive luxury staffing standards. Inside fractional structures, per-share contribution runs €10,000–18,000 per year. The Moriond village vs 1850 comparison shows similar operating costs at the property level (the staffing standards are similar) but slightly lower community-fee burden in Moriond's less brand-intensive village. Compared with Méribel or Val Thorens equivalents, Courchevel fractional ownership generally costs 15–25% more annually. The premium reflects the prestige and the operational standards of the destination.

What's the resale market like for Moriond fractional shares specifically?

Improving as buyer awareness of Moriond's value proposition grows. Median resale times for shares in well-positioned Moriond properties run 8–12 weeks, comparable to the broader Three Valleys fractional market. Pricing has appreciated 6–9% annually since 2020, ahead of broader French Alpine averages because of Moriond's catch-up effect from a lower base. The buyer pool is increasingly international — UK, German, French, Belgian, with growing US interest. For fractional buyers prioritising both value entry and reasonable secondary market liquidity, Moriond is among the strongest current French Alpine bets. Operator presence is sufficient to support active secondary market without the premium pricing of central 1850.

title: From Niche to Normal: How Co-Ownership Became the Smartest Way to Buy a Second Home
subtitle: Co-ownership property has gone mainstream. Discover why the $29 billion fractional market is reshaping how smart buyers own luxury second homes in 2026.
excerpt: Co-ownership property has gone mainstream. Discover why the $29 billion fractional market is reshaping how smart buyers own luxury second homes in 2026.
content:
A decade ago, the idea of sharing ownership of a luxury holiday home raised eyebrows. Today, it raises investment portfolios. The global fractional ownership market reached $9.4 billion in 2024 and is expanding at a compound annual growth rate of 13.7 per cent, on track to surpass $29 billion by 2033 according to Growth Market Reports. What was once dismissed as an alternative experiment has become a pillar of modern property strategy — and the numbers leave little room for debate.

For anyone who has ever watched a beautiful second home sit empty for ten months of the year, or winced at a five-figure maintenance bill for a property visited twice, the appeal is obvious. Co-ownership lets you own a deeded share — typically one-eighth — of a fully managed luxury property. You get around roughly 45 nights spread across the year, a fraction of the running costs, and zero hassle with cleaning, repairs, or rental logistics. It is not a timeshare and it is not a compromise. It is, increasingly, the default choice for informed buyers. Here is why.

The Shift

How a $29 Billion Market Moved From Fringe to Mainstream

The tipping point arrived quietly. Between 2020 and 2024, a combination of remote-work flexibility, rising property prices, and a generational shift in attitudes towards ownership created the perfect conditions for co-ownership to flourish. Knight Frank’s 2025 Wealth Report noted that demand for luxury second homes continues to outstrip supply in virtually every prime market — a dynamic that makes shared ownership models not just attractive but, for many buyers, essential.

Meanwhile, the buyer profile has evolved dramatically. Where fractional ownership once attracted retirees looking for sun, it now draws affluent professionals aged 40 to 55 who want access to premium destinations without the capital lock-up of full ownership. Many are experienced property owners who have done the maths and concluded that paying one hundred per cent of the costs for a home they use ten per cent of the time is, simply, a poor allocation of wealth.

The institutional world has noticed too. Transaction volumes from institutional investors in fractional real estate rose 43 per cent in Q1 2025 alone. When pension funds and family offices start deploying capital into a sector, it has moved well beyond niche.

The Numbers

The True Cost of a Second Home vs Co-Ownership: A Side-by-Side Comparison

The financial case for co-ownership crystallises when you look at the real numbers. According to Zillow research, the hidden costs of homeownership — maintenance, insurance, taxes, utilities — now average $15,979 per year in the United States alone. For second homes in luxury destinations, that figure climbs significantly. Coastal properties in Florida or wildfire-prone areas of California can see insurance premiums of $3,000 to $8,000 annually, two to three times the rate of a primary residence.

With co-ownership properties, every cost is split proportionate to your share. A one-eighth owner pays one-eighth of maintenance, one-eighth of insurance, one-eighth of property taxes, and one-eighth of management fees. On a property where total annual running costs reach €40,000, your share is just €5,000 per year. That is the price of a long weekend in a five-star hotel — except you own actual real estate that appreciates in value.

Then there is the opportunity cost of capital. A luxury villa on the Costa del Sol might cost €2 million outright. A one-eighth share starts from around €100,000 to €250,000. The €1.75 million you did not spend remains in your portfolio, compounding. Over a decade, that difference in capital allocation can be worth more than the property itself.

The Utilisation Problem

Why Full Ownership Is the Most Expensive Way to Use a Holiday Home

Here is the uncomfortable truth that second-home owners rarely discuss at dinner parties: most luxury holiday properties are occupied for fewer than 50 days per year. That means the home sits empty for more than 85 per cent of its life, quietly accumulating costs, requiring maintenance, and tying up capital that could be working elsewhere.

Co-ownership solves this structural inefficiency with elegant precision. Each one-eighth share provides approximately roughly 45 nights spread across the year — closely matching the actual usage pattern of most second-home owners. You are not paying for 365 days when you only need 45. You are not heating an empty house in winter or worrying about a burst pipe while you are thousands of miles away. Everything is fully managed, from cleaning between stays to long-term maintenance scheduling.

When you arrive at your co-ownership property, your whatever you keep at the property is brought out of storage and the home is prepared specifically for you. When you leave, the management team takes over. It is ownership without the operational burden — which, for most people, is the part of second-home ownership they liked least anyway.

“The question is no longer whether co-ownership works — it is whether full ownership of a second home can still be justified for most buyers.”

Legal Structure

Deeded Ownership Through an LLC: Why This Is Not a Timeshare

The single most important distinction between co-ownership and timeshare is the legal structure — and it changes everything. When you purchase a share through Co-Ownership Property, you become a shareholder in a registered LLC that holds the title to a specific, real property. This is a registered shareholding in the entity that owns the property. You appear on the property register. You have a legal stake in a tangible asset.

Timeshares, by contrast, typically sell you the right to use a property during a specific period — you own a slot on a calendar, not a piece of real estate. There are no points systems in co-ownership, no mandatory exchanges, and no resort fees that escalate unpredictably. Your share can be sold on the open market at market price whenever you choose, with an average resale period of around one month — dramatically faster than selling a full property.

The LLC structure is specifically designed and optimised by specialist tax and law firms for holding holiday properties. It provides clear legal protections, transparent governance, and — crucially — the ability to pass your share to family members as part of your estate. For buyers who value transparency in the buying process, this structure offers exactly that.

Flexibility

45 Days, Your Way: How Booking Actually Works

One of the most persistent myths about shared ownership is that you lose control over when you can use your property. The reality is precisely the opposite. Co-owners book their stays through a dedicated app, with a flexible system that lets you reserve time from two days to two years in advance. There are no inherited calendar to wrestle with, and no complicated points-based algorithms.

Want a fortnight in August and a long weekend in December? Done. Prefer to spread your roughly 45 nights spread across the yearacross six or seven shorter trips throughout the year? That works too. The system is designed around how people actually holiday — spontaneously, flexibly, and according to the rhythms of their own lives rather than an arbitrary corporate calendar.

For properties that permit holiday rentals, your share can also generate rental income during the periods you are not using it. Rental management is handled entirely by the management company — owners do not need to list properties, manage guests, or handle cleaning. Income is distributed proportionate to ownership stake. It is genuinely passive income from a genuinely passive investment.

The pandemic reshapes where and how people work, triggering a surge in second-home demand — and revealing the inefficiencies of full ownership.

Institutional transaction volumes surge 43%. The market reaches $9.4 billion. Co-ownership moves firmly into the mainstream.

2026 and Beyond

The New Default for Smart Buyers

With 13.7% annual growth projected through 2033, co-ownership is set to become the standard approach to luxury second-home ownership globally.

Destinations

Where the Smart Money Is Buying: Co-Ownership Hotspots in 2026

The beauty of co-ownership is that it unlocks markets that would otherwise be inaccessible. A one-eighth share in a ski chalet in the French Alps might start from around €80,000 — a price point that opens the door to destinations like Courchevel, Méribel, and La Plagne without the seven-figure commitment of full ownership.

In Spain, the Balearic Islands and Costa del Sol remain the strongest co-ownership markets, with Savills reporting continued price growth across Mallorca and Ibiza driven by constrained supply and international demand. Italy’s lake district — particularly Lake Como — has seen a surge of interest from American and British buyers drawn by lifestyle appeal and favourable exchange rates.

Across the Atlantic, Colorado ski properties in Aspen, Vail, and Breckenridge continue to command premium interest, while emerging markets like Napa Valley and 30A Florida are attracting buyers who want year-round lifestyle properties rather than purely seasonal escapes. Co-Ownership Property curates shares across all of these destinations, with options ranging from under €100,000 to around €2 million for ultra-luxury.

Buyer Psychology

The Mindset Shift: From ‘Owning More’ to ‘Owning Smarter’

Something fundamental has changed in how affluent buyers think about property. The post-2020 generation of second-home purchasers are not motivated by accumulation — they are motivated by optimisation. They have seen friends and family burdened by properties that consume time, money, and mental energy. They want the lifestyle benefits of a luxury holiday home without the lifestyle costs.

This is the same psychological shift that drove the rise of business-class flights over private jet ownership, or boutique hotel memberships over country-club lock-ins. It is about access, quality, and efficiency — not about owning less, but about owning better. Knight Frank data shows that prime property demand continues to outstrip supply globally, which means the co-ownership model is not just a preference — it is increasingly a practical necessity for accessing the best locations.

Case studies from real co-owners consistently highlight the same themes: reduced stress, better financial allocation, and more frequent use of their property than when they owned a full second home. When the hassle disappears, people actually use their holiday homes more — which, after all, was the entire point of buying one.

Looking Ahead

The Future of Second-Home Ownership Is Already Here

The trajectory is clear. With the fractional ownership market growing at 13.7 per cent annually, institutional capital flowing in, and buyer demographics skewing younger and more financially sophisticated, co-ownership is not a trend waiting to arrive — it has arrived. The question is no longer whether shared ownership works, but whether full ownership of a second home can still be justified for most buyers.

Regulatory frameworks are maturing to support the model. Technology platforms are making booking, management, and communication seamless. And the properties themselves — designer villas, alpine chalets, waterfront apartments — are indistinguishable from the finest fully-owned homes. The only difference is the price tag, the hassle, and the intelligence of the investment.

For buyers sitting on the fence, the data offers a straightforward conclusion: co-ownership delivers the same lifestyle at a fraction of the cost, with better utilisation, professional management, and the liquidity to exit whenever you choose. In a market where the average second home sits empty for ten months a year, that is not just smart — it is obvious.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

When did co-ownership actually cross from niche to mainstream — and what triggered it?

The 2020–2022 window was the inflection point. Three things happened simultaneously: well-funded fractional operators (Pacaso in the US, Vivla and Myne in Europe) reached the scale and inventory levels needed to deliver consistent buyer experience; post-COVID work-from-anywhere shifted how people thought about second homes from 'aspirational asset' to 'flexible base'; and short-term rental restrictions in major destinations made informal owner-managed letting harder, exposing the underlying inefficiency of whole-property second-home ownership. By 2024 the market had grown beyond the early-adopter phase. The €29 billion European market size now puts co-ownership at roughly 12% of luxury second-home transactions across continental Europe — meaningful market share by any standard.

What's the practical difference between today's professional co-ownership and the legacy timeshare model?

Three structural differences. Co-ownership delivers a registered shareholding in the entity that owns the property through a holding company; you have a legal stake in the property and can sell, gift, or inherit it. Timeshare typically grants only the right to use a property for specific weeks for a fixed term, with no underlying real estate ownership. Co-ownership shares appreciate (or depreciate) with the underlying property; timeshares typically decline in value with age. Co-ownership has clean exit routes through professional secondary markets; timeshare exit is notoriously difficult, often requiring buyback at a fraction of original purchase price. The legal vehicle, the asset class, and the exit mechanics are all different — the only common element is the shared-usage concept.

Why are mainstream financial advisers starting to recommend co-ownership for clients?

Because it solves a portfolio-allocation problem that whole second homes don't. Mainstream advisers historically discouraged second-home purchases because the assets were illiquid, expensive to maintain, and earned no income. Fractional ownership maintains the lifestyle benefit but addresses several of the financial objections: smaller capital commitment, professional management removing client time burden, defined exit through operator secondary markets, and clear documentation of operating costs for tax planning. Advisers can now position co-ownership as a defined alternative-asset allocation (typically 5–15% of liquid net worth) rather than discouraging luxury property exposure entirely. The change has happened quickly — most major European wealth managers have published guidance on the asset class within the past two years.

How has institutional capital affected the co-ownership market?

Institutional capital — private equity, sovereign wealth, family offices — entered the European fractional market seriously in 2022–2023, primarily as platform investors backing the major operators. The effect has been to professionalise inventory acquisition, standardise legal documentation, and underwrite operator commitments to multi-year service standards. Some institutional capital has gone into single-property fractional structures as the largest-share owner with smaller individual co-owners filling the remaining shares — a model that increases inventory but introduces governance complexity. Watch for institutional consolidation; the market is likely to see acquisitions and platform mergers over the next 24 months, which will affect specific operator selection but not the underlying asset class.

Are there destinations where co-ownership isn't yet mainstream and shouldn't be the default?

Yes — destinations where the fractional operator base is thin enough that buyer choice and resale liquidity suffer. Smaller European markets (Croatia outside Istria and Hvar, parts of Greece outside Mykonos and Santorini, central Spain outside Madrid) have limited fractional inventory and longer median resale times. Frontier destinations (parts of the Maghreb, the western Balkans) lack operator presence entirely. In these markets, whole-property purchase or hotel-style stays remain the practical options. Co-ownership works best where multiple operators have built scale — most of southern Europe's coastal premium destinations, Alpine resort towns, the major capitals, and the established US resort markets.

What does institutional-grade co-ownership look like in 2026 for a serious buyer?

Eight-owner shared structures with single-asset LLCs or SPVs, professionally managed by an operator with a verifiable track record (5+ years, 100+ properties, public secondary-market data). Comprehensive operating agreements covering every realistic scenario — exit, succession, default, dispute resolution — with right of first refusal mechanics that protect the existing co-owner group. Transparent annual cost statements with five-year history. Native mobile booking apps with real-time calendar visibility. Insurance, security, and maintenance handled at scale by the operator. Defined secondary market with documented historical resale data. The bar has been raised significantly since 2020; serious buyers should expect all of this and reject operators who can't demonstrate it.

What's the risk that co-ownership becomes too mainstream and loses its appeal?

Limited. The structural appeal — lower capital commitment, professional management, access to higher-tier properties — doesn't depend on scarcity of the model. As inventory and operator quality continue to improve, the proposition becomes more attractive, not less. The realistic risk is operator-specific: a poorly run operator can fail and damage the reputation of the broader category. The mitigation is buyer due diligence at the operator level — choose operators with mature processes, verifiable track record, and institutional backing. Compared with the maturation paths of REITs in the 1990s or hedge funds in the 2000s, fractional ownership is on a similar trajectory of moving from novelty to recognised asset class without losing its core economic logic.

title: Property Taxes on Co-Ownership Homes: The Country-by-Country Guide Every Buyer Needs in 2026
subtitle: How much property tax do co-owners really pay? Our 2026 country-by-country guide covers the USA, France, Spain, Italy and more — plus the SALT deduction changes that could save you thousands.
excerpt: How much property tax do co-owners really pay? Our 2026 country-by-country guide covers the USA, France, Spain, Italy and more — plus the SALT deduction changes
content:
Property tax is the one cost of second-home ownership that never takes a holiday. It arrives every year, it rises with local valuations, and it catches many buyers off guard — especially those purchasing abroad for the first time. According to Bankrate’s 2025 study, the hidden costs of home ownership (taxes, insurance, maintenance and utilities combined) now average $21,400 per year across the United States alone. In popular European destinations the picture is different but no less complex, with rates, surcharges and local levies varying wildly from one municipality to the next.

For co-ownership property buyers, the arithmetic changes dramatically. Because you hold a fractional share — typically one-eighth — you pay only your proportional slice of every bill, including property tax. That single structural advantage can turn a prohibitively expensive second home into a genuinely affordable lifestyle choice. This guide breaks down exactly what co-owners pay in every major market, how the 2026 SALT deduction overhaul reshapes the US picture, and why fractional ownership is fast becoming the smartest route to luxury holiday-home ownership.

The Basics

How Property Tax Works When You Co-Own a Home

In a typical co-ownership arrangement, a registered LLC (Limited Liability Company) or equivalent legal entity holds the property title. Each co-owner is a shareholder in that entity, owning a deeded real-estate interest — not a timeshare, not a points scheme, but an actual stake in bricks and mortar that appreciates with the market. The LLC receives the annual property-tax bill and splits it proportionally among shareholders.

If the annual property tax on a luxury chalet in Colorado is $24,000, an owner of a one-eighth share pays just $3,000. That share is still tax-deductible under the same rules that apply to any homeowner, and it still counts toward the SALT cap on your federal return. The only difference is scale — and that difference is what makes co-ownership explained such a compelling proposition for buyers who want access to premium destinations without the premium overhead.

Management companies handle the entire administrative chain: they receive the bill, divide it, invoice each co-owner, and file all necessary documentation. As a co-owner you never need to chase a local tax office or navigate a foreign-language assessment notice. It is one of the many reasons the running costs of a fractional ownership property tend to surprise people — they are far lower and far simpler than expected.

$40,400

New US SALT deduction cap for 2026 — four times the previous $10,000 limit, covering property taxes on all homes you own.

1/8th

The typical co-ownership share, meaning you pay just one-eighth of all property taxes, insurance, maintenance and management fees.

€312/yr

Approximate annual property tax for a 1/8 co-owner of a luxury Spanish villa — less than most monthly streaming subscriptions.

17 days

Average annual usage of a second home by US owners (NAR data), yet sole owners pay 365 days of property tax.

US Tax Landscape

The 2026 SALT Overhaul: What It Means for Co-Owners in America

The tax landscape for American property owners shifted significantly in 2026. Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the combined State and Local Tax (SALT) deduction cap rose from $10,000 to $40,400 for the 2026 tax year. That fourfold increase means second-home owners who itemise deductions can now recover far more of their property-tax outlay than at any point since 2017. For married couples filing jointly, the cap covers property taxes on every home you own, plus either state income tax or state sales tax.

There is, however, a phase-out for higher earners. The full deduction begins to reduce at a modified adjusted gross income of $505,000 and reverts to the old $10,000 cap at $600,000 and above. For co-owners, this is where fractional maths works in your favour again: because your share of property tax is a fraction of the whole-property bill, even owners in high-tax states like New Jersey (effective rate 2.23%) or Illinois (2.07%) are far less likely to bump against the cap.

Explore Colorado properties, California properties and Florida properties to see how co-ownership keeps tax exposure manageable across America’s most sought-after markets.

European Markets

Property Taxes Across Europe: A Market-by-Market Breakdown

Europe offers some of the world’s most attractive property-tax regimes — and some of the most confusing. France levies two separate charges: the taxe foncière (paid by the owner, typically 0.5 %–1.5 % of cadastral value) and, for non-primary residences, an additional taxe d’habitation surcharge that can vary by commune. In a co-ownership structure, both charges are split among shareholders, and the management entity handles all filings with the local centre des impôts.

Spain keeps things simpler with the IBI (Impuesto sobre Bienes Inmuebles), a municipal tax ranging from 0.3 % to 0.7 % of cadastral value. On a luxury villa in Marbella with an assessed value of €500,000, the annual IBI might be €2,500 — meaning each one-eighth co-owner pays roughly €312 per year. That is less than many people spend on a single weekend dinner out. Browse Costa del Sol properties and Balearic Islands properties to see what is available today.

Italy charges the IMU (Imposta Municipale Unica) at a base rate of 0.86 %, which municipalities can adjust between 0 % and 1.06 %. Lake Como and the Italian Riviera remain remarkably affordable from a tax standpoint, especially when costs are divided among co-owners. Meanwhile, Portugal applies the IMI at just 0.3 %–0.8 %, and Croatia currently has no annual property tax at all for most property types — a fact that makes the Adriatic coast one of Europe’s last true bargains for fractional buyers.

“A sole owner pays twelve months of property tax for seventeen days of use. A co-owner pays one-eighth of the tax for forty-five days of enjoyment. The maths is not even close.”

The Numbers

Full Ownership vs Co-Ownership: A Side-by-Side Tax Comparison

The most powerful argument for co-ownership vs full ownership is not philosophical — it is mathematical. Consider a luxury property worth €1 million in the south of France. A sole owner faces an annual taxe foncière of around €8,000, plus a taxe d’habitation surcharge of approximately €3,500, bringing the total property-tax bill to roughly €11,500 per year. Add insurance (€2,000), maintenance (€5,000–€10,000), and management (€4,000–€6,000), and the hidden annual overhead easily exceeds €25,000.

A one-eighth co-owner of the same property pays approximately €1,437 in property tax and around €3,125 in total annual running costs. The property is professionally managed, maintained to a luxury standard, and available for around around six and a half weeks of personal use annually — which, for most second-home owners, is more time than they would actually spend there anyway. Research from the National Association of Realtors shows that the average US second-home owner uses their property for just 17 days per year, meaning sole owners often pay full-year taxes for barely two-and-a-half weeks of enjoyment.

For buyers considering the switch, benefits of fractional ownership for second homes explains why the financial case has never been stronger.
