Smart Structuring

How the LLC Structure Optimises Your Tax Position

Every co-ownership property is held inside a purpose-built legal entity — typically an LLC in the US or an SCI (Société Civile Immobilière) in France. These structures are not tax-avoidance vehicles; they are tax-optimisation vehicles designed by specialist property-law firms to ensure each co-owner receives the most favourable treatment available under local legislation.

In the United States, the LLC is treated as a pass-through entity for federal tax purposes. Each co-owner reports their share of income and deductions on their individual return, which means you retain full access to mortgage-interest deductions (up to $750,000 of qualifying acquisition debt across all your homes) and property-tax deductions within the SALT cap. There are no additional corporate filings, no double taxation, and no partnership formalities to manage.

In France, the SCI achieves a similar result by allowing each co-owner to deduct their share of property taxes, mortgage interest, and maintenance costs against any rental income generated by the property. The management company files the SCI’s annual return and distributes individual tax statements to each shareholder. The entire process is hands-off — exactly the kind of hassle-free ownership that draws buyers to co-ownership buying process in the first place.

2017

TCJA Caps SALT at $10,000

The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act introduced a $10,000 cap on state and local tax deductions, hitting second-home owners in high-tax states hard.

2018–2024

Foreign Property Tax Deduction Eliminated

US taxpayers lost the ability to deduct property taxes paid on homes outside the United States, affecting European co-owners filing US returns.

2025

One Big Beautiful Bill Act Signed

The SALT cap quadrupled to $40,000 (indexed for inflation), restoring meaningful deductions for second-home owners who itemise.

2026

New Cap Takes Effect at $40,400

Inflation indexing pushes the cap to $40,400. Phase-out begins at $505,000 MAGI. Co-owners benefit from lower per-share tax exposure.

2029–2030

Sunset Provision Looms

The elevated cap is set to revert to $10,000 in 2030 unless Congress extends or replaces the legislation — creating urgency for buyers to act now.

Global Comparison

Where Do Co-Owners Get the Best Tax Deal in 2026?

Not all destinations are created equal when it comes to property tax. Savvy co-ownership buyers look beyond purchase price and lifestyle appeal to consider the full fiscal picture. Croatia, with no annual property tax on most residential properties, and Portugal, with IMI rates as low as 0.3 %, rank among Europe’s most tax-friendly markets for fractional buyers.

In the United States, Hawaii (0.27 % effective rate) and Colorado (0.51 %) offer strikingly low property-tax burdens compared to northeastern states. A one-eighth co-owner of a $2 million ski chalet in Vail might pay just $1,275 per year in property tax — a remarkable figure for a property of that calibre. Compare that to the same share of a $2 million home in New Jersey, where the bill would be closer to $5,575.

Across all markets, the pattern holds: fractional ownership turns what would be a major annual expense into a manageable line item. Explore all our homes to compare destinations side by side.

Common Pitfalls

Five Tax Mistakes Co-Ownership Buyers Should Avoid

Even with professional management, co-owners benefit from understanding the tax terrain. Mistake one: assuming foreign property taxes are deductible in the US. Since 2018, the TCJA has prohibited deductions for foreign real-property taxes, and the 2026 legislation continued that prohibition. If you co-own in Europe and file US taxes, your IBI or taxe foncière does not reduce your federal bill — though it may still be deductible in your state of residence.

Mistake two: ignoring the SALT phase-out. The new $40,400 cap is generous, but if your modified AGI exceeds $505,000 it begins to shrink. High-earning co-owners should model the phase-out with their accountant before assuming the full deduction. Mistake three: forgetting non-resident surcharges. Several French and Spanish municipalities impose additional levies on properties classified as secondary residences. These are built into your co-ownership cost structure, but it pays to know they exist.

Mistake four: conflating property tax with capital gains tax. They are entirely separate obligations — for a deep dive on the latter, see our guide to capital gains tax. Mistake five: not claiming rental-income offsets. If your co-owned property generates rental income through managed holiday lets, your share of property tax can often be offset against that income, reducing your net tax liability further. Speak with a tax adviser to ensure you are capturing every available benefit.

Future Outlook

What Is Changing in 2027 and Beyond?

Tax policy never stands still, and co-owners should keep one eye on the horizon. In the US, the SALT cap is set to rise by 1 % annually through 2029, reaching approximately $42,000 by 2029 before reverting to $10,000 in 2030 unless Congress intervenes. That sunset provision makes the next few years a particularly attractive window for American buyers to lock in co-ownership positions while deductions remain generous.

In Europe, Spain is reviewing its cadastral valuations in several regions, which could push IBI bills higher for luxury properties. France continues to phase out the taxe d’habitation for primary residences, but secondary-residence surcharges are rising in Paris and other major cities. Italy has signalled potential IMU adjustments for high-value properties in tourist-heavy municipalities around Lake Como and the Amalfi Coast.

The constant across all these markets is that co-ownership insulates buyers from the worst of any increase. A 20 % rise in property tax is painful when you own 100 % of a home; it is barely noticeable when you own one-eighth. That built-in resilience is why best fractional ownership properties continue to attract buyers who value both lifestyle and financial prudence.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What's the high-level property tax burden comparison across the main European fractional destinations?

Annual property taxes on a €2.5 million luxury property as a rough comparison: Spain (IBI plus IBI surcharges) €4,000–9,000; France (taxe foncière plus taxe d'habitation second-home surcharges) €4,500–11,000; Italy (IMU on second homes plus TARI) €6,000–14,000; Portugal (IMI plus AIMI on prime properties) €5,000–12,000; UK (council tax band H plus second-home premium) €4,500–8,500. Each jurisdiction has additional considerations — wealth tax in Spain (variable), IFI in France (above thresholds), no national property tax in Switzerland (canton-by-canton). Inside fractional structures, taxes are paid by the holding entity and divided per share, so per-share contributions are manageable; absolute totals matter more for operator-level cost statements than for buyer decisions.

How do transaction taxes (transfer tax) compare on fractional share acquisition across countries?

Spain (ITP for resale property): 6–11% depending on autonomous community, applied to share value when share-of-SL acquisition is structured. France (droits d'enregistrement on share transfers in SCI): around 5%, generally lower than direct property transfer. Italy (imposta di registro on share transactions): variable by structure, typically 3–9% depending on registration. Portugal (IMT plus stamp duty): around 6–8% on share value. The trend across jurisdictions is that share-of-company acquisitions for fractional ownership benefit from lower tax structures than direct property transfers; this is a meaningful structural cost saving versus whole-property purchase. Confirm specific structure with operator's local counsel before assuming particular treatment.

What's the wealth tax exposure for non-resident fractional owners across destinations?

Variable. Spain reactivated wealth tax in some autonomous communities (Catalonia, Asturias) with thresholds typically around €700,000 for non-residents; Madrid and Andalusia apply 100% bonification (effectively zero). France applies IFI on French real estate above €1.3 million. Italy has no national wealth tax. Portugal has no national wealth tax. For typical fractional shares (€200,000–500,000 each), most non-resident buyers stay below thresholds in most jurisdictions. Owners with multiple shares or substantial other foreign property may aggregate above thresholds. Specific advice from a local accountant familiar with non-resident wealth tax treatment is essential for owners with substantial holdings.

How do inheritance and gift tax rates compare across countries for fractional owners?

Substantial variation. Spain varies by autonomous community — Madrid and Andalusia have near-zero rates to direct heirs, Catalonia has steeper rates, regional differences materially affect planning. France applies graduated rates from 5% to 45% to direct heirs above thresholds. Italy is among the most favourable for direct heirs — €1 million exemption per heir, then 4% rate. Portugal has no inheritance tax for direct heirs. UK applies 40% above the nil-rate band on UK-domiciled estates worldwide. For fractional buyers thinking about multi-generational ownership, the destination's inheritance tax regime is one of the most important long-run considerations; Italy and Portugal currently offer the most favourable treatment for direct heirs.

What's the typical cost of professional tax representation across fractional jurisdictions?

Annual fiscal representation and filings for a non-resident fractional owner typically run €300–800 per year per share in Spain, €400–900 in France, €350–700 in Italy, €300–600 in Portugal. Cross-border buyers with multiple shares in different jurisdictions or with complex personal circumstances pay more. The operator's gestor or accountant typically handles the holding entity's filings; individual owners arrange their own personal-side representation. Specialist advisers familiar with both the destination jurisdiction and the buyer's home jurisdiction are worth the additional cost — the tax savings from clean structuring usually exceed the adviser fees.

How does VAT treatment work for fractional new-build properties?

VAT applies to new-build property transactions — Spain 10% (4% in some autonomous communities for primary residences); France 20% on new-build; Italy 10% (or 22% for luxury properties under €120,000 threshold); Portugal 23% with reduced rates for some categories. For resale property in fractional structures, VAT generally doesn't apply (transfer tax does instead). For new-build fractional inventory, the VAT is paid by the holding entity at acquisition and effectively built into the share price. Buyers don't pay VAT separately on share acquisition for resale property; for new-build shares, the VAT-inclusive cost is what's quoted in operator share offerings.

What's the practical advice for fractional buyers managing tax across borders?

Three principles. First, get specialist cross-border advice before any acquisition — the tax structuring choices made at purchase affect 7–10 years of subsequent treatment and are expensive to change later. Second, maintain clean documentation throughout ownership — purchase contracts, annual cost statements, distribution receipts, foreign tax credit documentation — all needed for both ongoing filings and eventual disposal. Third, treat the tax position as part of the asset analysis rather than as administrative afterthought — the wrong jurisdiction with the wrong structure can erode capital appreciation faster than market conditions might suggest. Most fractional operators have preferred adviser relationships in each jurisdiction; using them often delivers better outcomes than independent generalist advisers.

The Advantages of Buying a Home Through a fractional Ownership Platform

Purchasing a vacation home through a fractional ownership platform  (fractional ownership) comes with myriad upsides: getting more home for your money, combining purchase power to make a larger down payment, avoiding PMI, spending more time with friends or family, and the potential to build equity or even earn rental income from the unused time at the property.

 

 

However, as outlined above, there is also a long list of financial and legal hurdles to overcome before making your quintessential holiday home a reality.

A co-ownership platform like Co-Ownership Property can handle the hassle of not only purchasing a home through a joint limited company but can also help you manage all the complexities of property co-ownership, from taxes to paying bills to managing rentals when you are not staying in your home. The chosen company manages all elements of the home so that you can focus on your holiday, and that even includes paying the taxes.

Different companies allow foreigners to seamlessly co-own in Europe and the United States. Also, if you decide to sell your part in the co-owned property at some point, we will offer to manage it for you and find you the best buyer.

Liquidity Without Complexity

One of the most compelling aspects of fractional ownership lies in its resale flexibility – a feature that distinguishes sophisticated fractional arrangements from traditional property investment. Companies like co-ownership-property.com have developed streamlined resale mechanisms that eliminate the complexity typically associated with property transactions.

Rather than navigating the labyrinthine process of selling an entire property – with its attendant legal complications, marketing challenges, and timing uncertainties – fractional owners can exit their investment through established platforms that understand the unique dynamics of shared ownership. These specialist companies maintain databases of qualified buyers specifically seeking fractional opportunities, often enabling faster transactions at more predictable valuations than traditional property sales. The result is genuine liquidity in what has historically been an illiquid asset class, allowing owners to adjust their property portfolios with the sort of flexibility previously reserved for financial securities.

 Specialist fractional platforms maintain databases of qualified buyers actively seeking one-eighth or one-quarter shares, which can shorten transaction timelines and improve pricing transparency. Rather than marketing an entire €2 million property to a narrow buyer pool, you are offering a €200,000 share to a much broader audience.

This structured resale mechanism introduces a level of liquidity rarely associated with real estate. Owners can rebalance their capital, release funds, or adjust lifestyle priorities without the friction of selling a whole asset. For those who value both personal usage and financial flexibility, fractional ownership combines lifestyle access with a degree of capital mobility that traditional full ownership rarely provides.
